knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence under the upper-set extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates minimizers of a set-valued upper extension to minimal solutions of its point-valued generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the cone-ordered set-optimization setting hold, assume \(C\) is pointed, let \(f:S\to Y\), and define \(F(x):=\{y\in Y\mid f(x)\le_C y\}\) for every \(x\in S\). Then: (i) if \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a minimizer for \(F\), then \(\bar y=f(\bar x)\) and \(\bar x\) is a minimal solution for \(f\); (ii) if \(\bar x\) is a minimal solution for \(f\), then \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) is a minimizer for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointed ordering cone, replacing each vector value by its upper set preserves minimal solutions: every set-optimization minimizer lies at the generating value, and every minimal solution of the original vector problem yields such a minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \forall x\in S,\quad F(x)=\{y\in Y\mid f(x)\le_C y\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ minimizes }F\Rightarrow[\bar y=f(\bar x)\land\bar x\text{ is minimal for }f],\quad \bar x\text{ minimal for }f\Rightarrow(\bar x,f(\bar x))\text{ minimizes }F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Regularity and Uniform-Growth Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A forward stability theorem for parameterized critical pairs and a converse under canonical uniform growth and surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (f(x,u),G(x,u)) be a C^2-smooth parameterization. If (x_0,\lambda_0) is a strongly regular solution of the associated generalized equation, x_0 is locally optimal for the reference problem, and every choice \lambda(u)\in\Lambda(x,u) satisfies \lambda(u)\to\lambda_0 whenever (x,u)\to(x_0,u_0), then there exist neighborhoods \mathcal V_X of x_0 and \mathcal V_U of u_0 such that each P_u with u\in\mathcal V_U has a unique critical pair (\bar x(u),\bar\lambda(u))\in\mathcal V_X\times Y^*. This critical-pair map is Lipschitz continuous, each \bar x(u) is locally optimal, and uniform second-order growth holds at x_0. Conversely, if (x_0,\lambda_0) is a critical point, uniform second-order growth holds at x_0 for the canonical parameterization, and DG(x_0) is onto, then (x_0,\lambda_0) is a strongly regular solution of the generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity, reference local optimality, and convergence of nearby multipliers give a unique Lipschitz critical-pair map, persistence of local optimality, and uniform quadratic growth. Conversely, canonical uniform quadratic growth together with surjectivity of the constraint derivative implies strong regularity.
assumptions_latex: \text{Forward direction: }(f(x,u),G(x,u))\text{ is }C^2\text{-smooth},\ (x_0,\lambda_0)\text{ is strongly regular},\ x_0\text{ is locally optimal},\text{ and }[(x,u)\to(x_0,u_0),\ \lambda(u)\in\Lambda(x,u)]\Rightarrow\lambda(u)\to\lambda_0
\text{Converse direction: }(x_0,\lambda_0)\text{ is critical, canonical uniform second-order growth holds at }x_0,\text{ and }DG(x_0)\text{ is onto}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Forward: locally there is a unique Lipschitz critical-pair map }(\bar x(u),\bar\lambda(u)),\ \bar x(u)\text{ is locally optimal, and uniform second-order growth holds};\quad \text{Converse: canonical uniform growth and surjective }DG(x_0)\Rightarrow\text{strong regularity}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak critical sequence at a biconjugate minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted assumption F^{**}=F is retained literally; derivative convergence is in V^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V be a Banach space and let F:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and Gâteaux differentiable on \operatorname{dom}F. Assume F^{**}=F and that \bar v minimizes F^{**} over V. Then there exists (v_n)\subset\operatorname{dom}F such that v_n\rightharpoonup\bar v, F(v_n)\to\inf_VF=F^{**}(\bar v), and F'(v_n)\to0 in V^*, where 0\in\partial F^{**}(\bar v).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the extracted biconjugacy assumption, a minimizer of the biconjugate admits a weakly convergent minimizing sequence whose derivatives tend to zero; zero is a subgradient of the biconjugate at the minimizer.
assumptions_latex: F:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is lower semicontinuous and Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{dom}F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(v_n)\subset\operatorname{dom}F:\quad v_n\rightharpoonup\bar v,\quad F(v_n)\to\inf_VF=F^{**}(\bar v),\quad F'(v_n)\to0,\quad 0\in\partial F^{**}(\bar v).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is that the dual ball of radius k is contained in the closure of the derivative range.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier-Free Generalized-Equation Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of a convex lower-level optimal response by a normal-cone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\in X\), let \(M(x)=\{y:g(x,y)\le 0\}\). If \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) and \(M(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are convex, then \(y\in\Psi(x)\) if and only if \(0\in\partial_y f(x,y)+N_{M(x)}(y)\), where \(N_A(z)=\{d:d^\top(w-z)\le 0\ \forall w\in A\}\) and \(N_A(z)=\varnothing\) for \(z\notin A\). Consequently, replacing \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Psi\) by this inclusion gives a fully equivalent formulation of the optimistic bilevel graph problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the lower objective and lower feasible set are convex in the lower variable, lower-level optimality is equivalent to a zero-subgradient-plus-normal-cone inclusion. Substituting this generalized equation gives a fully equivalent bilevel formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in\Psi(x)\iff 0\in\partial_y f(x,y)+N_{M(x)}(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximately stationary minimizing sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability and the Banach-space setting are inherited from the immediately preceding setup; derivative convergence is in the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V be a Banach space and let F:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous, Gâteaux differentiable on \operatorname{dom}F, and satisfy \inf_{v\in V}F(v)>-\infty. Then there exists (v_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subset\operatorname{dom}F such that F(v_n)\to\inf_{v\in V}F(v) and \|F'(v_n)\|_{V^*}\to0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous differentiable functional with finite infimum has a minimizing sequence whose derivatives converge to zero in dual norm.
assumptions_latex: F:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is lower semicontinuous and Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{dom}F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(v_n)\subset\operatorname{dom}F:\quad F(v_n)\to\inf_{v\in V}F(v),\qquad \|F'(v_n)\|_{V^*}\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity and convex sufficiency for unconstrained minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the stated failure boundary: the assumptions do not imply existence of a minimizer or stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V be a Banach space and let F:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and Gâteaux differentiable at every point of \operatorname{dom}F. If \bar v minimizes F over V, then F'(\bar v)=0. If, additionally, F is convex, every v\in\operatorname{dom}F satisfying F'(v)=0 minimizes F over V. These hypotheses alone do not ensure existence of a minimizer or of a solution to F'(v)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every unconstrained minimizer of the stated differentiable functional is stationary. Under convexity, stationarity is also sufficient for global minimality. Neither a minimizer nor a stationary point is guaranteed to exist.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable at every point of }\operatorname{dom}F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar v\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in V}F(u)\Rightarrow F'(\bar v)=0;\qquad F\text{ convex and }F'(v)=0\Rightarrow v\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in V}F(u).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a single-valued mapping \(f:X\to Y\) and a set-valued mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), an unparameterized generalized equation is the problem of finding \(x\in X\) such that \[0\in f(x)+F(x).\] Equivalently, \(-f(x)\in F(x)\). Its solution set is \[\operatorname{Sol}(f,F):=\{x\in X\mid 0\in f(x)+F(x)\}.\] The mapping data are fixed; no external parameter indexes either \(f\) or \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unparameterized generalized equation seeks a point where the negative single-valued term belongs to the fixed set-valued term.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Cone Generalized Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unparameterized normal-cone form of a generalized equation and identifies its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^k be continuous and let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k be nonempty, closed, and convex. The inclusion 0\in C(z)+N_Q(z) is a generalized equation, where N_Q(z) denotes the normal cone to Q at z; Q is called the feasible set of the generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a continuous mapping C from R^k to R^k and a nonempty closed convex set Q, the inclusion 0 in C(z) plus the normal cone to Q at z is a generalized equation. The set Q is called its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in C(z)+N_Q(z)\text{ is a generalized equation with feasible set }Q.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parametric generalized equation associated with \(f:P\times X\to Y\) and \(F:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\) assigns to each parameter \(p\in P\) the problem \[0\in f(p,x)+F(p,x),\qquad x\in X.\] The corresponding solution mapping is \[S(p):=\{x\in X\mid 0\in f(p,x)+F(p,x)\}.\] Parameter sensitivity concerns the local behavior of this set-valued mapping as \(p\) varies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional certificate for generalized-Jacobian membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides sufficient strict-sign and linear-system conditions for an active-set matrix to belong to the solution map's generalized Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 6.12 and fix \(i\in\mathbb K(x_0,y_0)\). If there exist \(h\in\mathbb R^n\), \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), \(w\in\mathbb R^\ell\), and \(u_{I^+\cup M_i}\in\mathbb R^{a^++a_i^0}\) such that \[D_{I^+\cup M_i}(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\begin{bmatrix}v\\w\\u_{I^+\cup M_i}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\mathcal J_x\mathcal L(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\\-\mathcal J_xH(x_0,y_0)\\\mathcal J_xG_{I^+\cup M_i}(x_0,y_0)\end{bmatrix}h,\] \[u_{M_i}>0,\qquad \mathcal J_xG_{I^0\setminus M_i}(x_0,y_0)h+\mathcal J_yG_{I^0\setminus M_i}(x_0,y_0)v<0,\] then \(R_i(x_0,y_0)\in\partial\sigma(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an admissible index selection, solvability of the specified directional linearized system together with strict positivity on selected weakly active indices and strict decrease on the remaining indices certifies that the associated matrix belongs to the solution map's generalized Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \exists(h,v,w,u_{I^+\cup M_i})\text{ satisfying the displayed linear system and strict inequalities.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_i(x_0,y_0)\in\partial\sigma(x_0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Regularity Sensitivity of a Parametric Generalized Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local existence, uniqueness, Lipschitz stability, and first-order expansion of the solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let z_0 be a strongly regular solution of the abstract generalized equation at u_0, and let \zeta(\delta) denote the solution of the corresponding linearized generalized equation. Then there exist neighborhoods \mathcal V_Z of z_0 and \mathcal V_U of u_0 such that, for every u\in\mathcal V_U, the perturbed generalized equation has exactly one solution z(u)\in\mathcal V_Z. Moreover, for some \kappa>0 and all u,u'\in\mathcal V_U, \|z(u')-z(u)\|\leq\kappa\|u'-u\|, and z(u)=\zeta\!\left(-D_u\Phi(z_0,u_0)(u-u_0)\right)+o(\|u-u_0\|).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity yields a locally unique Lipschitz solution map for the perturbed generalized equation, with a first-order expansion determined by the linearized generalized equation.
assumptions_latex: z_0\text{ is a strongly regular solution of the reference generalized equation at }u_0
\zeta(\delta)\text{ solves the corresponding linearized generalized equation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal V_Z,\mathcal V_U,\kappa>0:\ \forall u\in\mathcal V_U\ \exists!z(u)\in\mathcal V_Z,\quad \|z(u')-z(u)\|\leq\kappa\|u'-u\|,\quad z(u)=\zeta(-D_u\Phi(z_0,u_0)(u-u_0))+o(\|u-u_0\|).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factorization of Uncoupled Block Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution-set factorization for the separable special case of a finite block generalized-equation system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), and for each \(i\), let \(f_i:X_i\to Y_i\) and \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\). For the block system \[0\in f_i(x_i)+F_i(x_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,\] define \(S_i:=\{x_i\in X_i:0\in f_i(x_i)+F_i(x_i)\}\). Then its solution set is \[S=\prod_{i=1}^m S_i.\] Thus componentwise dependence is sufficient for Cartesian factorization; without that separability, such a factorization does not follow from block structure alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each block depends only on its own variable, the full solution set is the Cartesian product of the component solution sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:0\in f_i(x_i)+F_i(x_i)\ \forall i\}=\prod_{i=1}^m\{x_i:0\in f_i(x_i)+F_i(x_i)\}.

notation.meaning: solution set of the full block system

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization of Uncoupled Block Systems

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\prod_{j=1}^m X_j\to Y_i\) and \(F_i:\prod_{j=1}^m X_j\rightrightarrows Y_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block system is equivalent to \(0\in f(x)+F(x)\) on the product spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite block systems encoded as one generalized equation on product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X:=\prod_{i=1}^m X_i\), consider the coupled system \[0\in f_i(x)+F_i(x),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Define \(f:X\to Y:=\prod_{i=1}^m Y_i\) by \(f(x):=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\) and define \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) by \(F(x):=\prod_{i=1}^m F_i(x)\). Then the entire coupled system is equivalent to the product-space generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+F(x).\] Coupling occurs because individual blocks may depend on the full vector \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite coupled system is one generalized equation on product spaces, with each block allowed to depend on all variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Generalized-Equation Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-space representation is mathematically plausible and the content kind fits, but no source is cited. A source-supported revision should also state that m is a positive integer.

children.title: Variational-Inclusion Forms
children.top_down_role: Generalized equations organized by the variational structure of their set-valued component.

children.title: Normal-Cone Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Constraint and equilibrium systems represented by normal-cone mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\) means \(x\in C\) and \(\langle f(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\) for all \(y\in C\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex Hilbert-space normal cone, avoiding ambiguity among nonconvex normal constructions.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define the convex normal cone by \[N_C(x):=\{v\in X\mid \langle v,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }y\in C\},\] and set \(N_C(x):=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin C\). The normal-cone generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\] is therefore equivalent to the variational inequality \[x\in C,\qquad \langle f(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex normal-cone inclusion is exactly a variational inequality over the underlying closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Generalized Equations

children.title: Subdifferential Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Optimization and equilibrium systems represented by subdifferential mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
\(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(f:X\to X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in f(x)+\partial\varphi(x)\) is equivalent to \(\varphi(y)\ge\varphi(x)-\langle f(x),y-x\rangle\) for all \(y\in X\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of phi at x
duality pairing between the dual and primal spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex subdifferential version in a Banach space.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex subdifferential of \(\varphi\) at \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) is \[\partial\varphi(x):=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \varphi(y)\ge\varphi(x)+\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in X\}.\] Hence the subdifferential generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+\partial\varphi(x)\] holds exactly when \(-f(x)\in\partial\varphi(x)\), equivalently when \[\varphi(y)\ge\varphi(x)-\langle f(x),y-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subdifferential inclusion is equivalent to the global subgradient inequality with subgradient equal to the negative residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Generalized Equations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel–Young Certificate for a Subdifferential Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual equality certificate for membership in a convex subdifferential, with the canonical Banach-space embedding made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_X:X\to X^{**}\) be the canonical embedding and let \(\varphi^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be the Fenchel conjugate. Then \[x^*\in\partial\varphi(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi(x)+\varphi^*(x^*)=\langle x^*,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J_Xx\in\partial\varphi^*(x^*).\] Hence \(0\in f(x)+\partial\varphi(x)\) is equivalent to \[\varphi(x)+\varphi^*(-f(x))=-\langle f(x),x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subdifferential inclusion is certified by equality in Fenchel–Young, equivalently by reciprocal subgradient membership in the bidual.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
\(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-f(x)\in\partial\varphi(x)\iff\varphi(x)+\varphi^*(-f(x))=-\langle f(x),x\rangle\).

notation.meaning: canonical embedding of X into its bidual

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Young Certificate for a Subdifferential Inclusion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Fermat Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-residual specialization of a convex subdifferential generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \[0\in\partial\varphi(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}\varphi.\] Thus the zero set of \(\partial\varphi\) is exactly \(\operatorname{argmin}\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function's subdifferential are exactly its global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial\varphi(\bar x)\iff\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}\varphi\).

notation.meaning: set of global minimizers of phi

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Fermat Principle

children.title: Monotone-Operator Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Inclusions governed by monotone or maximal-monotone operators.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone, and it is maximal monotone when explicitly stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized equation is \(0\in A(x)\); maximal monotonicity means no proper monotone graph extension exists.

notation.meaning: graph of the set-valued operator A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space inclusion governed by a monotone or maximal-monotone operator.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is monotone when \[\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for all }(x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gph}A.\] It is maximal monotone when its graph is not properly contained in the graph of another monotone operator. A monotone-operator generalized equation seeks \[x\in H\quad\text{such that}\quad 0\in A(x),\] so its solution set is \(\operatorname{zer}A:=\{x\in H\mid 0\in A(x)\}\). A sum inclusion \(0\in B(x)+C(x)\) has this form with \(A:=B+C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone-operator generalized equation seeks a zero of an operator whose graph satisfies the monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Operator Generalized Equations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Monotonicity Uniqueness and Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative certificate for zeros of a strongly monotone inclusion; existence is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone: \[\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq\mu\lVert x-y\rVert^2\quad((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gph}A)\] for some \(\mu>0\). Then \(A\) has at most one zero \(\bar x\). If that zero exists, every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gph}A\) satisfies \[\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\leq\mu^{-1}\lVert u\rVert,\] hence \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\leq\mu^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(0,A(x))\) whenever \(A(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes a zero unique and converts the inclusion residual into a distance-to-solution bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is at most one zero; conditional on existence, \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\leq\mu^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(0,A(x))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Uniqueness and Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity Alone Does Not Ensure a Convex Zero Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing why maximality is needed for the zero-set geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R\), define \(A(0)=A(1)=\{0\}\) and \(A(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. Then \(\operatorname{gph}A=\{(0,0),(1,0)\}\) is monotone, whereas \(\operatorname{zer}A=\{0,1\}\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone but nonmaximal two-point graph can have a nonconvex zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is monotone while \(\operatorname{zer}A=\{0,1\}\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Alone Does Not Ensure a Convex Zero Set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry of the Zero Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-set geometry of maximal-monotone Hilbert-space inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, then \(\operatorname{zer}A=A^{-1}(0)\) is a closed convex subset of \(H\), possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero set of a maximal monotone operator is closed and convex, but may be empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}A\) is closed and convex, but may be empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry of the Zero Set

children.title: Nonmonotone Variational Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Variational inclusions outside monotone-operator regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to H\) and \(F:H\rightrightarrows H\) are arbitrary unless additional structure is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusion \(0\in f(x)+F(x)\) is nonmonotone whenever the sum mapping fails the monotonicity inequality on its graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by failure of monotonicity of the aggregate inclusion mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonmonotone variational inclusion is a generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+F(x)\] for which the aggregate mapping \(T:=f+F\) is not monotone on the region under consideration. Explicitly, monotonicity fails if there exist \((x,u),(y,v)\in\operatorname{gph}T\) such that \[\langle u-v,x-y\rangle<0.\] The designation imposes no replacement regularity by itself: existence, stability, and algorithms require separately stated assumptions such as hypomonotonicity, metric regularity, compactness, or degree conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inclusion is nonmonotone when its aggregate set-valued mapping violates the monotonicity inequality; further analysis requires separate structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Variational Inclusions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence supports the proposed classification. Moreover, the phrase 'region under consideration' must be formalized as a restricted domain or removed so that it agrees with the global graph-based failure condition.

children.title: Variational-Inequality Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Variational inequalities represented through generalized-equation structure.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(f,C)\) is equivalent to \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: variational inequality with field f and feasible set C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stampacchia variational inequality on a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(f,C)\) asks for \(x\in C\) satisfying \[\langle f(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.\] With the convex normal cone \[N_C(x):=\{v\in H\mid \langle v,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}\] for \(x\in C\), this condition is equivalent to the generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+N_C(x).\] Thus the feasible-set constraint and inequality are jointly encoded by the normal-cone term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Stampacchia variational inequality is exactly the generalized equation obtained by adding the feasible set's convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Generalized Equations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minty–Stampacchia Equivalence for Monotone Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty equivalent formulation accompanying the normal-cone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), the Stampacchia inequality is \[\langle f(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\qquad(\forall y\in C),\] and the Minty inequality is \[\langle f(y),y-x\rangle\geq0\qquad(\forall y\in C).\] If \(f\) is monotone and continuous on line segments in \(C\), these inequalities are equivalent. Hence each is equivalent to \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\). Monotonicity suffices for the Stampacchia-to-Minty implication; the stated continuity supports the converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone, segment-continuous field, the Minty and Stampacchia variational inequalities and the normal-cone generalized equation have the same solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f:C\to H\) is monotone and continuous on every line segment in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Stampacchia VI, Minty VI, and \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\) have the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty–Stampacchia Equivalence for Monotone Fields

children.title: Complementarity Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Complementarity problems represented as generalized equations.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone with dual cone \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in K\), \(F(x)\in K^*\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\) are equivalent to \(0\in F(x)+N_K(x)\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of K under the nonnegative pairing convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone complementarity under the nonnegative dual-cone convention.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Constrained Optimization and Equilibria p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone complementarity problem is to find \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[x\in K,\qquad F(x)\in K^*,\qquad \langle x,F(x)\rangle=0.\] For \(x\in K\), the convex normal cone satisfies \[N_K(x)=\{v\in -K^*\mid \langle v,x\rangle=0\}.\] Consequently, the complementarity conditions are equivalent to \(-F(x)\in N_K(x)\), or to the generalized equation \[0\in F(x)+N_K(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone complementarity is equivalent to a normal-cone generalized equation, with the sign determined by the chosen dual-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Generalized Equations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Constrained Optimization and Equilibria p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed Complementarity as a Box-Normal Generalized Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mixed complementarity with finite or infinite component bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B:=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), where \(-\infty\leq\ell_i<u_i\leq+\infty\). Then \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\) is equivalent componentwise to \[\ell_i\leq x_i\leq u_i,\qquad \begin{cases}F_i(x)\geq0,&x_i=\ell_i,\\F_i(x)=0,&\ell_i<x_i<u_i,\\F_i(x)\leq0,&x_i=u_i.\end{cases}\] Conditions involving an infinite endpoint are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed complementarity over component bounds is exactly a generalized equation with the box normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_i[\ell_i,u_i]\) is a nonempty closed box, allowing infinite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed-complementarity conditions are equivalent to \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\).

notation.meaning: box defined by the component bounds
convex normal-cone mapping of the box

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Complementarity as a Box-Normal Generalized Equation

children.title: KKT Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Primal-dual optimality systems viewed as generalized equations.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Generalized Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional KKT system for inequality and equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem of minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g(x)\le 0\) and \(h(x)=0\), seek a primal-dual triple \((x,\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^q\). Define \(L(x,\lambda,\mu):=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}h(x)\). The KKT conditions are represented by \[0\in \begin{pmatrix}\nabla_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\\-g(x)\\h(x)\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\{0\}\\N_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}(\lambda)\\\{0\}\end{pmatrix}.\] This inclusion encodes stationarity, equality feasibility, multiplier nonnegativity, inequality feasibility, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smooth KKT conditions form one primal-dual generalized equation whose normal-cone block encodes inequality feasibility and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: The variables satisfy \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}^q\); inequality constraints use \(g(x)\le 0\) and the multiplier cone \(\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT system is the generalized equation \(0\in \Phi(x,\lambda,\mu)+\{0\}\times N_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}(\lambda)\times\{0\}\).

children.title: Equilibrium-Constrained Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Nested variational systems arising in equilibrium-constrained optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(\Psi:X\times Y\to Z\), \(Q:X\times Y\rightrightarrows Z\), and \(\phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{(x,y)\mid 0\in\Psi(x,y)+Q(x,y)\}\), and optimization of \(\phi\) over it is equilibrium-constrained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional upper-level optimization constrained by a lower-level generalized equation.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An equilibrium-constrained generalized-equation problem has the form \[\min_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}\ \phi(x,y)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad 0\in\Psi(x,y)+Q(x,y).\] Defining the lower-level solution mapping by \[S(x):=\{y\in Y\mid 0\in\Psi(x,y)+Q(x,y)\},\] the same problem is \(\min\{\phi(x,y)\mid y\in S(x)\}\). Thus feasibility is determined by a parameterized equilibrium system, while the upper level selects among its graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equilibrium-constrained optimization minimizes an upper-level objective over the graph of a solution mapping defined by a generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium-Constrained Generalized Equations

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.2 Variational Systems as Equilibrium Constraints p. 51
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of the Equilibrium Feasible Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-feasibility property for an optimization problem constrained by a lower-level generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S(x):=\{y\mid0\in\Psi(x,y)+Q(x,y)\}\). If \(\Psi\) is continuous and \(Q\) has closed graph, then \[\operatorname{gph}S=\{(x,y)\mid-\Psi(x,y)\in Q(x,y)\}\] is closed. If additionally \(\phi\) is lower semicontinuous and, for some \(\alpha\), the set \(\{(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}S\mid\phi(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\) is nonempty and compact, then the upper-level problem attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity of the single-valued term and closedness of the multifunction graph make the equilibrium-feasible graph closed; a compact feasible lower level set yields attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(\Psi:X\times Y\to Z\) is continuous and \(Q:X\times Y\rightrightarrows Z\) has closed graph.
For attainment, \(\phi\) is lower semicontinuous and has a nonempty compact feasible lower level set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is closed, and the stated compactness condition implies attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of the Equilibrium Feasible Graph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong regularity characterized by a single-valued linearized solution map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization for generalized equation (5.24) at the stated primal-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generalized equation (5.24) is strongly regular at $(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)$ if and only if the map
\[
\widetilde\Lambda(\xi):=\left\{\widetilde\eta\in\mathbb R^{m+\ell+a^++a^0}\mid \xi\in D_{(I)}(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\widetilde\eta+N_{\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^\ell\times\mathbb R^{a^+}\times\mathbb R^{a^0}}(\widetilde\eta)\right\}
\]
is single-valued on $\mathbb R^{m+\ell+a^++a^0}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized equation is strongly regular at the reference primal-dual point exactly when the displayed linearized normal-cone solution map is single-valued on its whole perturbation space.
assumptions_latex: (x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\text{ is the reference point of generalized equation (5.24).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SR}_{(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)}(\mathrm{GE}\ (5.24))\iff \widetilde\Lambda\text{ is single-valued on }\mathbb R^{m+\ell+a^++a^0}.

children.title: Normal-Map Equations
children.top_down_role: Normal-map representations of normal-cone generalized equations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaled Normal-Map Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space normal-map representation of a closed-convex normal-cone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), define \(M_\lambda(z):=F(P_Cz)+\lambda^{-1}(z-P_Cz)\). Then \[M_\lambda(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x:=P_Cz\text{ satisfies }0\in F(x)+N_C(x),\] with the corresponding variables related by \(z=x-\lambda F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of the scaled normal map project exactly to solutions of the normal-cone generalized equation, and every solution produces a normal-map zero.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_\lambda(z)=0\iff 0\in F(P_Cz)+N_C(P_Cz).
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Normal-Map Equation

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f:H\to H\) is single-valued and \(P_C\) is the metric projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\) is equivalent, via \(z=x-f(x)\), to \(f(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space normal map for a closed convex constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the normal map associated with \(f\) and \(C\) by \[f_C(z):=f(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz.\] If \(f_C(z)=0\) and \(x:=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-f(x)\). The projection characterization \(x=P_Cz\) gives \(z-x\in N_C(x)\), hence \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\). Conversely, if \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\), set \(z:=x-f(x)\); then \(-f(x)\in N_C(x)\), so \(P_Cz=x\) and \(f_C(z)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of the normal map correspond exactly to solutions of the normal-cone generalized equation through projection onto the constraint set.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Equations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-map correspondence is mathematically standard and fits the representation container, but the record has no cited source. Its explanatory converse derivation should also be replaced by a concise equivalence statement when a sourced revision is prepared.

children.title: Metric Projection Representations

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\iff x=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\).

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto the closed convex set C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space representation for a variational inequality over a closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(N_C(x):=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq 0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\). The projection characterization \(z=P_C(u)\iff u-z\in N_C(z)\) yields, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=P_C\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] Thus the constrained generalized equation has an equivalent single-valued metric-projection representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained generalized equation is solved exactly when the point equals the projection of a forward step onto the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Projection Representations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Convex Single-Valuedness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an ordinary single-valued metric-projection representation for a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\), the set of nearest points to \(0\) is \[P_C(0)=\{-1,1\}.\] Hence closedness without convexity does not make metric projection single-valued, and \(x=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\) is not an ordinary single-valued equation without an additional selection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed nonconvex set can have multiple nearest points, so its metric projection need not be single-valued.
assumptions_latex: \(P_C(u)\) denotes the set of nearest points when projection is not unique.

notation.meaning: Possibly set-valued metric projection onto C.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex Single-Valuedness Boundary

children.title: Projected Fixed-Point Forms
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point formulations built from projected mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:H\to H\).
\(\lambda>0\), and \(T_\lambda:H\to C\) is defined by \(T_\lambda(x):=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\iff x\in\operatorname{Fix}T_\lambda\) for every \(x\in H\).

notation.meaning: Projected forward map with stepsize lambda.
Convex-analytic normal cone to C, taken to be empty outside C.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed \(\lambda>0\), define the projected forward map \(T_\lambda:H\to C\) by \(T_\lambda(x):=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\). Then, for every \(x\in H\), \[0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_\lambda(x)=x.\] Consequently, the solution set is \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\lambda:=\{x\in H:T_\lambda(x)=x\}\). This zero-set identity holds for every positive stepsize; convergence of the iteration \(x^{k+1}=T_\lambda(x^k)\) requires additional assumptions and is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real Hilbert space and a nonempty closed convex feasible set, solutions are precisely the fixed points of the map obtained by taking a forward step and projecting it onto the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Fixed-Point Forms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Point Equivalence Does Not Imply Iterative Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between an exact fixed-point representation and convergence of its Picard iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=C=\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=-x\), and \(\lambda>0\). The generalized equation has the unique solution \(0\), while \[T_\lambda(x)=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))=(1+\lambda)x.\] Thus \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\lambda=\{0\}\), but \(x^{k+1}=T_\lambda(x^k)\) gives \(x^k=(1+\lambda)^kx^0\), which diverges for \(x^0\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projected fixed-point equivalence does not ensure convergence of the associated iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Fix}T_\lambda=\{0\},\qquad |x^k|\to\infty\text{ for }x^0\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Equivalence Does Not Imply Iterative Convergence

children.title: Projection–Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between projection-based forms and resolvent representations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C=(I+\lambda N_C)^{-1}=J_{\lambda N_C}\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled normal-cone operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone resolvent identity in a Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: I.2 The Characterization of the Projection onto a Convex Set p. 8
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u,z\in H\), the projection characterization gives \[z=P_C(u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u-z\in N_C(z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in (I+\lambda N_C)(z),\] where the middle inclusion may be multiplied by any \(\lambda>0\) because \(N_C(z)\) is a cone. Hence \[P_C=(I+\lambda N_C)^{-1}=J_{\lambda N_C}.\] Therefore the projection fixed-point equation is the normal-cone specialization of a resolvent equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex set is exactly the resolvent of its normal-cone operator, for every positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Resolvent Correspondence

children.title: Resolvent Equations
children.top_down_role: Resolvent and proximal fixed-point forms of operator inclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Global Single-Valuedness Without Maximal Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a global single-valued resolvent equation for a nonmonotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(A(x)=\{-x\}\), and \(\lambda=1\). Then \[(I+A)^{-1}(u)=\begin{cases}\mathbb R,&u=0,\\ \varnothing,&u\ne0.\end{cases}\] Thus the inverse relation is multivalued at \(0\) and undefined elsewhere, so it is not a global single-valued resolvent equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a suitable well-posedness condition such as maximal monotonicity, a resolvent can be multivalued or undefined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J_A(0)=\mathbb R,\qquad J_A(u)=\varnothing\text{ for }u\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Global Single-Valuedness Without Maximal Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward–Resolvent Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued resolvent representation of a maximal-monotone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), \[0\in F(x)+A(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda F(x))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda F(x))=0.\] Maximal monotonicity makes \(J_{\lambda A}:=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) single-valued and defined on all of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal-monotone inclusion is equivalent to a fixed-point equation obtained by applying its resolvent after a forward step.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, and \(F:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in F(x)+A(x)\iff x=J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda F(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Forward–Resolvent Equation

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, and \(F:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+A(x)\iff x=J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda F(x))\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled maximal monotone operator A.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic resolvent reformulation of a maximal-monotone inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-resolvent equation for a maximal-monotone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maximal monotonicity makes \(J_{\lambda A}\) single-valued and defined on all of \(H\). For every \(x\in H\), \[0\in F(x)+A(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-\lambda F(x)\in x+\lambda A(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\lambda A}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] Equivalently, the resolvent residual \(R_\lambda(x):=x-J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda F(x))\) vanishes exactly at the solutions of the inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator inclusion is equivalent to a fixed-point equation formed by applying the resolvent after a forward step.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Equations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-resolvent equivalence is mathematically standard and precisely stated, but the record supplies no source. An authoritative locator for maximal-monotone resolvents and their full-domain single-valuedness is required.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\lambda(x)=0\iff 0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Natural residual associated with C, F, and lambda.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural map for a finite-dimensional variational inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the natural residual by \[R_\lambda(x):=x-P_C\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] Its zero equation is equivalent to the variational inequality generalized equation: \[R_\lambda(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=P_C\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+N_C(x).\] The residual is defined for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), including infeasible points, while every zero necessarily belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural residual subtracts a projected forward step from the current point; its zeros are exactly the variational-inequality solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural Residual Equations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity of the Natural Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary global regularity of the finite-dimensional natural residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \[R_\lambda(x):=x-P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\] satisfies \[\|R_\lambda(x)-R_\lambda(y)\|\le (2+\lambda L)\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally Lipschitz field produces a globally Lipschitz natural residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}(R_\lambda)\le 2+\lambda L.

children.title: Complementarity-Function Equations
children.top_down_role: Equation forms induced by complementarity functions.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), and the nonlinear complementarity problem requires \(x\geq0\), \(F(x)\geq0\), and \(x_iF_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) solves the complementarity problem if and only if \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fischer-Burmeister equation for the nonlinear complementarity problem.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8. Global Methods for Nonsmooth Equations p. 723

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b):=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\). Then \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0\) holds exactly when \(a\geq0\), \(b\geq0\), and \(ab=0\). Define \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) componentwise by \[\bigl(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\bigr)_i:=\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}\bigl(x_i,F_i(x)\bigr).\] Consequently, \[\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\geq0,\quad F(x)\geq0,\quad x_iF_i(x)=0\text{ for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the Fischer-Burmeister function componentwise converts nonnegativity and complementary slackness into one nonsmooth equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity-Function Equations

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar Fischer–Burmeister function is Lipschitz but nonsmooth at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_{\mathrm{FB}}\in C^1(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\})\text{ and is not differentiable at }(0,0).

children.title: Residual-Representation Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting interchange among residual-based representations.

assumptions_latex: \(R_\lambda(x)=x-P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\), while \(\Phi\) is built from a scalar complementarity function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The zero sets coincide for \(C=\mathbb R_+^n\), but this componentwise complementarity representation does not extend unchanged to arbitrary closed convex \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between orthant complementarity equations and general convex-set residuals.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8. Global Methods for Nonsmooth Equations p. 723
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the orthant, \[R_\lambda(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+N_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Phi(x)=0,\] provided the scalar function defining \(\Phi\) vanishes exactly on complementary nonnegative pairs. This establishes equality of zero sets, not equality of residual values, derivatives, error-bound constants, or conditioning. For a general non-product closed convex set \(C\), coordinatewise complementarity functions do not encode \(N_C\); the projection residual remains valid, whereas the same componentwise equation need not be equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural and complementarity residuals share zeros on the nonnegative orthant, but their values and conditioning differ, and componentwise formulas fail for general convex sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Representation Equivalence Boundaries

children.title: Solution-Set Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence confined to the set of solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are sets, and \(S_1,S_2:P\rightrightarrows X\) are solution multifunctions for two formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulations are solution-set equivalent on \(D\subset P\) exactly when \(S_1(p)=S_2(p)\) for every \(p\in D\).

notation.meaning: Parameter domain on which equivalence is asserted.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct equality of parameterized solution sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-set equivalence without claims about neighborhoods, regularity, or conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The two formulations are solution-set equivalent on \(D\subset P\) if \[S_1(p)=S_2(p)\qquad\text{for every }p\in D.\] Equivalently, for all \((p,x)\in D\times X\), \[x\in S_1(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in S_2(p).\] This predicate compares only exact solutions. It does not require the defining residuals or multifunctions to agree away from their zero sets, nor does it imply preservation of local branches, metric regularity, error bounds, or numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations are solution-set equivalent when they have exactly the same solutions for every parameter under consideration.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Equivalence

children.title: Localization-Preserving Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence preserving designated local solution branches.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, \(S_1,S_2:P\rightrightarrows X\), and \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S_1\cap\operatorname{gph}S_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Localization is preserved when \(S_1(p)\cap V=S_2(p)\cap V\) for every \(p\in U\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhood selecting the reference solution branch.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph equality near a designated parameter-solution pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The formulations preserve the localization of the solution map at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[S_1(p)\cap V=S_2(p)\cap V\qquad\text{for every }p\in U.\] Equivalently, their graphs coincide in \(U\times V\). This condition preserves the designated local solution branches while permitting the global solution sets to differ outside the localization neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations preserve a designated localization when their solution graphs coincide near the chosen parameter and solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Localization-Preserving Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localization Equivalence Is an Equivalence Relation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property of local graph-germ equality at a fixed parameter-solution pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \((\bar p,\bar x)\). Define \(S_1\sim_{(\bar p,\bar x)}S_2\) when their graphs coincide on some neighborhood of \((\bar p,\bar x)\). Then \(\sim_{(\bar p,\bar x)}\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; hence localization-preserving formulations represent the same solution-map graph germ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality of localized solution graphs is an equivalence relation and identifies the same graph germ at the reference pair.
assumptions_latex: \(S_i:P\rightrightarrows X\) all contain \((\bar p,\bar x)\) in their graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local graph equality at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

notation.meaning: equality of solution-map graph germs at the reference pair

children.title: Regularity-Preserving Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence preserving the regularity properties used in stability analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(G_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\) are set-valued formulations on metric spaces, with \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}G_i\) for \(i=1,2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regularity-preserving equivalence requires the designated regularity property of \(G_1\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) to hold if and only if it holds for \(G_2\) there.

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a named local regularity property \(\mathcal R\), such as metric regularity, strong metric regularity, or metric subregularity. Two representations are \(\mathcal R\)-preserving equivalent at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) when \[G_1\text{ has }\mathcal R\text{ at }(\bar x,\bar y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_2\text{ has }\mathcal R\text{ at }(\bar x,\bar y).\] Equality of solution sets alone does not establish this condition. Preservation of the qualitative property also need not preserve its exact modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulations preserve regularity only when the specified local stability property holds for one exactly when it holds for the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Preserving Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph-Germ Equality Preserves Local Regularity and Exact Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient mechanism for preserving standard local regularity properties of a multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_1,G_2:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have the same graph on a neighborhood of \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then metric regularity, metric subregularity, and strong metric regularity have the same truth values for \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and their exact local moduli coincide. Equivalently for metric regularity, the localized inverses have the same Aubin property and exact local Aubin modulus. Equality of only the fibers \(G_1^{-1}(\bar y)=G_2^{-1}(\bar y)\) does not imply these conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical local graph germs preserve the principal metric regularity properties and their exact local moduli; identical solution fibers alone do not.
assumptions_latex: There are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that \(\operatorname{gph}G_1\cap(U\times V)=\operatorname{gph}G_2\cap(U\times V)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity, metric subregularity, strong metric regularity, and the corresponding exact local moduli coincide for \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Germ Equality Preserves Local Regularity and Exact Moduli

children.title: Conditioning-Distorting Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent formulations with materially different local conditioning.

assumptions_latex: \(R:X\to Y\) is a residual between normed spaces, \(R(\bar x)=0\), and \(D:Y\to Y\) is a bounded linear isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde R^{-1}(\{0\})=R^{-1}(\{0\})\), while residual norms and associated error-bound constants are changed according to bounds involving \(\lVert D\rVert\) and \(\lVert D^{-1}\rVert\).

notation.meaning: Common zero set of the two residuals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible residual scaling as a precise zero-set versus conditioning boundary.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(D\) is injective, \[\widetilde R(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(x)=0,\] and hence \(\widetilde R^{-1}(\{0\})=R^{-1}(\{0\})=Z\). Nevertheless, for every \(x\in X\), \[\lVert D^{-1}\rVert^{-1}\lVert R(x)\rVert\leq\lVert\widetilde R(x)\rVert\leq\lVert D\rVert\lVert R(x)\rVert.\] Thus a local error bound expressed using one residual transfers to the other with constants involving \(\lVert D\rVert\) or \(\lVert D^{-1}\rVert\), so its numerical constant need not be preserved. In finite dimensions, if \(R\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(\widetilde R'(\bar x)=D R'(\bar x)\); consequently derivative conditioning also need not be preserved. For example, when \(X=Y=\mathbb R^m\), \(m\geq2\), and \(R(x)=x-\bar x\), one has \(\operatorname{cond}(\widetilde R'(\bar x))=\operatorname{cond}(D)\), which can be arbitrarily large over invertible choices of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible output scaling preserves every zero, but it changes residual norms and error-bound constants; in finite-dimensional differentiable examples it can also worsen derivative conditioning arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning-Distorting Reformulations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Set Equivalence Can Destroy an Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample separating common zeros from preservation of metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R,\widetilde R:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(R(x)=x\) and \(\widetilde R(x)=x^3\). Then \[R^{-1}(0)=\widetilde R^{-1}(0)=\{0\}.\] The residual \(R\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})=|R(x)|\), whereas no finite \(\kappa\) gives \[|x|\leq\kappa|\widetilde R(x)|\] throughout any neighborhood of zero. Thus \(\widetilde R\) is not metrically subregular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residuals x and x cubed have the same zero, but only the first has a local linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) and \(\widetilde R\) are zero-set equivalent, but only \(R\) is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Set Equivalence Can Destroy an Error Bound

children.title: Solution-Map Objects
children.top_down_role: The principal global and local objects attached to a parametric generalized equation.

children.title: Global Solution Multifunction
children.top_down_role: The full parameter-to-solution correspondence.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a parameter set, \(X,Y\) are spaces, \(f:P\times X\to Y\), and \(Q:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+Q(p,x)\}\) for every \(p\in P\).

notation.meaning: Set-valued term in the generalized equation.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical parameter-to-solution multifunction of a generalized equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full, unlocalized solution correspondence of a parameterized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parameterized generalized equation \[0\in f(p,x)+Q(p,x),\] its global solution multifunction is the mapping \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) defined by \[S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+Q(p,x)\}.\] Its graph is \[\operatorname{gph}S=\{(p,x)\in P\times X:0\in f(p,x)+Q(p,x)\}.\] No neighborhood of a reference solution is imposed, so \(S(p)\) contains every solution and may be empty, singleton, or set-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global solution multifunction assigns to each parameter the complete set of points satisfying the generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Solution Multifunction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically correct, fully quantified, and well matched to the global solution-multifunction container, but the record has no citation. A specific authoritative generalized-equation or solution-map locator is required.

children.title: Graphical Localizations
children.top_down_role: Local restrictions of a solution graph around a reference pair.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
\((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), with neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S_{U,V}=\operatorname{gph}S\cap(U\times V)\).

notation.meaning: graphical localization of the solution map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization is relative to neighborhoods of a fixed graph point.

source_refs.locator: B. Continuity and Semicontinuity p. 152

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical localization of \(S\) to \(U\times V\) is the multifunction \(S_{U,V}:P\rightrightarrows X\) defined by \(S_{U,V}(p)=S(p)\cap V\) for \(p\in U\), and \(S_{U,V}(p)=\varnothing\) for \(p\notin U\). Equivalently, its graph is the local restriction \[\operatorname{gph}S_{U,V}=\operatorname{gph}S\cap(U\times V).\] Thus only solution pairs whose parameter and solution components lie in the prescribed neighborhoods are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphical localization retains exactly the solution pairs lying near a specified reference parameter-solution pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Localizations

source_witnesses.locator: B. Continuity and Semicontinuity p. 152

children.title: Single-Valued Localizations
children.top_down_role: Localized solution correspondences represented by a unique branch.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)\cap V=\{s(p)\}\) for every \(p\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness are required throughout the parameter neighborhood.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Local Uniqueness of Solutions p. 266
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-valued localization of \(S\) around \((\bar p,\bar x)\) consists of neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\), together with a mapping \(s:U\to V\), such that \[S(p)\cap V=\{s(p)\}\quad\text{for every }p\in U,\qquad s(\bar p)=\bar x.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{gph}S\cap(U\times V)=\operatorname{gph}s\). No continuity of \(s\) is included unless imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-valued localization represents all nearby localized solutions by one uniquely determined branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Localizations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Local Uniqueness of Solutions p. 266
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness Does Not Imply Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the purely set-theoretic localization definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=X=\mathbb R\) and \(S(0)=\{0\}\), \(S(p)=\{1\}\) for \(p\ne0\). On neighborhoods \(U=(-1,1)\) and \(V=(-2,2)\), \(S(p)\cap V=\{s(p)\}\), where \(s(0)=0\) and \(s(p)=1\) for \(p\ne0\); nevertheless, \(s\) is discontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unique localized solution branch need not be continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) has a discontinuous single-valued localization at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Does Not Imply Continuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit Mapping Theorem for Generalized Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient generalized-derivative conditions for stability and differentiation of the solution map R(p)={x:0∈S(x,p)}.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^d\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m be outer semicontinuous, define R(p)=\{x\mid0\in S(x,p)\}, and let \bar x\in R(\bar p). If
(0,r)\in D^*S(\bar x,\bar p\mid0)(y)\Rightarrow y=0,\ r=0,
then R has the Aubin property at \bar p for \bar x. If also
0\in D_*S(\bar x,\bar p\mid0)(w,0)\Rightarrow w=0,
then R has a Lipschitz continuous single-valued localization there. Under the coderivative condition, if S is proto-differentiable at (\bar x,\bar p) for 0, then R is semidifferentiable and
DR(\bar p\mid\bar x)(q)=\{w\mid0\in DS(\bar x,\bar p\mid0)(w,q)\};
under both conditions this derivative is single-valued and Lipschitz continuous. In the single-valued strictly differentiable square case, the two conditions are equivalent to nonsingularity of \nabla_xS(\bar x,\bar p), and R is strictly differentiable with its Jacobian determined by
\nabla_xS(\bar x,\bar p)\nabla R(\bar p)+\nabla_pS(\bar x,\bar p)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an outer-semicontinuous parameterized generalized equation, a coderivative nondegeneracy condition guarantees the Aubin property of its solution map. Adding a strict-derivative kernel condition guarantees a locally unique Lipschitz solution branch. Proto-differentiability gives an explicit graphical-derivative formula, while the smooth square case reduces to nonsingularity of the partial Jacobian with respect to the solution variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\text{ has the Aubin property; with }0\in D_*S(\bar x,\bar p\mid0)(w,0)\Rightarrow w=0,\ R\text{ has a Lipschitz continuous single-valued localization}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint representations of reduced-objective subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four alternative adjoint constructions, each conditional on relation (7.25) and its own stated structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that (7.25) holds for each \(i\in\mathbb K(x_0,y_0)\). (i) If \(f\) is independent of \(\mu,\lambda\) and \((\widehat p_i,\widehat q_i,\widehat r_i)\) is the unique solution of (7.5) evaluated at \((x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\), then for \(\Theta(x)=f(x,S_1(x))\), \[
abla_x f(x_0,y_0)-\mathcal J_x\mathcal L(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)^T\widehat p_i-\mathcal J_xH(x_0,y_0)^T\widehat q_i+\mathcal J_xG_{I^+\cup M_i}(x_0,y_0)^T\widehat r_i\in\partial\Theta(\widehat x).\] (ii) If \((\widehat p_i,\widehat q_i,\widehat r_i)\) is the unique solution of (7.9) at the same reference point, then for \(\Theta(x)=f(x,S_1(x),S_2(x),S_3(x))\), the analogous expression with \(
abla_xf(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\) belongs to \(\partial\Theta(\widehat x)\). (iii) If \(f\) is independent of \(\mu,\lambda\), \(H\) and \(G\) are independent of \(x\), and \(\widehat p_i\) is the unique solution of GE (7.12) at the reference point, then for \(\Theta(x)=f(x,S_1(x))\), \[
abla_xf(x_0,y_0)-\mathcal J_xF(x_0,y_0)^T\widehat p_i\in\partial\Theta(\widehat x).\] (iv) If \(f\) is independent of \(\mu,\lambda\), \(\mathcal J_yF(x_0,y_0)\) is symmetric, and \((\widehat p_i,\widehat q_i,-\widehat r_i)\) is the solution with unique KKT vector of adjoint QP (7.15) at the reference point, then the inclusion in (i) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming relation (7.25), four case-specific adjoint constructions produce subgradients of objectives reduced through equilibrium-solution mappings. The cases use two adjoint equations, a generalized equation under x-independence of H and G, and an adjoint quadratic program under symmetry of the y-Jacobian of F.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each of cases (i)--(iv) additionally requires its stated independence, uniqueness, or symmetry hypotheses.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{In each case, the corresponding displayed vector belongs to the stated }\partial\Theta(\widehat x).

children.title: Solution Selections
children.top_down_role: Selected branches of a set-valued solution map.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(p)\in S(p)\) for all \(p\in D\).

notation.meaning: domain on which solutions are selected

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition imposes no continuity, measurability, or uniqueness by itself.

source_refs.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solution selection of \(S\) on \(D\) is a single-valued mapping \(s:D\to X\) satisfying \[s(p)\in S(p)\quad\text{for every }p\in D.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{gph}s\subset\operatorname{gph}S\) over \(D\). A local selection through \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) additionally has a neighborhood domain \(D\) of \(\bar p\) and satisfies \(s(\bar p)=\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution selection chooses one admissible solution from each nonempty solution set in its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Selections

source_witnesses.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Selection Need Not Be a Localization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates branch choice from exhaustive representation of nearby solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(p)=\{0,p\}\) and \(s(p)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(s(p)\in S(p)\) and \(s(0)=0\). For every neighborhoods \(U,V\) of \(0\), some nonzero \(p\in U\cap V\) satisfies \(S(p)\cap V\supset\{0,p\}\); hence \(s\) is not a single-valued localization around \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected branch may coexist with other arbitrarily close solutions and need not be a localization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is a solution selection but not a single-valued localization at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: A Selection Need Not Be a Localization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of an Unrestricted Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely set-theoretic existence; no regularity or uniqueness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assuming the axiom of choice, if \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in D\), then there exists \(s:D\to X\) satisfying \(s(p)\in S(p)\) for every \(p\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the axiom of choice, every nonempty-valued multifunction admits an unrestricted selection.
assumptions_latex: The axiom of choice is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists s:D\to X\;\forall p\in D:\ s(p)\in S(p)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Existence of an Unrestricted Selection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint subgradient formula for GE (5.37)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-objective subgradient representation conditional on relation (7.38).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider GE (5.37). Assume that (7.38) holds and that \(f\) is independent of \(\lambda\). Let \(\Theta(x)=f(x,S_1(x))\), and let \(\widehat\pi_i\) be the unique solution of adjoint equation (7.20) with \((\widehat x,\widehat y)\) replaced by \((x_0,y_0)\). Then \[\xi:=\nabla_xf(x_0,y_0)-\mathcal J_xF_{L\cup(I^0\setminus M_i)}(x_0,y_0)^T\widehat\pi_i\in\partial\Theta(x_0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For GE (5.37), relation (7.38), independence of f from lambda, and the unique adjoint solution specified by (7.20) yield the displayed subgradient of the reduced objective at x0.
assumptions_latex: \widehat\pi_i\text{ is the unique solution of adjoint equation (7.20) at }(x_0,y_0).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in\partial\Theta(x_0),\qquad \Theta(x)=f(x,S_1(x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonzero Degree of a VI Residual Map Implies Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both natural-map and normal-map degree certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, and let F:\mathcal D\supseteq K\to\mathbb R^n be continuous on the open set \mathcal D. If a bounded open set \mathcal U satisfies \operatorname{cl}\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal D and \deg(\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}},\mathcal U) is well defined and nonzero, then \operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\cap\mathcal U\neq\varnothing. If a bounded open set \mathcal U' satisfies that \deg(\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nor}},\mathcal U') is well defined and nonzero, then there exists x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F) such that x-F(x)\in\mathcal U'.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous variational inequality on a closed convex set, a well-defined nonzero degree of the natural map on a bounded admissible open set guarantees a solution in that set. A well-defined nonzero degree of the normal map guarantees a solution whose normal-map variable lies in the specified open set.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is open},\quad K\subseteq\mathcal D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\deg(\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}},\mathcal U)
eq0\Rightarrow\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\cap\mathcal U
eq\varnothing,\qquad \deg(\mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nor}},\mathcal U')
eq0\Rightarrow\exists x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F):x-F(x)\in\mathcal U'
