children.title: Graphical Convergence of Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Convergence of solution correspondences through their graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k\to_g S\iff\liminf_k\operatorname{gph}S_k=\limsup_k\operatorname{gph}S_k=\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of graphs is used.

source_refs.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109
E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution maps \(S_k\) converge graphically to \(S\), written \(S_k\to_g S\), when their graphs converge in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense: \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}S_k=\limsup_{k\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}S_k=\operatorname{gph}S.\] Hence every \((p,x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) is approximated by points \((p_k,x_k)\in\operatorname{gph}S_k\), while every convergent subsequence of graph points from \(S_k\) has its limit in \(\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution maps converge graphically when their graphs have the same inner and outer set limit, equal to the limiting solution graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Convergence of Solution Maps

source_witnesses.locator: A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109
E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical Convergence Need Not Give Fixed-Fiber Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convergence in the product space from convergence at a fixed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{gph}S_k=\{(0,1),(1/k,0)\}\). Then \(S_k\to_g S\) with \(\operatorname{gph}S=\{(0,1),(0,0)\}\). However, \(S_k(0)=\{1\}\) for every \(k\), so the Painlev\'e--Kuratowski limit of the fixed fibers is \(\{1\}\ne S(0)=\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving parameter coordinates can create limiting graph points absent from the limits of fixed fibers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k\to_g S\) while \(S_k(0)\not\to S(0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Convergence Need Not Give Fixed-Fiber Convergence

children.title: Outer Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Upper limiting stability of nearby solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{p\to\bar p}S(p)\subset S(\bar p)\).

notation.meaning: outer limit of solution sets as the parameter approaches the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential outer semicontinuity in metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: B. Continuity and Semicontinuity p. 152

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution map \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar p\) when \[\limsup_{p\to\bar p}S(p)\subset S(\bar p).\] Equivalently, whenever \(p_k\to\bar p\), \(x_k\in S(p_k)\), and \(x_k\to x\), one has \(x\in S(\bar p)\). Thus no convergent sequence of nearby solutions can produce a limit outside the reference solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limit of convergent nearby solutions remains a solution at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Semicontinuity

source_witnesses.locator: B. Continuity and Semicontinuity p. 152

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer Semicontinuity Does Not Prevent Escape to Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompactness boundary of the sequential outer-limit condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(S(p)=\{0,1/|p|\}\) for \(p\ne0\). Any convergent sequence \(p_k\to0\), \(x_k\in S(p_k)\), must eventually select a bounded subsequence whose only possible limit is \(0\); hence \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(0\). Nevertheless, \(S\) is not locally bounded there because the solutions \(1/|p|\) escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer semicontinuity controls convergent solution sequences but does not prevent other solutions from escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is outer semicontinuous but not locally bounded at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Semicontinuity Does Not Prevent Escape to Infinity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Local Lipschitz Continuity of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided and pairwise local Lipschitz inclusions for a nonempty compact-valued multifunction; the extract explicitly calls \(\mathcal B^l\) the unit sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma:\mathbb{R}^k\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^l\) have nonempty compact values and let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^k\). It is upper Lipschitz continuous at \(z\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) and \(L<\infty\) such that \(\Gamma(z')\subseteq\Gamma(z)+L\lVert z-z'\rVert\mathcal B^l\) for every \(z'\in U\). It is locally Lipschitz continuous at \(z\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) and \(L<\infty\) such that \(\Gamma(z')\subseteq\Gamma(z'')+L\lVert z''-z'\rVert\mathcal B^l\) for all \(z',z''\in U\), where \(\mathcal B^l\) denotes the unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^l\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper Lipschitz continuity controls nearby images by proportional enlargements of the reference image. Local Lipschitz continuity imposes the analogous inclusion for every ordered pair of nearby parameters.
assumptions_latex: \Gamma(u)\text{ is nonempty and compact for every }u
\mathcal B^l\text{ is the unit sphere in }\mathbb{R}^l
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni z,\ L<\infty\text{ satisfying the stated one-sided or pairwise Lipschitz inclusion.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz estimate for primal–dual solutions under MFCQ and SSOC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative stability near a local optimum of the parametrized nonlinear program (4.1); the extract's final neighborhood center is interpreted as \(y^0\), consistently with the parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0\in\Psi_{\mathrm{loc}}(y^0)\), and suppose \(\mathrm{MFCQ}\) and \(\mathrm{SSOC}\) hold at \((x^0,y^0)\). Then there exist open neighborhoods \(U_\delta(y^0)\), \(V_\varepsilon(x^0)\), and \(L<\infty\) such that, for every \(y\in U_\delta(y^0)\), every \(x\in\Psi_{\mathrm{loc}}(y)\cap V_\varepsilon(x^0)\), and every \((\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(x,y)\), \[\varrho\!\left((x,\lambda,\mu),\{x^0\}\times\Lambda(x^0,y^0)\right)\le L\lVert y-y^0\rVert.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ and SSOC, every nearby localized primal solution and associated multiplier pair lies within a constant times the parameter perturbation of the reference primal–multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varrho\!\left((x,\lambda,\mu),\{x^0\}\times\Lambda(x^0,y^0)\right)\le L\lVert y-y^0\rVert.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Semicontinuity of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-set definitions for a multifunction between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma:\mathbb{R}^k\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^l\) and \(z\in\mathbb{R}^k\). It is upper semicontinuous at \(z\) if, for every open set \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^l\) satisfying \(\Gamma(z)\subset Z\), there is an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) such that \(\Gamma(z')\subset Z\) for every \(z'\in U\). It is lower semicontinuous at \(z\) if, for every open set \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^l\) satisfying \(\Gamma(z)\cap Z\neq\varnothing\), there is an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(z\) such that \(\Gamma(z')\cap Z\neq\varnothing\) for every \(z'\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper semicontinuity keeps nearby images inside every open set containing the reference image. Lower semicontinuity preserves intersection with every open set meeting the reference image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma\text{ satisfies the respective open-set condition for upper or lower semicontinuity at }z.

children.title: Inner Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Approximation of reference solutions by nearby solution branches.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(\bar p)\subset\liminf_{p\to\bar p}S(p)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential inner semicontinuity in metric spaces; approximating selections are required on a sufficiently large tail of each parameter sequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution map \(S\) is inner semicontinuous at \(\bar p\) when \[S(\bar p)\subset\liminf_{p\to\bar p}S(p).\] Equivalently, for every \(x\in S(\bar p)\) and every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\), there exist an index \(k_0\) and points \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) for all \(k\ge k_0\) such that \(x_k\to x\). Thus each reference solution can be approximated along the tail of every nearby parameter sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every reference solution can be approximated by solutions along a sufficiently large tail of any sequence of parameters converging to the reference parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty Reference Value Is Vacuous
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of the pointwise definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S(\bar p)=\varnothing\), then \(S(\bar p)\subset\liminf_{p\to\bar p}S(p)\) holds automatically. Inner semicontinuity at \(\bar p\) therefore asserts neither existence nor persistence of a solution in this case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner semicontinuity is vacuous at an empty reference value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is inner semicontinuous at \(\bar p\) vacuously.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty Reference Value Is Vacuous

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood-Hitting Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological formulation of inner semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is inner semicontinuous at \(\bar p\) if and only if, for every \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) and every neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\), there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar p\) such that \(S(p)\cap V\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every neighborhood of each reference solution is hit by every sufficiently nearby solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }\bar p\iff \forall\bar x\in S(\bar p),\ \forall V\in\mathcal N(\bar x),\ \exists U\in\mathcal N(\bar p):\ \forall p\in U,\ S(p)\cap V\ne\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Hitting Characterization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner semicontinuity and inner semicompactness of a multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definitions at a graph point or base point, together with their basic comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S:X\rightrightarrows Y$ and $\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S$. For $\bar y\in S(\bar x)$, $S$ is inner semicontinuous at $(\bar x,\bar y)$ if, for every sequence $x_k\to\bar x$ with $x_k\in\operatorname{dom}S$, there exist $y_k\in S(x_k)$ such that $y_k\to\bar y$. The mapping $S$ is inner semicompact at $\bar x$ if, for every sequence $x_k\to\bar x$, there exist $y_k\in S(x_k)$ having a convergent subsequence. Inner semicontinuity at every $(\bar x,\bar y)$ with $\bar y\in S(\bar x)$ implies inner semicompactness at $\bar x$. Inner semicompactness generally requires passage to a subsequence and cannot be replaced by convergence of the whole selected sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner semicontinuity lets every nearby domain sequence select values converging to a prescribed reference value. Inner semicompactness only requires selectable values with a convergent subsequence. Pointwise inner semicontinuity for every reference value implies inner semicompactness, but the latter does not generally permit convergence of the whole sequence.
assumptions_latex: \bar y\in S(\bar x)\text{ for inner semicontinuity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ under the stated selection condition; }S\text{ is inner semicompact at }\bar x\text{ under the stated subsequential selection condition; inner semicontinuity at every }\bar y\in S(\bar x)\Rightarrow\text{ inner semicompactness}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Boundedness Does Not Imply Outer Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates size control from limiting-membership stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(S(p)=\{1\}\) for \(p\ne0\). Then \(S\) is locally bounded at \(0\), but for nonzero \(p_k\to0\), the solutions \(x_k=1\) converge to \(1\notin S(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform boundedness of nearby solutions does not force their limits to remain reference solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is locally bounded but not outer semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Boundedness Does Not Imply Outer Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Characterization of Local Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-domain characterization for a normed range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be metric and \(X\) normed. Then \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is locally bounded at \(\bar p\) if and only if every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\) and every choice \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) produce a bounded sequence \((x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local boundedness is equivalent to boundedness of every solution sequence selected along parameters converging to the reference point.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a metric space and \(X\) is a normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is locally bounded at }\bar p\iff \forall p_k\to\bar p,\ \forall x_k\in S(p_k),\ \sup_k\lVert x_k\rVert<\infty.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Characterization of Local Boundedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon criterion for local boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a sufficient horizon-mapping condition and a graph-convex outer-semicontinuous specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\). If \(S^\infty(0)=\{0\}\), then \(S\) is locally bounded and its horizon mapping \(S^\infty\) is locally bounded. Moreover, if \(S\) is graph-convex and outer semicontinuous and there exists \(\bar x\) such that \(S(\bar x)\) is nonempty and bounded, then \(S^\infty(0)=\{0\}\), so the preceding conclusions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triviality of the horizon value at zero is sufficient for a multifunction and its horizon mapping to be locally bounded. For a graph-convex outer-semicontinuous mapping, one nonempty bounded value ensures this horizon condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ and }S^\infty\text{ are locally bounded};\quad [S\text{ graph-convex and osc},\ \exists\bar x:\varnothing\ne S(\bar x)\text{ bounded}]\Rightarrow S^\infty(0)=\{0\}.

children.title: Outer Lipschitz Continuity
children.top_down_role: One-sided quantitative continuity of localized solution sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer Semicontinuity Does Not Imply an Outer Lipschitz Estimate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar separation between qualitative and linear-rate outer stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(p)=\{\sqrt{|p|}\}\) and \((\bar p,\bar x)=(0,0)\). The single-valued map is continuous, hence outer semicontinuous, at \(0\). However, no \(\kappa<\infty\) satisfies \(\sqrt{|p|}\le\kappa|p|\) for every sufficiently small nonzero \(p\), so the localized outer Lipschitz property fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity and outer semicontinuity do not supply the required linear rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is outer semicontinuous but not outer Lipschitz continuous at \(0\) for \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Semicontinuity Does Not Imply an Outer Lipschitz Estimate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Outer Lipschitz Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The convention is explicitly localized at a graph point; this one-base-parameter estimate is also commonly called calmness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,X\) be normed spaces and \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\). The solution map \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is outer Lipschitz continuous at \(\bar p\) for \(\bar x\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\), \(V\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that \[S(p)\cap V\subset S(\bar p)+\kappa\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\mathbb B_X\qquad(p\in U).\] Equivalently, \[\sup_{x\in S(p)\cap V}\operatorname{dist}(x,S(\bar p))\le \kappa\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\qquad(p\in U),\] with the supremum over an empty set interpreted as zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nearby localized solution lies within a linearly parameter-controlled distance of the reference solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)\cap V\subset S(\bar p)+\kappa\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\mathbb B_X\) for all \(p\in U\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the solution space

knowledge_statements.title: Localized Outer Lipschitz Continuity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution map \(S\) is outer Lipschitz continuous at \(\bar p\) for \(\bar x\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\ge0\), such that \[S(p)\cap V\subset S(\bar p)+\kappa\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\mathbb B_X\quad\text{for every }p\in U.\] Hence every localized nearby solution lies within a distance proportional to the parameter displacement from some reference solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal recovery from a smooth-envelope dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Under a strong-relative-interior qualification, the dual is attained and every dual solution recovers the unique minimizer of a quadratically regularized composite problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(\psi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), \(z\in\mathcal H\), \(r\in\mathcal K\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), with \(r\in\operatorname{sri}(L(\operatorname{dom}\varphi)-\operatorname{dom}\psi)\). Consider \[\min_x\left\{\varphi(x)+\psi(Lx-r)+\tfrac12\|x-z\|^2\right\}\] and \[\min_v\left\{{}^{1}(\varphi^*)(z-L^*v)+\psi^*(v)+\langle v,r\rangle\right\},\] whose objective is equivalently \(\tfrac12\|z-L^*v\|^2-{}^{1}\varphi(z-L^*v)+\psi^*(v)+\langle v,r\rangle\). The dual problem has a solution, and for every dual solution \(v\), \(x=\operatorname{Prox}_{\varphi}(z-L^*v)\) is the unique primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratically regularized convex composite problem satisfying the strong-relative-interior qualification, the Moreau-envelope dual is attained. Every dual minimizer recovers the unique primal minimizer by one proximal evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Argmin}_v\left[{}^{1}(\varphi^*)(z-L^*v)+\psi^*(v)+\langle v,r\rangle\right]\ne\varnothing,\quad \forall v\text{ in this set},\quad \operatorname{Argmin}_x\left[\varphi(x)+\psi(Lx-r)+\tfrac12\|x-z\|^2\right]=\{\operatorname{Prox}_{\varphi}(z-L^*v)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity Characterizations of Local Uniqueness for Polyhedral VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates a homogeneous critical-cone complementarity problem, a directional implication, and local uniqueness; affinity makes all three equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a polyhedron, \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\), and suppose \(F\) is B-differentiable at \(x\). Define: \(A\): the homogeneous complementarity problem \[v\in\mathcal C(x;K,F),\quad F'(x;v)\in\mathcal C(x;K,F)^*,\quad v\perp F'(x;v)\] has only the solution \(v=0\); \(B\): whenever \(x+d\in K\), \(d\perp F(x)\), \(d\ne0\), and \[(F(x)+F'(x;d))^T(y-x)\ge0\quad\forall y\in K,\] one has \(d^TF'(x;d)>0\); and \(C\): \(x\) is locally unique. Then \[A\iff B\implies C.\] If, in addition, \(F\) is affine, then \[A\iff B\iff C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral VI with F B-differentiable at x, uniqueness of the zero solution to the homogeneous critical-cone complementarity problem is equivalent to the stated directional positivity implication, and either condition implies local uniqueness. When F is affine, local uniqueness is equivalent to both conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\iff B\implies C;\qquad F\text{ affine}\implies(A\iff B\iff C)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: b-Regular Nonlinear Complementarity Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by the equivalent conditions of Corollary 3.3.9, together with the implication and nonconverse for local uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) solve \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\). The matrix \(J_\gamma F_\gamma(x)\) is called the basic matrix of \(x\). The solution \(x\) is b-regular when it satisfies either of the equivalent conditions: the basic matrix is nonsingular and its associated Schur complement is nondegenerate; or \(JF(x)_{\gamma'\gamma'}\) is nonsingular for every \(\gamma\subseteq\gamma'\subseteq\gamma\cup\beta\). Every b-regular solution is locally unique, but a locally unique solution need not be b-regular and its basic matrix need not be nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NCP solution is b-regular when it satisfies the equivalent basic-matrix/Schur-complement and principal-submatrix conditions. B-regularity implies local uniqueness, but local uniqueness does not imply b-regularity or nonsingularity of the basic matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ b-regular}\Rightarrow x\text{ locally unique},\qquad x\text{ locally unique}\nRightarrow x\text{ b-regular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-System Criterion for Local Uniqueness of an LCP Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes isolation using the positive-support and biactive index sets of a fixed LCP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(q,M)\), \(\alpha=\{i:z_i^*>0\}=\operatorname{supp}z^*\), and \(\beta=\{i:z_i^*=0,\ (q+Mz^*)_i=0\}\). Then \(z^*\) is locally unique if and only if \((u_\alpha,u_\beta)=(0,0)\) is the only solution of \(M_{\alpha\alpha}u_\alpha+M_{\alpha\beta}u_\beta=0\), \(v_\beta=M_{\beta\alpha}u_\alpha+M_{\beta\beta}u_\beta\ge 0\), \(u_\beta\ge0\), and \(v_\beta^{\mathsf T}u_\beta=0\). In particular, if \(z^*\) is nondegenerate and \(M_{\alpha\alpha}\) is nonsingular, then \(z^*\) is locally unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP solution is isolated exactly when its homogeneous reduced complementarity system on the positive-support and biactive indices has only the zero solution. In particular, a nondegenerate solution is locally unique when its principal support submatrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^*\text{ is locally unique}\iff (0,0)\text{ is the unique solution of the stated reduced system};\quad z^*\text{ nondegenerate and }M_{\alpha\alpha}\text{ nonsingular}\implies z^*\text{ locally unique}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of Fréchet differentiability of a GE solution map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded equivalence for GE (5.1) with the structured set $Q$ specified by (6.17).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider GE (5.1) at $(x_0,z_0)$, with $Q$ given by (6.17). Suppose LICQ holds at $z_0$ and
\[\langle d,\mathcal J_zF(x_0,z_0)d\rangle>0\quad\text{for every nonzero }d\in\operatorname{Ker}^{1}A\cap\operatorname{Ker}^{2}A_{I^+}.\]
Then the following are equivalent: (i) $\sigma$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x_0$; (ii) for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $v=\sigma'(x_0;h)$ satisfies ${}^{2}A_Iv=0$; (iii) for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $v=\sigma'(x_0;h)$ is the unique solution of
\[0\in\mathcal J_xF(x_0,z_0)h+\mathcal J_zF(x_0,z_0)v+N_L(v);\]
(iv) for every $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $v=\sigma'(x_0;h)$ satisfies
\[\langle z,\mathcal J_xF(x_0,z_0)h+\mathcal J_zF(x_0,z_0)v\rangle=0\quad\text{for every }z\in K.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under LICQ and strict positivity of the z-Jacobian on the specified intersection of kernels, Fréchet differentiability of the solution map is equivalent to an all-directions linear constraint, unique solvability of a linearized generalized equation, and the stated orthogonality condition over K.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(iv) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform approximation of regular solution branches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded existence, local uniqueness, regularity, and uniform error estimate for discrete branches of parameterized nonlinear Banach-space equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\) be Banach spaces and \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb R\) compact. Suppose \(\mathcal G\in C^2(\Lambda\times\mathcal X;\mathcal Y)\), \(D^2\mathcal G\) is bounded on bounded subsets, conditions (6.31), (6.33), and (6.34) hold, and \(\{(\lambda,\psi(\lambda)):\lambda\in\Lambda\}\) is a regular solution branch of (6.30). Then there exist a neighborhood \(\mathcal O\) of \(0\) in \(\mathcal X\) and \(h_0>0\) such that, for every sufficiently small \(h\le h_0\), there is a unique \(C^2\) map \(\psi^h:\Lambda\to\mathcal X^h\) whose graph is a regular solution branch of (6.32) and satisfies
\[
\psi^h(\lambda)-\psi(\lambda)\in\mathcal O\quad\forall\lambda\in\Lambda.
\]
Moreover, there is a constant \(C>0\), independent of \(h\) and \(\lambda\), such that
\[
\|\psi^h(\lambda)-\psi(\lambda)\|_{\mathcal X}
\le C\|(\mathcal T^h-mathcal T)\mathcal G(\lambda,psi(\lambda))\|_{\mathcal X}
\quad\forall\lambda\in\Lambda.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every sufficiently fine discretization, a regular continuous solution branch has a unique nearby twice continuously differentiable regular discrete branch. Its error is uniformly bounded by the operator consistency error evaluated along the continuous branch.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X,\mathcal Y\text{ are Banach spaces and }\Lambda\subset\mathbb R\text{ is compact}
D^2\mathcal G\text{ is bounded on bounded subsets of }\Lambda\times\mathcal X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal O\ni0,\ h_0>0\ \forall h\le h_0\ \exists!\psi^h\in C^2(\Lambda;\mathcal X^h)\text{ satisfying the regular-branch, proximity, and uniform error conclusions}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness conditions ensuring a directional solution limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for directional convergence of nearby solutions of a parametric VI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the standing setting and MFCQ, fix \(dp\in\mathbb R^p\), and suppose that for some \(c>0\), every sufficiently small \(\tau>0\) and every \(x(\tau)\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(p^*+\tau dp),F(\cdot,p^*+\tau dp))\cap\mathcal N\) satisfy \(\|x(\tau)-x^*\|\le c\tau\). Then \((x(\tau)-x^*)/\tau\to\bar v\) if any one of the following holds: (a) for every \(\lambda\in\mathcal M^c(x^*,p^*;dp)\), \(\bar v\) is the unique solution of the associated critical AVI; (b) SMFCQ holds, \(\mathcal M(x^*,p^*)=\{\lambda\}\), and \(\bar v\) uniquely solves that AVI; or (c) \(K(p)=K\) is locally constant and finitely representable, and for every \(\lambda\in\mathcal M(x^*,p^*)\), \(\bar v\) uniquely solves \[\mathcal C\ni v\perp J_pF(x^*,p^*)dp+J_x\mathbf L(x^*,\lambda,p^*)v\in\mathcal C^*,\] where \(\mathcal C\) is the critical cone of \((K,F(\cdot,p^*))\) at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all nearby solutions move at most linearly with the perturbation, then their normalized displacement converges to a common vector whenever that vector is uniquely determined by every relevant critical AVI, by the single-multiplier AVI under SMFCQ, or—when the feasible set is fixed and finitely representable—by every relevant homogeneous critical-cone complementarity problem.
assumptions_latex: \text{The standing parametric-VI assumptions, including MFCQ, hold.}
\exists c>0\ \forall\tau>0\text{ sufficiently small}\ \forall x(\tau)\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(p^*+\tau dp),F(\cdot,p^*+\tau dp))\cap\mathcal N:\ \|x(\tau)-x^*\|\le c\tau.
\text{At least one of conditions (a), (b), or (c) stated above holds.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{x(\tau)-x^*}{\tau}=\bar v\quad\text{for every admissible nearby solution selection }x(\tau).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Primal-Dual Uniqueness, Quadratic Growth, and Smooth Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained parametric optimization under surjectivity of the constraint derivative and the stated second-order sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_0$ be a locally optimal solution of $(P_{u_0})$ and let $\lambda_0$ be an associated Lagrange multiplier. Suppose that $D_xG(x_0,u_0)$ is onto and that the second-order sufficient condition (4.344) holds with constant $\alpha>0$. Then there are neighborhoods $\mathcal V_X$ of $x_0$ and $\mathcal V_U$ of $u_0$ such that, for every $u\in\mathcal V_U$, the system $D_xL(x,\lambda,u)=0$, $G(x,u)=0$ has a unique solution $(\bar x(u),\bar\lambda(u))\in\mathcal V_X\times Y^*$. These neighborhoods can be chosen so that $f(x)\ge f(\bar x(u))+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-\bar x(u)\|^2$ for every $x\in\Phi(u)\cap\mathcal V_X$. Moreover, $(\bar x(\cdot),\bar\lambda(\cdot))$ is Fréchet differentiable near $u_0$, and for each parameter direction $d$, $(h,\mu)=(D\bar x(u_0)d,D\bar\lambda(u_0)d)$ solves $D^2L(x_0,\lambda_0,u_0)(h,d)+D_xG(x_0,u_0)^*\mu=0$ and $DG(x_0,u_0)(h,d)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Surjectivity and the stated second-order sufficient condition yield a locally unique primal-dual branch, local quadratic growth, and Fréchet differentiability characterized by the linearized optimality system.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is a locally optimal solution of }(P_{u_0})
\text{the second-order sufficient condition }(4.344)\text{ holds with constant }\alpha>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal V_X,\mathcal V_U\;\forall u\in\mathcal V_U:\ \exists!(\bar x(u),\bar\lambda(u))\in\mathcal V_X\times Y^*\text{ satisfying the optimality system, with quadratic growth and a Fréchet-differentiable primal-dual solution map characterized by the linearized system}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Value and First-Order Solution Asymptotics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the perturbed problems \((\widetilde{\mathcal P}_\varepsilon)\) near the limit problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \(V^b\leq\mathbf 1\leq V^z\) and \((\widetilde{\mathcal P}_0)\) satisfies Gollan’s condition. For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), \((\widetilde{\mathcal P}_\varepsilon)\) has a unique optimal solution \((\widetilde V^\varepsilon,\widetilde P^\varepsilon)\), and
\[\operatorname{val}(\widetilde{\mathcal P}_\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\varepsilon^2(\overline{dV})^T Z^R\overline{dV}+o(\varepsilon^2),\]
\[(\widetilde V^\varepsilon,\widetilde P^\varepsilon)=(\widetilde V^0,\widetilde P^0)+\varepsilon(\widetilde{dV},\widetilde{dP})+o(\varepsilon).\]
The associated multiplier set \(\Lambda_\varepsilon\) is nonempty and uniformly bounded. Moreover, if \(\lambda^\varepsilon\in\Lambda_\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), then \(\lambda^\varepsilon\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the bounds and Gollan’s condition, every sufficiently small perturbed problem has a unique optimizer. Its value has the stated second-order expansion, its optimizer has the stated first-order expansion, and its nonempty uniformly bounded multiplier sets converge to zero selectionwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}\mathcal S(\widetilde{\mathcal P}_\varepsilon)=\{(\widetilde V^\varepsilon,\widetilde P^\varepsilon)\},\\ \operatorname{val}(\widetilde{\mathcal P}_\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\varepsilon^2(\overline{dV})^T Z^R\overline{dV}+o(\varepsilon^2),\\ (\widetilde V^\varepsilon,\widetilde P^\varepsilon)=(\widetilde V^0,\widetilde P^0)+\varepsilon(\widetilde{dV},\widetilde{dP})+o(\varepsilon),\\ \varnothing\neq\Lambda_\varepsilon\text{ is uniformly bounded},\quad \lambda^\varepsilon\in\Lambda_\varepsilon,\ \varepsilon\downarrow0\Rightarrow\lambda^\varepsilon\to0.\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian and MLCP Criteria for Local Uniqueness of an NCP Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implication chain for a continuously differentiable NCP, including an affine-case equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) solve \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\), where \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(x\), and let \(\gamma,\beta\) be the associated index sets. Consider: (a) \(J_{\gamma}F_{\gamma}(x)\) is nonsingular and the Schur complement \(J_{\beta}F_{\beta}(x)-J_{\gamma}F_{\beta}(x)[J_{\gamma}F_{\gamma}(x)]^{-1}J_{\beta}F_{\gamma}(x)\) is nondegenerate; (b) \(JF(x)_{\gamma'\gamma'}\) is nonsingular for every \(\gamma\subseteq\gamma'\subseteq\gamma\cup\beta\); (c) the stated MLCP in \((v_\gamma,v_\beta)\) has \((0,0)\) as its unique solution; and (d) \(x\) is locally unique. Then \((a)\iff(b)\Rightarrow(c)\Rightarrow(d)\). If \(F\) is affine, then \((c)\iff(d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic-matrix and Schur-complement condition is equivalent to nonsingularity of every relevant principal Jacobian submatrix. These conditions imply uniqueness of the zero solution of the linearized MLCP, which implies local uniqueness of the NCP solution. For affine F, MLCP uniqueness and local uniqueness are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: F\in C^1(U)\text{ for an open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b)\Rightarrow(c)\Rightarrow(d),\qquad F\text{ affine}\Rightarrow[(c)\iff(d)].

children.title: Multiple Solution Branches
children.top_down_role: Coexisting local branches of a solution correspondence.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are topological spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)\cap V=\{s_1(p),\ldots,s_m(p)\}\) on \(U\), where \(m\ge2\) and the branches are distinct somewhere in every neighborhood of \(\bar p\).
review_flags: A precise authoritative locator for the finite continuous-branch decomposition is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a finite continuous-branch decomposition of the localized solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The localized solution map has multiple solution branches around \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\), an integer \(m\ge2\), and continuous selections \(s_i:U\to V\) satisfying \[S(p)\cap V=\{s_1(p),\ldots,s_m(p)\}\quad\text{for every }p\in U.\] Moreover, for every neighborhood \(U'\subset U\) of \(\bar p\), some \(p\in U'\) and indices \(i\ne j\) satisfy \(s_i(p)\ne s_j(p)\). Branches may coincide at \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple branches are distinct continuous selections that together exhaust the localized solutions and remain distinct arbitrarily near the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Solution Branches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition imposes a finite exhaustive decomposition into continuous selections, which is substantially stronger than the informal notion of coexisting local branches and is not a universally standard definition. No source is supplied to justify this exact convention.

children.title: Solution-Branch Creation
children.top_down_role: Local emergence of additional solution branches.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\), and \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
\(V\) is a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), and \(S(\gamma(t))\cap V\) is finite for sufficiently small \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_+>N_-\), where \(N(t)=\#(S(\gamma(t))\cap V)\) and \(N(t)=N_\pm\) on the corresponding sides of \(0\).

notation.meaning: localized number of solutions along the parameter path

review_flags: No supplied locator identifies a standard definition of branch creation; the pathwise finite-cardinality convention requires source review.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise finite-branch creation across a local bifurcation boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reference pair lies at a pathwise solution-branch creation boundary if, for some \(\delta>0\), the localized count \[N(t):=\#\bigl(S(\gamma(t))\cap V\bigr)\] is constant with value \(N_-\) for \(-\delta<t<0\), constant with value \(N_+\) for \(0<t<\delta\), and satisfies \(N_+>N_-\). The orientation of \(\gamma\) designates the positive side as the creation side. This criterion records an increase in distinct localized solutions and does not by itself specify smoothness or multiplicity of the branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing the boundary along a parameter path creates branches when the finite number of localized solutions increases on the designated side.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Branch Creation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits a branch-creation phenomenon, but the finite pathwise cardinality jump is a particular convention rather than a source-independent standard definition. An authoritative source must support the exact hypotheses, orientation convention, and conclusion.

children.title: Solution-Branch Collision
children.top_down_role: Local intersections or mergers of distinct solution branches.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is the solution map of a parameterized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar p,\bar x)\) is a solution-branch collision point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential local definition for two distinct solution branches meeting at one reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) is a solution-branch collision if there exist sequences \(p_k\to\bar p\), \(x_k^1,x_k^2\in S(p_k)\), and distinctness \(x_k^1\ne x_k^2\) such that \(x_k^1\to\bar x\), \(x_k^2\to\bar x\), and \(d_X(x_k^1,x_k^2)\to0\). Thus two distinct solutions at each perturbed parameter become indistinguishable at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collision occurs when two distinct nearby solutions for the same perturbed parameters converge to one reference solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Branch Collision

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential condition is mathematically coherent, but it is not a standard source-independent definition of a solution-branch collision: it identifies coalescing solution sequences without defining branches or a bifurcation framework. An authoritative source must establish the intended terminology and criterion.

children.title: Bifurcation Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Parameter boundaries associated with changes in local solution structure.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a metric space and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar p\in\partial\mathcal R_{\bar x}\) is a local bifurcation threshold.

notation.meaning: parameters admitting a regular local solution branch near the reference solution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold relative to a chosen regularity class for local single-valued solution branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a prescribed regularity class \(\mathscr C\), such as continuous or Lipschitz mappings, and let \(\mathcal R_{\bar x}\) contain those parameters \(p\) near \(\bar p\) for which the localization of \(S\) near \(\bar x\) is represented by a unique branch \(s_p\) of class \(\mathscr C\). The reference parameter \(\bar p\) is a bifurcation threshold when \(\bar p\in\partial\mathcal R_{\bar x}\); equivalently, every neighborhood of \(\bar p\) contains both parameters possessing and parameters lacking such a regular branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bifurcation threshold lies on the boundary between parameters with and without a chosen type of regular local solution branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Bifurcation Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed threshold depends on the undefined set of parameters admitting a regular branch. In particular, a branch s_p and its domain are not specified, and the regularity class is left variable. A source and framework-specific definition are needed before the boundary characterization can be assessed.

children.title: Moving-Constraint Parameterization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameter-dependent closed convex set \(C(p)\subset X\), a moving-constraint generalized equation has the form \[0\in f(p,x)+N_{C(p)}(x),\qquad S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+N_{C(p)}(x)\}.\] Here \(N_{C(p)}(x):=\{v:\langle v,z-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }z\in C(p)\}\) when \(x\in C(p)\), and \(N_{C(p)}(x):=\varnothing\) otherwise. Thus parameter dependence of feasibility is encoded by a varying normal-cone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving feasible set is encoded by its parameter-dependent normal cone inside the generalized equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-Inequality Form of a Moving Convex Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise equivalence in the closed-convex moving-set regime fixed by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\in P\), \[0\in f(p,x)+N_{C(p)}(x)\] if and only if \[x\in C(p)\quad\text{and}\quad \langle f(p,x),z-x\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }z\in C(p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving convex normal-cone inclusion is equivalent, parameter by parameter, to a variational inequality on the moving feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(C(p)\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for the parameter under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in f(p,x)+N_{C(p)}(x)\iff x\in C(p)\ \text{and}\ \langle f(p,x),z-x\rangle\ge0\ \forall z\in C(p).

children.title: Ample Parameter Families
children.top_down_role: Parameter families rich enough to expose full local inverse behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(P,Y\) are normed spaces and \(\Phi:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) satisfies \(\bar y\in\Phi(\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed covering property defines ampleness at \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ampleness formalized as linear local coverage of target perturbations by parameter variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parameter family is ample at \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist \(c>0\) and \(r_0>0\) such that, for every \(0<r<r_0\), \[B(\bar y,cr)\subset\bigcup_{p\in B(\bar p,r)}\Phi(p,\bar x).\] Hence all sufficiently small target perturbations, in every direction of \(Y\), can be generated at the fixed state \(\bar x\) by parameter changes of proportional size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ample family can generate every sufficiently small target perturbation through proportionally small parameter changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Ample Parameter Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed covering property is precise, but no evidence establishes that it is the intended meaning of an ample parameter family in this taxonomy. Because the terminology and chosen linear-openness formulation are framework-dependent, a source is required.

children.title: Restricted Parameter Families
children.top_down_role: Parameter families confined to selected perturbation directions.

assumptions_latex: \(P,Y\) are normed spaces and \(\Phi:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) satisfies \(\bar y\in\Phi(\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable first-order target directions form a proper subset of \(Y\).

notation.meaning: locally attainable target set at the reference state

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction expressed by failure to expose every first-order target direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r>0\), set \(A_r:=\bigcup_{p\in B(\bar p,r)}\Phi(p,\bar x)\). The parameter family is restricted at \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) when, for every sufficiently small \(r>0\), \[T_{A_r}(\bar y)\ne Y.\] Equivalently, at least one target direction is not attainable to first order by locally admissible parameter variations while the state remains fixed at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted family misses at least one first-order target direction, so it probes only part of the generalized equation's perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Parameter Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangent-cone condition is syntactically precise, but no source establishes it as the intended definition of a restricted parameter family or as the proper counterpart of ampleness. Its mathematical role and equivalence depend on the missing exposure framework.

children.title: Inverse-Behavior Exposure
children.top_down_role: Variation in observable inverse behavior across parameter families.

assumptions_latex: \(e:P\to Y\) is a local perturbation map with \(e(\bar p)=\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=G^{-1}\circ e\), and local surjectivity of \(e\) exposes the full local inverse of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full inverse behavior is visible when parameters locally cover all right-hand-side perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parameterized equation \(e(p)\in G(x)\), the solution map satisfies \[S(p)=G^{-1}(e(p)).\] If \(e\) maps every neighborhood of \(\bar p\) onto a neighborhood of \(\bar y\), then the family exposes every sufficiently local fiber of \(G^{-1}\) near \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Consequently, any local inverse pathology of \(G\)—including emptiness, multiplicity, or loss of a Lipschitz localization—appears along some parameter sequence approaching \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally target-surjective parameterization reveals every nearby inverse fiber and therefore cannot hide local inverse pathologies.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Behavior Exposure

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity \(S=G^{-1}\circ e\) is correct, but the cited generic set-valued-mapping page does not specifically support the stronger exposure conclusion. Neighborhood-surjectivity alone also does not provide quantitative control relating parameter distance to target distance, so claims involving exposure of Lipschitz-localization pathologies require a precise theorem and additional hypotheses or a source establishing the intended weaker meaning.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse Problems and Hadamard Ill-Posedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A qualitative definition for inverse recovery problems on specified admissible classes, not a local metric-regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a forward relation between causes or parameters $x\in X$ and effects or observations $y\in Y$, an inverse problem seeks a cause $x$ corresponding to an observed or desired effect $y$. The problem is Hadamard well posed on specified admissible classes if, for every admissible datum, a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the datum. It is ill posed if at least one of these conditions fails; regularization methods aim in particular to restore stability when continuous dependence fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inverse problem determines causes, states, or parameters from observed or desired effects. It is Hadamard well posed when every admissible datum has a solution, that solution is unique, and it changes continuously with the data. Failure of any condition makes the problem ill posed; regularization is used especially to address instability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{well\mbox{-}posed}\iff(\text{existence})\land(\text{uniqueness})\land(\text{continuous dependence on }y);\qquad \operatorname{ill\mbox{-}posed}\iff\text{at least one condition fails}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Inverse Function Theorem at a Regular Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion guarantees nearby solvability with a linear displacement estimate; it does not assert uniqueness or a single-valued inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset X\) be open, where \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces, and let \(T:D\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable. If \(x_0\in D\) and \(T'(x_0):X\to Y\) is surjective, then, with \(y_0=T(x_0)\), there exist a neighborhood \(N(y_0)\) and a constant \(K>0\) such that for every \(y\in N(y_0)\) there exists \(x\in D\) satisfying \(T(x)=y\) and \(\lVert x-x_0\rVert_X\le K\lVert y-y_0\rVert_Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular point of a continuously Fréchet differentiable mapping between Banach spaces, every sufficiently nearby target has at least one preimage whose displacement from the reference point is bounded linearly by the target displacement. Uniqueness is not claimed.
assumptions_latex: T:D\to Y\text{ is continuously Fréchet differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,N(y_0),\ K>0\ \forall y\in N(y_0)\ \exists x\in D:\ T(x)=y\ \land\ \lVert x-x_0\rVert_X\le K\lVert y-y_0\rVert_Y

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multifunction \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq \kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\qquad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V.\]
The estimate simultaneously permits variation of the input \(x\) and target \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds distance to a nearby inverse image by a uniform multiple of the residual distance to the multifunction value.

The multifunction \(F\) has the covering property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c>0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that

for every \(x\in U\) and every \(0<r<\varepsilon\). The intersections with \(V\) localize both the centers being covered and the covered output points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covering, local covering, and semi-local covering properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative image-ball covering regimes for a set-valued mapping and their exact covering bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) with \(\operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing\). For nonempty \(U\subset X\) and \(V\subset Y\), \(F\) has the covering property on \(U\) relative to \(V\) with modulus \(\kappa>0\) if, whenever \(r>0\) and \(x+r\mathbb B\subset U\), \[(F(x)\cap V)+\kappa r\mathbb B\subset F(x+r\mathbb B).\] It has the local covering property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) with modulus \(\kappa\) if this inclusion holds for neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\); the supremum of all such moduli is \(\operatorname{cov}F(\bar x,\bar y)\). It has the semi-local covering property around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) with modulus \(\kappa\) if the inclusion holds for a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) with \(V=Y\); the corresponding supremum is \(\operatorname{cov}F(\bar x)\). Local covering is also called openness at a linear rate or linear openness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction has the covering property when every admissible input ball covers, at a uniform linear rate, an enlargement of the relevant part of its value. Local covering imposes this near a graph point, whereas semi-local covering uses the whole output space near a domain point. Their exact bounds are the suprema of admissible rates.
assumptions_latex: U\subset X\text{ and }V\subset Y\text{ are nonempty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x+r\mathbb B\subset U,\ r>0\Longrightarrow (F(x)\cap V)+\kappa r\mathbb B\subset F(x+r\mathbb B),\quad \operatorname{cov}F=\sup\{\kappa:\kappa\text{ is admissible}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C(F;\bar x,\bar y)\) be the set of all \(c>0\) for which \(F\) has the covering property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c\). The exact covering modulus is
\[\operatorname{cov}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\sup\mathcal C(F;\bar x,\bar y).\]
The conventions are \(\sup\varnothing=0\) and an unbounded set of admissible rates has supremum \(+\infty\). By openness–covering equivalence, the same value is obtained from admissible linear-openness rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact covering modulus is the largest achievable local covering rate, defined as the supremum of all valid rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Covering Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multifunction \(S\) has the Aubin property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with constant \(L\geq0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(y,S(u))\leq Ld_X(x,u)\qquad\text{for all }x,u\in U\text{ and }y\in S(x)\cap V.\]
Only values near \(\bar y\) are required to satisfy the estimate; the comparison set \(S(u)\) itself need not be localized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin property requires nearby multifunction values to vary Lipschitzly after localizing the values around the reference output.
knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Property

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin Property Is Strictly Stronger Than Calmness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed comparison between two-parameter Aubin control and one-base-point calmness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has the Aubin property around \((\bar x,\bar y)\), then fixing one input at \(\bar x\) yields calmness at the reference graph point. Conversely, the function \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x\sin(x^{-2})\) for \(x\ne0\) is calm at \((0,0)\) but is not locally Lipschitz and hence lacks the Aubin property there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin property implies calmness, while an oscillatory scalar function shows that calmness does not imply the Aubin property.
assumptions_latex: \(S:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is a multifunction between metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Aubin}(S;\bar x,\bar y)\Rightarrow\operatorname{calm}(S;\bar x,\bar y),\quad\text{but not conversely.}
knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Property Is Strictly Stronger Than Calmness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative characterizations of the Aubin property for regular generalized equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular generalized equations, adjoint-kernel criteria, and exact Lipschitz moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S(x):=\{y\mid 0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\}, let ( ar x, ar y)\in\operatorname{gph}S, and set  ar z=-f( ar x, ar y). Suppose f is strictly differentiable at ( ar x, ar y), Q has locally closed graph and is SNC at ( ar x, ar y, ar z), and X,Y are Asplund. (i) If Z is Banach, 
abla_xf( ar x, ar y) is surjective, and Q is independent of x, triviality of the partial adjoint generalized equation implies that S is Lipschitz-like around ( ar x, ar y). It is also necessary when S is strongly coderivatively normal there, in particular when Y is finite-dimensional. If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}S( ar x, ar y)=\sup\{\|
abla_xf( ar x, ar y)^*z^*\|\mid \exists y^*\in D_N^*Q( ar y, ar z)(z^*),\ \|
abla_yf( ar x, ar y)^*z^*+y^*\|\le1\}; the supremum is attained under the stated local norm	imes weak^* closedness condition. (ii) If Z is Asplund and Q is N-regular at the reference point, then S is N-regular, and [(x^*,0)\in
abla f( ar x, ar y)^*z^*+D^*Q( ar x, ar y, ar z)(z^*)]\Rightarrow x^*=z^*=0 is sufficient for the Lipschitz-like property and is necessary when the adjoint generalized equation has only the trivial solution. If \dim X<\infty, the theorem gives the corresponding exact coderivative formula for \operatorname{lip}S. For Q=Q(y), triviality of the partial adjoint equation is sufficient and is necessary when that equation has only the trivial solution on \ker
abla_xf( ar x, ar y)^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For regular generalized equations, specified adjoint-kernel conditions guarantee—and under additional normality assumptions characterize—the Aubin property of the solution map. Finite-dimensional parameter spaces admit exact coderivative formulas for the Lipschitz modulus.
assumptions_latex: S(x)=\{y\mid0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\},\quad (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}S,\quad \bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y)
f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }(\bar x,\bar y)
Q\text{ has locally closed graph and is SNC at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated adjoint-kernel conditions imply, and under the specified additional hypotheses characterize, the Aubin property of }S;\ \dim X<\infty\text{ yields the stated exact modulus formulas.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin criteria for generalized equations with convex-graph fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone range criteria and exact Lipschitz moduli for convex-graph generalized equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S be the generalized-equation solution map under the common assumptions of Theorem 4.56, additionally suppose \operatorname{gph}Q is convex, and let M,\widetilde M,L be the mappings specified in the source. (i) If Z is Banach, \nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y) is surjective, and Q is independent of x, then S is Lipschitz-like around (\bar x,\bar y) if and only if (0,z^*)\in N((0,0);\operatorname{rge}\widetilde M)\Rightarrow z^*=0. If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)=\sup\{\|\nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y)^*z^*\|\mid -(y^*,z^*)\in N((0,0);\operatorname{rge}\widetilde M),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}. (ii) If Z is Asplund, then (x^*,0,z^*)\in N((0,0,0);\operatorname{rge}M)\Rightarrow x^*=z^*=0 is sufficient for the Lipschitz-like property and is necessary when N(0;\operatorname{rge}L)=\{0\}. If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)=\sup\{\|x^*\|\mid \exists(y^*,z^*),\ (x^*,-y^*,-z^*)\in N((0,0,0);\operatorname{rge}M),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For generalized equations with convex-graph fields, normal-cone conditions on ranges of associated mappings provide necessary-and-sufficient or sufficient Aubin criteria. In finite-dimensional parameter spaces they yield exact Lipschitz-modulus formulas.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }(\bar x,\bar y)
Q\text{ has locally closed convex graph and is SNC at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
M,\widetilde M,L\text{ are the mappings defined in the cited framework}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated normal-cone range conditions characterize or imply the Aubin property and, when }\dim X<\infty,\text{ yield the displayed exact Lipschitz moduli.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal R(F;\bar x,\bar y)\) consist of all \(\kappa\geq0\) for which there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\qquad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V.\]
The metric-regularity modulus is
\[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\inf\mathcal R(F;\bar x,\bar y),\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). A finite modulus is equivalent to metric regularity at the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric-regularity modulus is the smallest local residual-to-solution-distance constant, interpreted as infinity when no such constant exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Strong Monotonicity Gives Lipschitz VI Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric variational inequality over a fixed closed convex set, assuming the unique solution exists for every parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\to\mathbb{R}^m and let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m be closed and convex. Suppose F(\cdot,x) is strongly monotone with a modulus independent of x\in X, and F(y,\cdot) is Lipschitz continuous on X with a modulus independent of y\in Y. If y(x) denotes the unique solution of \operatorname{VI}(F(\cdot,x),K), then x\mapsto y(x) is Lipschitz continuous on X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a variational inequality over a fixed closed convex set, uniform strong monotonicity in the decision variable and uniform Lipschitz dependence on the parameter imply that the unique solution varies Lipschitz-continuously with the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \exists L_F<\infty\ \forall y\in Y\ \forall x_1,x_2\in X:\ \lVert F(y,x_1)-F(y,x_2)\rVert\leq L_F\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
\forall x\in X,\ y(x)\text{ is the unique solution of }\operatorname{VI}(F(\cdot,x),K)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists L_y<\infty\ \forall x_1,x_2\in X:\ \lVert y(x_1)-y(x_2)\rVert\leq L_y\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal O(F;\bar x,\bar y)\) be the set of all \(c>0\) for which there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that
\[B(y,cr)\subset F(B(x,r))\]
for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(0<r<\varepsilon\). The linear-openness modulus is
\[\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\sup\mathcal O(F;\bar x,\bar y),\]
where \(\sup\varnothing=0\) and an unbounded set of rates has supremum \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linear-openness modulus is the supremum of all rates at which nearby input balls uniformly cover output balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Openness Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A(S;\bar x,\bar y)\) consist of all \(L\geq0\) for which there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{dist}(y,S(u))\leq Ld_X(x,u)\qquad\text{for all }x,u\in U\text{ and }y\in S(x)\cap V.\]
The Aubin modulus is
\[\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\inf\mathcal A(S;\bar x,\bar y),\]
with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). It is finite exactly when \(S\) has the Aubin property around the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin modulus is the smallest constant governing the local Lipschitz-like estimate, or infinity if the Aubin property fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Exact Aubin Modulus Need Not Be Attained
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal nature of the exact local Lipschitz-like bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=x+x^2\), considered at \((0,0)\). Its Aubin modulus is \[\operatorname{lip}f(0\mid0)=1.\] Nevertheless, no neighborhood of \(0\) admits Aubin constant \(1\): every neighborhood contains positive \(x\) at which the local slope \(f'(x)=1+2x\) exceeds \(1\), while every constant strictly larger than \(1\) is admissible after sufficiently shrinking the neighborhood. Thus the exact modulus is an infimum and need not itself be an admissible local bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact Aubin modulus can be the limit of admissible neighborhood constants without itself being valid on any neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lip}f(0\mid0)=1\quad\text{and}\quad1\notin\mathcal A(f;0,0).

notation.meaning: constants admissible in an Aubin estimate on some reference neighborhood

knowledge_statements.title: The Exact Aubin Modulus Need Not Be Attained

children.top_down_role: Sharp relationships among the moduli of equivalent regularity views.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The exact moduli use the stated extended-real conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=1/\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quantitative correspondence for a multifunction and its inverse.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multifunction \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\), and these properties are equivalent to linear openness of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Their exact bounds satisfy
\[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)}.\]
Here \(1/0:=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty):=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity, the Aubin property of the inverse, and linear openness are equivalent; their exact constants agree after reciprocating the openness rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Bound Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multifunction \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
Unlike metric regularity, the target is fixed at \(\bar y\); only the input \(x\) varies locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity bounds distance to the reference solution set by the residual measured against one fixed target value.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse mapping \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq 0\), such that, for every \(y\in V\), \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U\subset F^{-1}(\bar y)+\kappa\lVert y-\bar y\rVert\mathbb B_X.\] The calmness modulus is the infimum of all constants \(\kappa\) for which such neighborhoods exist.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calmness Does Not Ensure Nearby Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vacuous-calmness example separating the estimate from persistence of solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(S(p)=\varnothing\) for \(p\neq0\). Then \(S\) is calm at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(0\), while no nonzero parameter has a solution. Thus solution-map calmness alone does not imply persistence or inner semicontinuity of solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution map may be calm because all nearby nonreference values are empty; calmness alone does not guarantee nearby solvability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clm}S(0\mid0)=0\), but \(S(p)=\varnothing\) for all nonzero \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) agree after simultaneous localization of parameters and values, then calmness is invariant under replacing one mapping by the other. Precisely, \[S_1\text{ is calm at }(\bar p,\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_2\text{ is calm at }(\bar p,\bar x),\] and their exact moduli satisfy \[\operatorname{clm}S_1(\bar p\mid\bar x)=\operatorname{clm}S_2(\bar p\mid\bar x).\] Shrinking either localization preserves every already valid calmness estimate, although enlarging a localization need not preserve it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mappings with the same localized graph have identical calmness behavior and exact local modulus; enlarging the localization may destroy an estimate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local error bound for the inclusion \(\bar y\in F(x)\) at \(\bar x\) is the existence of a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq 0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)\qquad(x\in U).\] This inequality is exactly metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). children.title: Single-Valued Lipschitz Inverse Localizations
children.top_down_role: The local inverse geometry defining the strong property.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localized inverse is single-valued and Lipschitz, equivalently \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse characterization defining strong metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-valued Lipschitz inverse localization of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) consists of neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a Lipschitz mapping \(s:V\to U\), such that \(s(\bar y)=\bar x\) and \[\operatorname{gph}s=\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\cap(V\times U).\] Thus, for every \(y\in V\), the inclusion \(y\in F(x)\) has exactly one solution \(x\in U\), namely \(x=s(y)\). Existence of such a localization is strong metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity means that every nearby right-hand side has one nearby solution and this localized solution depends Lipschitz continuously on that right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Lipschitz Inverse Localizations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Strong Metric-Regularity Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best Lipschitz modulus attached to the single-valued inverse-localization characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), define \[\operatorname{reg}_{\mathrm s}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\inf\{\kappa:\text{some inverse localization }s\text{ through }(\bar y,\bar x)\text{ satisfies }\|s(y_1)-s(y_2)\|\leq\kappa\|y_1-y_2\|\text{ locally}\}.\] Equivalently, it is the infimum of the local Lipschitz constants of all single-valued inverse localizations through the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact strong metric-regularity modulus is the best local Lipschitz constant of an inverse localization through the reference point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}_{\mathrm s}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is the infimum of the local Lipschitz constants of inverse branches through \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Strong Metric-Regularity Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Valued Lipschitz Invertibility via the Strict Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonsmooth inverse-function criterion with exact Lipschitz modulus and semiderivative consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let O\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open, F:O\to\mathbb{R}^n continuous, \bar x\in O, and \bar u=F(\bar x). Then F^{-1} has a Lipschitz continuous single-valued localization at \bar u for \bar x if and only if
D_*F(\bar x)(w)=0\Rightarrow w=0.
In that case,
D^*F(\bar x)(y)=0\Rightarrow y=0,
\qquad \operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar u\mid\bar x)=|D_*F(\bar x)^{-1}|^+=|D^*F(\bar x)^{-1}|^+.
If F is semidifferentiable at \bar x, the localized inverse is semidifferentiable at \bar u, with single-valued Lipschitz derivative DF(\bar x)^{-1}. If F is strictly differentiable at \bar x, these nonsingularity conditions are equivalent to \nabla F(\bar x) being nonsingular, and the localized inverse is strictly differentiable with
\nabla F^{-1}(\bar u)=\nabla F(\bar x)^{-1},\qquad \operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar u\mid\bar x)=|\nabla F(\bar x)^{-1}|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous square mapping has a locally single-valued Lipschitz inverse exactly when its strict derivative has trivial kernel. The inverse modulus is determined by the inverse strict derivative or coderivative. Semidifferentiability passes to the inverse; in the strictly differentiable case this reduces to the classical nonsingular-Jacobian inverse theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{-1}\text{ has a Lipschitz continuous single-valued localization at }(\bar u,\bar x)\iff \ker D_*F(\bar x)=\{0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Inverse Function Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz invertibility under maximal rank of the Clarke generalized Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x_0\). If every \(M\in\partial F(x_0)\) is nonsingular, then there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(x_0\) and \(V\) of \(F(x_0)\), and a Lipschitz mapping \(G:V\to\mathbb{R}^n\), such that \(G(F(u))=u\) for every \(u\in U\) and \(F(G(v))=v\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz square mapping, nonsingularity of every matrix in the generalized Jacobian at the base point guarantees a Lipschitz local inverse satisfying both inverse identities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists U\ni x_0,\;\exists V\ni F(x_0),\;\exists G:V\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ Lipschitz}: (\forall u\in U)\,G(F(u))=u\ \land\ (\forall v\in V)\,F(G(v))=v.\)

children.title: Perturbation Stability of Strong Metric Regularity
children.top_down_role: Persistence of strong inverse behavior under controlled perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with inverse-localization Lipschitz constant \(\kappa\).
\(g:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), with local constant \(\ell\), and \(\kappa\ell<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\), with inverse-localization constant at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\ell)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the original inverse localization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After restricting the neighborhoods so that the stated Lipschitz bounds hold, the perturbed mapping \(H:=F+g\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\). Its local inverse is single-valued, and for nearby \(z_1,z_2\) it satisfies \[\lVert H^{-1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(z_1)-H^{-1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(z_2)\rVert\leq\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\ell}\lVert z_1-z_2\rVert.\] Hence every additive perturbation whose local Lipschitz constant is strictly smaller than \(1/\kappa\) preserves strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity survives a sufficiently small Lipschitz additive perturbation, with inverse Lipschitz constant bounded by the standard contraction denominator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Small-Gain Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform sharpness of the strict perturbation bound for additive Lipschitz perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=x\), and \(g(x)=-x\). Then \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\) with inverse modulus \(\kappa=1\), while \(g\) has Lipschitz constant \(\ell=1\). Thus \(\kappa\ell=1\), but \((F+g)(x)=0\) has no single-valued inverse localization at \((0,0)\). Hence the strict condition \(\kappa\ell<1\) cannot uniformly be replaced by \(\kappa\ell\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the threshold κℓ=1, cancellation can destroy strong metric regularity, so the strict small-gain condition is uniformly sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically regular with \(\kappa=1\), whereas \(F+g\) is not strongly metrically regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Small-Gain Threshold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Regularity Characterization under Cone Reducibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constraint-space characterization for a set locally reducible to a pointed closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x_0 be a locally optimal solution and \lambda_0 a corresponding Lagrange multiplier. Suppose Y is finite-dimensional and K is C^2-reducible at G(x_0) to a pointed closed convex cone \mathcal C\subset Z. Then (x_0,\lambda_0) is a strongly regular solution of the associated generalized equation if and only if x_0 is nondegenerate and the uniform second-order growth condition holds at x_0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the constraint space is finite-dimensional and the feasible set is twice-smoothly reducible to a pointed closed convex cone, the KKT generalized equation is strongly regular exactly when the solution is nondegenerate and satisfies uniform second-order growth.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_0,\lambda_0)\text{ is strongly regular}\iff\bigl(x_0\text{ is nondegenerate and }\operatorname{USOG}(x_0)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of Local Lipschitz Homeomorphisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization using local Lipschitz continuity and a uniform lower Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(x\in\mathcal O\), and \(\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^n\). Then \(\Phi\) is a locally Lipschitz homeomorphism at \(x\) if and only if \(\Phi\) is locally Lipschitz continuous at \(x\) and there exist an open neighborhood \(\mathcal N\) of \(x\) and \(c>0\) such that \(\|\Phi(y)-\Phi(z)\|\ge c\|y-z\|\) for all \(y,z\in\mathcal N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mapping is a locally Lipschitz homeomorphism at the point exactly when it is locally Lipschitz there and uniformly expands no nearby pair by less than a fixed positive multiple of its original distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ is a locally Lipschitz homeomorphism at }x\iff\left[\Phi\text{ is locally Lipschitz at }x\ \land\ \exists\mathcal N\ni x\text{ open},\ \exists c>0,\ \forall y,z\in\mathcal N:\ \|\Phi(y)-\Phi(z)\|\ge c\|y-z\|\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Fréchet Inverse-Function Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between Jacobian nonsingularity and local Lipschitz invertibility under strong Fréchet differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(x\in\mathcal O\), and let \(\Phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^n\) be strongly Fréchet differentiable at \(x\). There are neighborhoods \(V_0\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U_0\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\ell\geq0\) with \(\kappa\ell<1\), such that \(\lVert[f(p,x_1)-f(\bar p,x_1)]-[f(p,x_2)-f(\bar p,x_2)]\rVert\leq\ell\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\) for all \(p\in V_0\) and \(x_1,x_2\in U_0\).
\(f(p,\bar x)\to f(\bar p,\bar x)\) as \(p\to\bar p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) by \[S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\}.\] Then there are neighborhoods \(V\subset V_0\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\subset U_0\) of \(\bar x\), and a unique mapping \(s:V\to U\), such that \[S(p)\cap U=\{s(p)\}\qquad(p\in V),\qquad s(\bar p)=\bar x.\] Thus \(s\) is a single-valued implicit solution localization, and \(\operatorname{gph}s=\operatorname{gph}S\cap(V\times U)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity of the reference generalized equation, together with a sufficiently small uniform state perturbation and continuity at the reference state, yields one localized solution for every nearby parameter.
