children.title: Lipschitz Implicit Functions
children.top_down_role: Lipschitz implicit mappings arising from stable inverse localizations.

assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(f:P\times X\to Y\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\(0\in f(\bar p,\bar x)+F(\bar x)\), and \(R(x):=f(\bar p,x)+F(x)\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,0)\) with an inverse-localization Lipschitz constant \(\kappa\).

There are neighborhoods \(V_0\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U_0\) of \(\bar x\), and constants \(L_p,\ell\geq0\) with \(\kappa\ell<1\), such that \(\lVert f(p,x)-f(q,x)\rVert\leq L_p\lVert p-q\rVert\) for all \(p,q\in V_0\) and \(x\in U_0\), and \(\lVert[f(p,x_1)-f(\bar p,x_1)]-[f(p,x_2)-f(\bar p,x_2)]\rVert\leq\ell\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\) for all \(p\in V_0\) and \(x_1,x_2\in U_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implicit solution localization \(s\) is Lipschitz with local constant at most \(\kappa L_p/(1-\kappa\ell)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke implicit function theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, local uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuity of an implicit solution branch under partial generalized-Jacobian nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be open, let \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally Lipschitz, and suppose \((x_0,y_0)\in X\times Y\) satisfies \(F(x_0,y_0)=0\). If every matrix in \(\pi_2\partial_{\mathrm{Cl}}F(x_0,y_0)\) is nonsingular, then there exist \(\eta,\delta>0\) such that, for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(x_0)\), the equation \(F(x,y)=0\) has a unique solution \(y=\widetilde y(x)\) in \(\mathcal B_\delta(y_0)\), and the mapping \(\widetilde y\) is Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally Lipschitz equation F(x,y)=0, if all generalized-Jacobian matrices associated with the y variables are nonsingular at a zero (x₀,y₀), then nearby x values admit a unique nearby solution ỹ(x), and this implicit solution mapping is Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\eta,\delta>0\ \exists\widetilde y:\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(x_0)\to\mathcal B_\delta(y_0):\quad \forall x\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal B_\eta(x_0),\ \{y\in\mathcal B_\delta(y_0):F(x,y)=0\}=\{\widetilde y(x)\},\quad \widetilde y\text{ is Lipschitz}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability of a Lipschitz Homeomorphism Under a Small Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative invertibility and image-coverage result for a Lipschitz perturbation of a Lipschitz homeomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A,A':U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n. Suppose A is a Lipschitz homeomorphism, A-A' is Lipschitz on U, and the Lipschitz moduli of A^{-1} and A-A' are L>0 and L'>0, respectively. If d^*\in U and \delta>0 satisfy \[\operatorname{cl}B(d^*,\delta)\subseteq U,\qquad \operatorname{cl}B(A(d^*),\delta/L)\subseteq A(U),\qquad LL'<1,\] then A' is a Lipschitz homeomorphism from U onto A'(U), its inverse has Lipschitz modulus at most \[\frac{L}{1-LL'},\] and \[B\!\left(A'(d^*),\frac{(1-LL')\delta}{L}\right)\subseteq A'(U).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz homeomorphism remains a Lipschitz homeomorphism after a perturbation whose Lipschitz modulus is smaller than the reciprocal inverse modulus. The theorem gives an explicit inverse modulus and a ball contained in the perturbed image.

A-A'\text{ is Lipschitz on }U\text{ with modulus }L'>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Implicit-Solution Existence Under a Uniform Determinant Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded theorem; the extract does not define the matrix family \(\mathfrak B(x_0,y_0)\) or neighborhood notation \(S_{1\delta}(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\lvert\det C\rvert\geq\alpha_0>0\) for every \(C\in\mathfrak B(x_0,y_0)\), then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(\delta>0\) and a function \(y_\varepsilon:S_{1\delta}(x_0)\to\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\|y_\varepsilon(x)-y_0\|\leq\varepsilon\) and \(f(x,y_\varepsilon(x))=0_n\) for every \(x\in S_{1\delta}(x_0)\subset\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Continuous Directional Implicit Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional implicit-function theorem using upper semicontinuity and uniform nonsingularity of the matrix family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each $f_i(x,y)$ is Lipschitz in $y$, $\mathfrak{B}(\alpha,q)$ is upper semicontinuous at $(0,q_0)$, and there is $\beta>0$ such that $|\det A|\geq\beta$ for every $A\in\mathfrak{B}(0,q_0)$. Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist $\alpha_0>0$ and a unique continuous function $q:[0,\alpha_0]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ such that, for every $\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0]$, $\|q(\alpha)-q_0\|\leq\varepsilon$ and $f(x_0+\alpha g,y_0+\alpha q(\alpha))=0_n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the components of f are Lipschitz in y, the matrix-family mapping is upper semicontinuous at (0,q0), and all matrices in B(0,q0) are uniformly nonsingular, then for every tolerance there is a short interval carrying a unique continuous correction q(alpha), uniformly close to q0, that solves the directional implicit equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\alpha_0>0\ \exists!q\in C([0,\alpha_0];\mathbb{R}^n)\ \forall\alpha\in[0,\alpha_0],\quad \|q(\alpha)-q_0\|\leq\varepsilon,\quad f(x_0+\alpha g,y_0+\alpha q(\alpha))=0_n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsingular Uniform Newton Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary and strong uniform Newton approximations for a square mapping on an open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, where $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open. A nonsingular uniform Newton approximation consists of $\varepsilon,L>0$, a function $\Delta:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $\Delta(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and, for every $x\in\Omega$, a family $\mathcal A(x)$ of maps $A(x,\cdot):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that: (i) $A(x,0)=0$; (ii) for all distinct $x,x'\in\Omega$ and all $A(x,\cdot)\in\mathcal A(x)$, $\|G(x)+A(x,x'-x)-G(x')\|/\|x-x'\|\leq\Delta(\|x-x'\|)$; and (iii) each $A(x,\cdot)$ restricts to a Lipschitz homeomorphism $U_x\to V_x$, where $U_x,V_x$ are open and contain $\mathbb B(0,\varepsilon)$, and the restricted inverse has Lipschitz modulus at most $L$. It is strong if (ii) is replaced by the existence of $L'>0$ such that $\|G(x)+A(x,x'-x)-G(x')\|/\|x-x'\|^2\leq L'$ for all such $x,x'$ and $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular uniform Newton approximation uniformly combines a vanishing first-order model error with local homeomorphic Newton models whose inverses have a common Lipschitz bound. It is strong when the model error is uniformly quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a nonsingular uniform Newton approximation; under the quadratic error bound it has a nonsingular uniform strong Newton approximation.}

children.title: Isolated Calmness
children.top_down_role: The inverse-mapping counterpart of strong metric subregularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}\) has the isolated calmness property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-mapping formulation equivalent to strong metric subregularity.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse mapping \(F^{-1}\) is isolated calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\geq0\), such that \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U\subset\bar x+\kappa\lVert y-\bar y\rVert\mathbb B_X\qquad(y\in V).\] Taking \(y=\bar y\) gives \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\cap U=\{\bar x\}\), so the reference solution is locally isolated. This property is equivalent to strong metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby inverse images cluster linearly around one isolated reference solution; equivalently, the original mapping is strongly metrically subregular.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Calmness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality of Isolated-Calmness and Strong-Subregularity Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quantitative inverse equivalence at the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the same local metric conventions, the exact isolated-calmness modulus of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) equals the exact strong metric-subregularity modulus of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\): \[\operatorname{clm}_{\mathrm{iso}}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\operatorname{subreg}_{\mathrm s}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolated calmness of the inverse and strong metric subregularity of the original mapping have the same best local modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces with the same distance conventions in both properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clm}_{\mathrm{iso}}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\operatorname{subreg}_{\mathrm s}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolated Calmness Does Not Ensure Nearby Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between control of existing nearby values and their existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(S(y)=\varnothing\) for \(y\neq0\). Then \(S\) is isolated calm at \((0,0)\), with modulus zero, but has no value at any nonzero nearby \(y\). Thus isolated calmness controls existing localized values but does not ensure nearby nonemptiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isolated calmness may hold while every nonreference nearby parameter has no solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is isolated calm at \((0,0)\) but is not locally nonempty around \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Calmness Does Not Ensure Nearby Solvability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Growth Form of the Isolated Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent positive-growth representation of the point-centered residual inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\). For \(\kappa>0\), the local isolated error bound \[\|x-\bar x\|\leq\kappa r(x)\] is equivalent to \[r(x)\geq\kappa^{-1}\|x-\bar x\|.\] Consequently, the best positive local residual-growth rate is the reciprocal of the exact strong metric-subregularity modulus, with the usual extended-real reciprocal conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity is equivalently linear positive growth of the residual away from the isolated reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-\bar x\|\leq\kappa r(x)\) locally if and only if \(r(x)\geq\kappa^{-1}\|x-\bar x\|\) locally.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Growth Form of the Isolated Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Strong metric subregularity means that, on some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(d(x,\bar x)\leq\kappa\,\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\) for every \(x\in U\). If \(\|g(x)-g(\bar x)\|\leq\lambda d(x,\bar x)\) locally and \(\kappa\lambda<1\), then, after possibly shrinking \(U\),
\[
d(x,\bar x)\leq \frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y+g(\bar x),(F+g)(x)\bigr)\qquad(x\in U).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently small Lipschitz perturbation preserves strong metric subregularity, with the modulus enlarged by the factor determined by the perturbation size.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Subregularity Perturbations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Strictness of the Perturbation Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar cancellation at the boundary of the additive Lipschitz perturbation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=\{x\}\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)=(0,0)\), and let \(g(x)=-x\). Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular with exact modulus \(1\), while \(\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\). Nevertheless, \((F+g)(x)=\{0\}\) for every \(x\), so \(F+g\) is not strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equality in the perturbation-size bound, cancellation can destroy strong metric subregularity, so the strict inequality is sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{subreg}F(0\mid0)=1\), \(\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\), but \(F+g\) is not strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Exact strong metric subregularity modulus at the reference graph point.

children.title: Strong Metric q-Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Hölder-type strong subregularity variants.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Hölder error bound defines strong metric \(q\)-subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to infinity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention with residual raised to the power \(q\); reciprocal-exponent conventions also occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically \(q\)-subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d_X(x,\bar x)\leq \kappa\bigl[\operatorname{dist}_Y(\bar y,F(x))\bigr]^q\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
This inequality implies that \(\bar x\) is an isolated point of \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric q-subregularity is a Hölder residual bound that controls distance to the isolated reference solution by the qth power of the residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Metric q-Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent under the explicitly stated residual-to-the-power-q convention, and the isolation conclusion follows from it. However, conventions for strong metric q-subregularity vary, and no source is supplied to establish that this convention is intended for the terminal container.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric regularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) requires neighborhoods \(U,V\) and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\qquad((x,y)\in U\times V).
\]
Fixing \(y=\bar y\) yields metric subregularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). The converse fails: for \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=|x|\), the reference-value inequality at \((0,0)\) holds with modulus \(1\), whereas metric regularity fails because nearby negative targets have empty inverse images.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform control for all nearby targets implies the fixed-target error bound. The absolute-value mapping shows that fixed-target regularity does not imply full metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Full Versus Reference-Value Regularity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to the Aubin property of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\), which permits several nearby inverse values. Strong metric regularity additionally requires neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that
\[
s(y):=F^{-1}(y)\cap U
\]
is a singleton for every \(y\in V\), and the resulting function \(s:V\to U\) is Lipschitz. Thus Lipschitz-like set-valued behavior alone does not produce a unique local solution branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inverse may vary Lipschitzly while retaining several values. Strong metric regularity requires those localized inverse values to form one Lipschitz solution branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Versus Single-Valued Inverse Behavior

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse characterization for strictly differentiable mappings in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:X	o Y$ be strictly differentiable at $ ar x$, and let $ ar y=f( ar x)$. Then $f^{-1}$ is locally single-valued around $ ar y$ and strictly differentiable at $ ar y$ if and only if $
abla f( ar x)$ is invertible. In this case, $$
abla f^{-1}( ar y)=
abla f( ar x)^{-1},\qquad \operatorname{lip}f^{-1}( ar y)=\left\| ig(
abla f( ar x)^* ig)^{-1}ight\|,$$ $$\operatorname{reg}f^{-1}( ar y)=\|
abla f( ar x)^*\|,$$ and $$\operatorname{cov}f^{-1}( ar y)=\inf_{\|x^*\|=1}\|
abla f^{-1}( ar y)^*x^*\|.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly differentiable mapping has a locally single-valued, strictly differentiable inverse exactly when its derivative is invertible. The inverse derivative and the stated Lipschitz, regularity, and covering moduli then admit exact adjoint formulas.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{-1}\text{ is locally single-valued around }\bar y\text{ and strictly differentiable at }\bar y\iff \nabla f(\bar x)\text{ is invertible, with the stated derivative and modulus formulas}

assumptions_latex: All mappings below are considered at the reference pair \((0,0)\) in \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric subregularity, strong metric subregularity, metric regularity, and strong metric regularity are genuinely distinct notions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F_0\) is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\), since \(F_0^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\), but it is not strongly subregular because the reference solution is not isolated. The mapping \(F_1\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\), since \(|x|=\operatorname{dist}(0,F_1(x))\), but it is not metrically regular because negative nearby targets have no preimages. The mapping \(F_2\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\), but it is not strongly metrically regular because \(F_2^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\) for \(y\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant, absolute-value, and two-branch mappings respectively separate subregularity from isolation, strong subregularity from full regularity, and metric regularity from a unique inverse branch.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full and Strong Reference-Value Regularity Do Not Ensure a Unique Branch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict failure of strong metric regularity despite simultaneous metric regularity and strong metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the seed mapping \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=\{x,-x\}\), one also has \(F^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\) and \[|x|=\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x)),\] so \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(1\). Together with the seed's metric regularity calculation, this shows that \(F\) is both metrically regular and strongly metrically subregular. Nevertheless, \(F^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\) for every \(y\ne0\), so no inverse localization through \((0,0)\) is single-valued on a neighborhood of \(0\); hence \(F\) is not strongly metrically regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The seed's two-branch mapping is both metrically regular and strongly metrically subregular but is not strongly metrically regular, so the two former properties together do not ensure a unique inverse branch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is metrically regular and strongly metrically subregular at }(0,0)\text{, but not strongly metrically regular there.}

notation.meaning: the two-valued inverse for nonzero right-hand sides

knowledge_statements.title: Full and Strong Reference-Value Regularity Do Not Ensure a Unique Branch

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Regularity Without Strong Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation of full metric regularity from reference-solution isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(P(u,v)=u\), with reference pair \(((0,0),0)\). For every \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(y\in\mathbb R\), \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl((u,v),P^{-1}(y)\bigr)=|u-y|=\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,P(u,v)\bigr),\] so \(P\) is metrically regular with modulus \(1\). It is not strongly metrically subregular at the reference pair because \(P^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\) is not locally reduced to \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate projection is metrically regular but has a nonisolated reference fiber, so metric regularity need not imply strong metric subregularity.
assumptions_latex: \(P:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is the coordinate projection \(P(u,v)=u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is metrically regular at }((0,0),0)\text{ but is not strongly metrically subregular there.}
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity Without Strong Subregularity

children.title: Generalized-Equation Linearizations
children.top_down_role: Local generalized-equation models used in strong-regularity analysis.

children.title: Partial Linearization
children.top_down_role: Linearization of the single-valued component with the set-valued component retained.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial linearization is the generalized equation \(y\in f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of the single-valued component at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only the smooth single-valued component is linearized; the multifunction is retained exactly.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the generalized equation \(y\in f(x)+F(x)\), its partial linearization at \(\bar x\) is the set-valued mapping
\[
L_{\bar x}(x):=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x).
\]
For a target \(y\) near \(\bar y\), the associated partially linearized generalized equation is \(y\in L_{\bar x}(x)\). This construction replaces the increment of \(f\) by its first-order linear approximation while leaving the dependence of \(F(x)\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial linearization replaces the smooth term by its affine first-order model while keeping the set-valued term unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Linearization

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Accuracy of Partial Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation property obtained by linearizing only the smooth component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x):=f(x)+F(x)\) and
\[
L_{\bar x}(x):=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x).
\]
If \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\), then
\[
G(x)=L_{\bar x}(x)+r(x),\qquad r(x):=f(x)-f(\bar x)-Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x),
\]
where
\[
\frac{\|r(x)\|}{\|x-\bar x\|}\to0\quad\text{as }x\to\bar x.
\]
The equality denotes translation of every value of \(L_{\bar x}(x)\) by \(r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonlinear generalized-equation mapping differs from its partial linearization only by the little-o remainder of the smooth component.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+F(x)=L_{\bar x}(x)+o(\|x-\bar x\|)\) through a single-valued translation remainder.

notation.meaning: First-order Taylor remainder of the smooth component.
Partial linearization at the reference state.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Accuracy of Partial Linearization

children.title: Affine Variational Linearization
children.top_down_role: Affine generalized equations serving as local variational models.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded linear, \(a\in Y\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine variational model is the generalized equation \(y\in a+Ax+F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Bounded linear part of the affine model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine generalized equations used as local first-order variational models.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine variational generalized equation has the form
\[
y\in M(x):=a+Ax+F(x).
\]
If it models \(y\in f(x)+F(x)\) around \(\bar x\), then one takes \(A=Df(\bar x)\) and \(a=f(\bar x)-Df(\bar x)\bar x\), giving
\[
M(x)=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x).
\]
Thus the affine variational equation is precisely the partial first-order model of the smooth component together with the original multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine variational model combines a bounded affine map with the original multifunction; derivative data produce the usual partial linearization.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Variational Linearization

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

children.title: Graphical-Derivative Linearization
children.top_down_role: Set-valued linearization based on tangent geometry of a graph.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graphical-derivative linearization of \(y\in F(x)\) is \(v\in DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u)\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to the graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order set-valued model obtained directly from tangent geometry of the graph.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The graphical derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the positively homogeneous multifunction defined by
\[
DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u):=\{v\in Y:(u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Consequently, the tangent or graphical-derivative linearization of the inclusion \(y\in F(x)\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
v\in DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u),
\]
where \(u\) and \(v\) represent first-order increments of \(x\) and \(y\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent cone to the graph defines a positively homogeneous multifunction relating first-order input and output increments.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Linearization

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical Linearization of a Smooth-Plus-Set-Valued Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical graphical-derivative model for a generalized equation with a smooth single-valued component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x):=f(x)+F(x)\), let \(\bar z\in F(\bar x)\), and set \(\bar y=f(\bar x)+\bar z\). If \(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), then
\[
DG(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u)=Df(\bar x)u+DF(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u).
\]
Consequently, at a solution \(0\in f(\bar x)+F(\bar x)\), the graphical-derivative linearization is
\[
0\in Df(\bar x)u+DF(\bar x\mid-f(\bar x))(u).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth-plus-set-valued generalized equation, the graphical linearization adds the smooth derivative to the graphical derivative of the multifunction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(f+F)(\bar x\mid f(\bar x)+\bar z)(u)=Df(\bar x)u+DF(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u)\).

notation.meaning: Reference value selected from the multifunction.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Linearization of a Smooth-Plus-Set-Valued Equation

children.title: Critical-Cone Linearization
children.top_down_role: Linearized variational models organized by critical-cone geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a convex polyhedral set.
\(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), with \(0\in f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graphical linearization is \(0\in Df(\bar x)u+N_K(u)\).

notation.meaning: Critical cone at the reference solution and normal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral normal-cone equations, where the normal graphical derivative reduces to a critical-cone normal.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 The critical cone p. 267
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the polyhedral normal-cone generalized equation \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\), the graphical derivative satisfies
\[
DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u)=N_K(u),
\]
with the convention that \(N_K(u)=\varnothing\) when \(u\notin K\). Hence the graphical-derivative linearization at \(\bar x\) is
\[
0\in Df(\bar x)u+N_K(u).
\]
The cone \(K\) retains exactly those tangent directions orthogonal to the active reference normal \(\bar z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral constraint set, the normal-cone derivative is the normal cone to the critical cone, yielding a critical-cone generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Cone Linearization

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 The critical cone p. 267
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpolyhedral Curvature Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the pure critical-cone normal formula when a smooth convex boundary contributes curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x\|\le1\}\), \(\bar x=(1,0)\), and \(\bar z=\lambda\bar x\) with \(\lambda>0\). Then
\[
K=T_C(\bar x)\cap\bar z^\perp=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
For \(u\in K\),
\[
DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u)=\lambda u+K^\perp,
\qquad N_K(u)=K^\perp.
\]
Thus \(DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u)=N_K(u)\) generally fails outside the polyhedral regime because curvature adds the term \(\lambda u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the Euclidean ball at a boundary point with a positive normal multiplier, the normal-cone derivative contains a curvature term absent from the critical-cone normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the closed Euclidean unit ball in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DN_C(\bar x\mid\bar z)(u)=\lambda u+K^\perp\ne N_K(u)\) for every nonzero \(u\in K\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal complement of the critical cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Curvature Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Critical-Cone Complementarity Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent primal and cone-complementarity forms of the critical-cone linearized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear. With \(K^*:=\{w:\langle w,v\rangle\ge0\ \forall v\in K\}\),
\[
0\in Au+N_K(u)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
u\in K,\qquad \langle Au,v-u\rangle\ge0\quad(\forall v\in K),
\]
and to
\[
u\in K,\qquad Au\in K^*,\qquad \langle Au,u\rangle=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical-cone generalized equation is equivalently a variational inequality on the critical cone or a cone-complementarity system.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in Au+N_K(u)\iff[\,u\in K,\ Au\in K^*,\ \langle Au,u\rangle=0\,]\).

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone of the critical cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Critical-Cone Complementarity Forms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly regular solution of an abstract generalized equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This records only Definition 5.12. Uniqueness is localized to \mathcal V_Z, and solutions of the linearized equation outside \mathcal V_Z are not excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solution z_0 of the abstract generalized equation is strongly regular if there exist neighborhoods \mathcal V_Z\subset Z of z_0 and \mathcal V_W\subset W of 0 such that, for every \delta\in\mathcal V_W, the linearized generalized equation (LE_\delta) has a unique solution \zeta(\delta) in \mathcal V_Z, and the mapping \zeta:\mathcal V_W\to\mathcal V_Z is Lipschitz continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is strongly regular when every sufficiently small perturbation of its linearized generalized equation has exactly one solution in a fixed neighborhood of the reference point and that localized solution varies Lipschitz continuously with the perturbation. Other solutions outside the neighborhood are allowed.
assumptions_latex: z_0\in Z\text{ is a solution of the abstract generalized equation}
\mathcal V_Z\text{ is a neighborhood of }z_0\text{ in }Z
\mathcal V_W\text{ is a neighborhood of }0\text{ in }W
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\delta\in\mathcal V_W,\ \exists!\,\zeta(\delta)\in\mathcal V_Z\text{ solving }(LE_\delta),\qquad \zeta:\mathcal V_W\to\mathcal V_Z\text{ is Lipschitz continuous}.

children.title: Strong Regularity of Linearized Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: The linearized inverse property underlying Robinson strong regularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Valued Linear Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong regularity specialized to a bounded linear equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\to Y\) be a bounded linear operator between Banach spaces. The equation
\[
y=Ax
\]
has a single-valued Lipschitz solution map on neighborhoods of \(0\in Y\) and \(0\in X\) if and only if \(A\) is a Banach-space isomorphism. In that case the localization is \(x=A^{-1}y\), and its exact Lipschitz modulus is \(\|A^{-1}\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded linear equation, strong regularity is exactly bounded invertibility of the operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear equation has the strong localized inverse property if and only if \(A\) is bijective, with modulus \(\|A^{-1}\|\).

notation.meaning: Bounded inverse of the linearized operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Linear Specialization

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong regularity holds exactly when the inverse of the partial linearization has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Partial linearization at the reference point.
Localized solution map of the linearized equation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson strong regularity formulated through the inverse of the partially linearized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generalized equation \(\bar y\in f(\bar x)+F(\bar x)\) is strongly regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that, for every \(y\in V\),
\[
y\in f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x),\qquad x\in U,
\]
has exactly one solution \(x=s_L(y)\), and the map \(s_L:V\to U\) is Lipschitz. Equivalently, \(L_{\bar x}^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robinson strong regularity requires the partially linearized generalized equation to possess a unique local solution depending Lipschitzly on its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Regularity of Linearized Generalized Equations

An exact section, definition, theorem, or page locator is required before accepting the convention and hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional sensitivity through a linearized generalized equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The linearized generalized equations (5.29) and the quadratic form Q_0 are retained as source-defined objects; normalized symbols h_* and \mu_* denote their unique solution in the final clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let u_t=u_0+td+o(t^2). Assume X is reflexive, \mathcal S(u_0)=\{(x_0,\lambda_0)\}, t\mapsto\mathcal S(u_t) is upper Lipschitzian at 0, Q_0 is a Legendre form, K is polyhedric at y_0=G(x_0,u_0), and Robinson's constraint qualification holds for G(\cdot,u_0)\in K at x_0. For any (x_t,\lambda_t)\in\mathcal S(u_t), every weak limit point (h_0,\mu_0) of t^{-1}(x_t-x_0,\lambda_t-\lambda_0) solves (5.29), and h_0 is a strong limit point of t^{-1}(x_t-x_0). If (5.29) has the unique solution (h_*,\mu_*), then x_t=x_0+th_*+o(t), while t^{-1}(\lambda_t-\lambda_0) converges weakly to \mu_*; the primal scaled displacement converges strongly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under reflexivity, isolated reference solvability, upper-Lipschitz stability, Legendre curvature, polyhedricity, and Robinson constraint qualification, weak first-order primal-dual displacement limits solve the linearized generalized equation, with strong convergence for the primal component. A unique linearized solution gives a first-order primal expansion and convergence of the scaled multiplier displacement.
assumptions_latex: t\mapsto\mathcal S(u_t)\text{ is upper Lipschitzian at }0
\text{Robinson's constraint qualification holds for }G(\cdot,u_0)\in K\text{ at }x_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (h_0,\mu_0)\in\operatorname*{w-LimPt}_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}(x_t-x_0,\lambda_t-\lambda_0)\Rightarrow (h_0,\mu_0)\in\operatorname{Sol}(5.29)\text{ and }h_0\in\operatorname*{s-LimPt}_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}(x_t-x_0);\quad \operatorname{Sol}(5.29)=\{(h_*,\mu_*)\}\Rightarrow x_t=x_0+th_*+o(t),\ t^{-1}(\lambda_t-\lambda_0)\rightharpoonup\mu_*.

children.title: Parametric Strong Regularity
children.top_down_role: Strong regularity for generalized equations with parameter-dependent data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Parameter Dependence Cannot Be Dropped
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the Lipschitz conclusion in a parametric strong-regularity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
0=x-|p|^{1/2}
\]
at \((\bar p,\bar x)=(0,0)\). The state linearization is \(u\mapsto u\), hence is strongly regular. For every nearby \(p\), the equation has the unique solution
\[
s(p)=|p|^{1/2},
\]
but \(s\) is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\). Thus strong regularity in the state variable alone does not yield Lipschitz parameter sensitivity when the parameter perturbation is not locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An identity state linearization can be strongly regular while a square-root parameter perturbation produces a non-Lipschitz solution branch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state linearization is strongly regular, but \(s(p)=|p|^{1/2}\) is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Parameter Dependence Cannot Be Dropped

assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(0\in f(\bar p,\bar x)+F(\bar x)\).
\(f\) is continuous near \((\bar p,\bar x)\), continuously Fréchet differentiable in \(x\), and locally Lipschitz in \(p\), uniformly in nearby \(x\).
The linearized equation at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) is strongly regular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parametric generalized equation has a unique local solution map \(s(p)\), and \(s\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space implicit mapping consequence of Robinson strong regularity under Lipschitz parameter dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for every \(p\in Q\), the generalized equation
\[
0\in f(p,x)+F(x),\qquad x\in U,
\]
has a unique solution \(x=s(p)\). Moreover, after shrinking \(Q\) if necessary, there is \(L\geq0\) such that
\[
\|s(p_1)-s(p_2)\|\leq L\|p_1-p_2\|\qquad(p_1,p_2\in Q).
\]
Thus strong regularity of the reference linearization yields a locally unique Lipschitz solution branch for the parameterized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity of the reference linearization yields a unique nearby solution for each nearby parameter, with Lipschitz dependence on that parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Strong Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive Banach-space implicit-mapping theorem, and no source is supplied. The exact uniformity and continuity assumptions needed to derive a unique Lipschitz parameter solution map from strong regularity must be checked against an authoritative theorem before the statement can be accepted.

children.title: Strong Stability of Generalized Equations
children.top_down_role: Strong-stability terminology and its relation to localized solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated convention, strong stability is the existence of a single-valued Lipschitz localization of \(G^{-1}\) at \((0,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Solution mapping of the generalized equation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses strong stability for unique Lipschitz response to right-hand-side perturbations; terminology varies across generalized-equation literature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generalized equation \(0\in G(x)\) is strongly stable at \(\bar x\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that, for every \(y\in V\), the perturbed equation
\[
y\in G(x),\qquad x\in U,
\]
has exactly one solution \(x=s(y)\), and \(s:V\to U\) is Lipschitz. Equivalently, \(G^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((0,\bar x)\). When \(G(x)=f(x)+F(x)\), this describes localized solution behavior; Robinson strong regularity instead tests the corresponding partial linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong stability means that small right-hand-side perturbations admit one nearby solution varying Lipschitzly; strong regularity imposes this inverse property on the linearized equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Stability of Generalized Equations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inverse-localization property is precise, but the term strong stability is not uniform across the generalized-equation literature and may coincide with or differ from strong metric regularity depending on the source. An exact terminology source and locator are necessary to validate this definition and its stated contrast with Robinson strong regularity.

children.title: Basic Robinson Implicit-Function Theorem
children.top_down_role: The foundational strong-regularity implicit-mapping result.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a normed space, \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \(f:P\times X\to Y\).
\(0\in f(\bar p,\bar x)+F(\bar x)\), and \(f\) is strictly Fréchet differentiable with respect to \(x\) at \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
The mapping \(L(x)=f(\bar p,\bar x)+D_xf(\bar p,\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x)\) has a single-valued Lipschitz inverse localization at \((0,\bar x)\).
Near \((\bar p,\bar x)\), the parameter variation of \(f\) is locally Lipschitz in \(p\), uniformly in \(x\), and the state-variable linearization remainder has sufficiently small Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a unique Lipschitz mapping \(s:Q\to U\) such that \(s(\bar p)=\bar x\) and \(S(p)\cap U=\{s(p)\}\) for every \(p\in Q\).

notation.meaning: solution mapping of the generalized equation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson's local theorem for a strongly regular partial linearization in normed parameter and Banach state spaces.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.1.4, Implicit-function theorems, p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(p)=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\}\). Under the stated strong-regularity, differentiability, and uniform parameter-variation hypotheses, there exist neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a unique Lipschitz mapping \(s:Q\to U\) such that \[0\in f(p,s(p))+F(s(p))\quad\text{and}\quad S(p)\cap U=\{s(p)\}\quad\text{for every }p\in Q.\] Moreover, \(s(\bar p)=\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity of the partial linearization, together with the stated uniform differentiability and parameter-Lipschitz hypotheses, yields a unique local Lipschitz solution branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Robinson Implicit-Function Theorem

source_witnesses.locator: Section 1.1.4, Implicit-function theorems, p. 19

children.title: Extended Robinson Perturbation Theorems
children.top_down_role: Extensions accommodating broader nonlinear perturbations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Uniform Small-Gain Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar boundary example for nonlinear additive perturbation theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa>0\), \(M(x)=x/\kappa\), and \(g(x)=-x/\kappa\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(M\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\) with inverse modulus \(\kappa\), while \(\operatorname{lip}g=\kappa^{-1}\) and \((M+g)(x)=0\) for every \(x\). Hence \(M+g\) is not strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\), so a uniform perturbation theorem cannot replace \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g<1\) by \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equality in the small-gain bound, a perturbation can cancel the regular mapping and destroy solvability and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) has inverse modulus \(\kappa\) and \(\operatorname{lip}g=\kappa^{-1}\), but \(M+g\) is not strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: inverse Lipschitz modulus of the unperturbed mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Uniform Small-Gain Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hölder-Parameter Nonlinear Perturbation Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear state perturbation with uniform Hölder parameter dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with localized inverse modulus \(\kappa\). Suppose \(g(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), \[\|g(p,x)-g(p,x')\|\le\eta\|x-x'\|,\qquad \kappa\eta<1,\] uniformly for nearby \(p,x,x'\), and \[\|g(p,x)-g(p',x)\|\le Ld(p,p')^\alpha\] uniformly for nearby \(x\), where \(0<\alpha\le1\). Then the localized solution of \[\bar y\in M(x)+g(p,x)\] is unique and satisfies \[\|s(p)-s(p')\|\le\frac{\kappa L}{1-\kappa\eta}d(p,p')^\alpha.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently small state-dependent perturbation preserves unique solvability, and uniform Hölder parameter dependence transfers to the solution with the contraction-denominator modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is strongly metrically regular with localized inverse modulus \(\kappa\).
The uniform state Lipschitz modulus satisfies \(\kappa\eta<1\).
The parameter Hölder estimate is uniform over nearby states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localized solution is unique and Hölder continuous with modulus at most \(\kappa L/(1-\kappa\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder-Parameter Nonlinear Perturbation Extension

assumptions_latex: \(M:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with inverse modulus \(\kappa\).
\(g:P\times X\to Y\), \(g(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), is locally Lipschitz in \(p\) with modulus \(L_p\).
Uniformly near \(\bar p\), \(g(p,\cdot)\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with modulus \(\eta<\kappa^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local solution \(s(p)\) of \(\bar y\in M(x)+g(p,x)\) is single-valued and satisfies \(\operatorname{lip}s\le \kappa L_p/(1-\kappa\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A contraction-type extension allowing nonlinear state-dependent perturbations.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Implicit-function theorems p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all \(p\) sufficiently near \(\bar p\), the perturbed inclusion \[\bar y\in M(x)+g(p,x)\] has exactly one solution \(x=s(p)\) near \(\bar x\). Moreover, \(s(\bar p)=\bar x\), the mapping \(s\) is locally Lipschitz, and its Lipschitz modulus may be bounded by \[\operatorname{lip}s\leq \frac{\kappa L_p}{1-\kappa\eta}.\] The strict inequality \(\kappa\eta<1\) is the small-perturbation condition ensuring contraction of the localized inverse equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity survives a nonlinear state perturbation whose Lipschitz modulus is smaller than the reciprocal regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Robinson Perturbation Theorems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Implicit-function theorems p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the perturbation-theorem container, and the contraction denominator is plausible. The supplied locator does not presently confirm this exact nonlinear perturbation variant or its modulus bound, while the assumption on Lipschitz dependence in p does not clearly state uniformity in x. Source confirmation is needed before choosing a reliable mathematical version.

children.title: Ample-Parameter Robustness Regime
children.top_down_role: Implicit-mapping results under sufficiently rich parameterizations.

children.title: Ample Parameter Families
children.top_down_role: Parameter families sufficiently rich for strong implicit-mapping conclusions.

assumptions_latex: \(P,Y\) are finite-dimensional spaces and \(q:P\to Y\) is differentiable at \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is ample at \(\bar p\) exactly when \(Dq(\bar p)P=Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth surjectivity sense of an ample perturbation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a generalized equation perturbed through \(q(p)\), the parameter family is called ample at \(\bar p\) when its first-order perturbation directions fill the ambient perturbation space: \[Dq(\bar p)P=Y.\] Equivalently, \(Dq(\bar p):P\to Y\) is surjective. Thus every sufficiently small first-order right-hand-side direction in \(Y\) is generated by some parameter direction in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth parameter family is ample when its derivative generates every ambient perturbation direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Ample Parameter Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, and derivative surjectivity is a coherent finite-dimensional ampleness condition. Because 'ample' varies across frameworks and no authoritative definition is cited, the claimed equivalence cannot be accepted without a source.

children.title: Robust Implicit Localizations
children.top_down_role: Persistence of implicit solution localizations across admissible perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(M:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
\(q:P\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar p\), with \(q(\bar p)=\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique Lipschitz localization \(s(p)\in M^{-1}(q(p))\) near \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization obtained by composing a regular inverse with a parameter perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(\bar p\), \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that, whenever \(p\in Q\) and \(q(p)\in V\), \[M^{-1}(q(p))\cap U=\{s(p)\}.\] The mapping \(s:Q\to U\) is Lipschitz and satisfies \[\|s(p_1)-s(p_2)\|\leq \kappa\|q(p_1)-q(p_2)\|.\] Hence the implicit localization persists uniformly over every sufficiently small parameter family, whether or not that family is ample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a strongly regular inverse localization with a Lipschitz parameter perturbation produces a unique Lipschitz solution localization.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Implicit Localizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the localization leaf, and the composition claim is mathematically standard under strong metric regularity. No source is supplied for the localization statement or its modulus estimate, so the nontrivial theorem remains unsupported.

children.title: Restricted-Parameter Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of parametric conclusions when perturbation families lack sufficient richness.

assumptions_latex: The admissible perturbations are restricted to \(q(p)=(p,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricted implicit uniqueness holds, but \(M\) is not strongly metrically regular at \((0,(0,0))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted perturbations cannot test regularity in missing ambient directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p\) near \(0\), the restricted equation \[q(p)\in M(x)\] has the unique solution \(x=p\), and this solution depends Lipschitzly on \(p\). Nevertheless, every neighborhood of \((0,0)\) in \(\mathbb R^2\) contains points \((y_1,y_2)\) with \(y_2\neq0\), for which \(M^{-1}(y_1,y_2)=\varnothing\). Thus no inverse localization defined as a single-valued solution on an ambient neighborhood exists; restricted-family robustness does not imply strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique Lipschitz solutions along a lower-dimensional parameter family do not establish regularity against all ambient perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Parameter Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is well matched to the leaf, and the example correctly separates restricted-family solvability from ambient strong metric regularity. The record nevertheless supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence contract.

children.title: Banach-Space Strong-Regularity Theorems
children.top_down_role: Strong-regularity implicit-mapping principles in Banach spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \(f:P\times X\to Y\).
\(f\) is strictly Fréchet differentiable in \(x\) at \((\bar p,\bar x)\), and \(0\in f(\bar p,\bar x)+F(\bar x)\).
The affine partial linearization is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized equation admits a unique local Lipschitz solution mapping \(p\mapsto s(p)\) near \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space form using strict Fréchet differentiability and localized inverse regularity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the parameter variation \(p\mapsto f(p,x)\) is locally Lipschitz uniformly for \(x\) near \(\bar x\), then there are neighborhoods \(Q\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(s:Q\to U\) satisfying \[0\in f(p,s(p))+F(s(p)),\qquad \{x\in U:0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\}=\{s(p)\}.\] Completeness of the Banach spaces supports the contraction argument implicit in the localized inverse construction.

children.title: Mapping-Level Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between strong regularity and strong metric regularity of associated mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mapping-Level Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for a fixed affine partial linearization, not an automatic assertion about the nonlinear mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[L(x)=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x),\qquad \bar y\in L(\bar x).\] The generalized equation is strongly regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) precisely when \(L^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization through \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Equivalently, \(L\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity of a generalized equation is strong metric regularity of its fixed affine partial linearization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong regularity is equivalent to strong metric regularity of \(L\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Mapping-Level Correspondence

children.title: Dependence on Linearization
children.top_down_role: Dependence of strong regularity on the chosen generalized-equation model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure for a Noncanonical Linear Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing dependence on arbitrary derivative approximations, rather than on admissible exact smooth redistributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar equation \(M(x)=x\) at \((0,0)\), the affine model \(L_B(x)=Bx\) is strongly metrically regular exactly when \(B\ne0\). Thus the exact derivative model \(B=1\) is strongly metrically regular, whereas the singular surrogate \(B=0\) is not. Strong regularity can therefore change when the selected linear model is changed without preserving the derivative of the underlying mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the exact derivative of the identity equation by the zero linear model destroys strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_B\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\) if and only if \(B\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure for a Noncanonical Linear Model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance Under Smooth Redistribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decompositions of the same generalized mapping whose smooth parts differ by a strictly differentiable term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(M=f_1+F_1=f_2+F_2\) near \(\bar x\), where \(f_1,f_2\) are strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), and put \(h=f_2-f_1\). Their partial linearizations satisfy \[L_2(x)=L_1(x)+h(\bar x)+Dh(\bar x)(x-\bar x)-h(x).\] The added term is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative zero. Hence strong metric regularity of \(L_1\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) holds if and only if strong metric regularity of \(L_2\) does. Thus admissible smooth redistribution within one exact mapping does not change strong regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity is invariant when a strictly differentiable term is redistributed between the smooth and set-valued parts of the same exact generalized mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_1\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(L_2\) is.

notation.meaning: term redistributed between the two decompositions

knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Under Smooth Redistribution

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong regularity is determined by \(x\mapsto f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x)\), so changing the decomposition or derivative can change the predicate.

notation.meaning: affine linearization associated with a chosen decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong regularity is attached to a specified generalized-equation linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the representation \(M=f+F\), strong regularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the strong metric regularity of \[L_{f,F}(x)=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x).\] Consequently, the phrase does not describe the graph of \(M\) alone unless hypotheses guarantee equivalence with strong metric regularity of \(M\). Two decompositions \(M=f_1+F_1=f_2+F_2\) need not yield the same strong-regularity test when their admissible linearizations differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity depends on the selected smooth-plus-set-valued model and its affine linearization.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependence on Linearization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the leaf. The stronger assertion that different decompositions can produce different strong-regularity tests is plausible but nontrivial and needs an authoritative source or a sourced counterexample; none is supplied.

children.title: Generalized-Equation Usage
children.top_down_role: Terminological conventions specific to generalized equations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \(\bar y\in f(\bar x)+F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Generalized-equation strong regularity means that the affine linearized inclusion has a single-valued Lipschitz solution localization.

notation.meaning: localized solution of the linearized inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson-style usage for a smooth-plus-set-valued generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generalized equation \(y\in f(x)+F(x)\) is strongly regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(\ell:V\to U\) such that \[\{x\in U:y\in L(x)\}=\{\ell(y)\}\quad\text{for every }y\in V.\] Thus the terminology refers to solvability of the affine linearized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In generalized-equation usage, strong regularity is unique Lipschitz solvability of the affine linearized inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Equation Usage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and statement match generalized-equation usage, with variables and quantifiers adequately specified. The terminology is framework-dependent and no definition-level citation is provided.

children.title: Variational-Inequality Usage
children.top_down_role: Terminological conventions specific to variational inequalities.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:H\to H\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong regularity of the variational inequality is strong regularity of \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\) under its affine linearization.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the feasible set

source_refs.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational inequality \[\langle f(x),z-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }z\in C\] is equivalent to \(0\in f(x)+N_C(x)\). It is strongly regular at \(\bar x\) when the inverse of \[L(x)=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+N_C(x)\] has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((0,\bar x)\). Hence variational-inequality usage is a specialization of generalized-equation usage with the convex normal-cone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex variational inequality, strong regularity concerns the inverse localization of the affine field plus the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Usage

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter II. Variational Inequalities in Hilbert Space p. 23

children.title: Mapping-Level Usage
children.top_down_role: Terminological conventions stated directly for mappings or inverse mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mapping-level strong metric regularity is the existence of a single-valued Lipschitz localization of \(M^{-1}\) around \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic mapping-level terminology, independent of a chosen smooth-plus-set-valued decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(M\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(m:V\to U\) satisfying \[M^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{m(y)\}\quad\text{for every }y\in V,\qquad m(\bar y)=\bar x.\] Unlike generalized-equation strong regularity, this definition is applied directly to \(M\), without selecting an affine linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is strongly metrically regular when its inverse is locally single-valued, everywhere defined, and Lipschitz near the reference pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Mapping-Level Usage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind exactly fits mapping-level usage, and the formulation includes local single-valuedness, local domain coverage, and Lipschitz continuity. It lacks the required authoritative definition citation or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Cross-Framework Scope Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring terminology among the three frameworks.

assumptions_latex: \(M:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is given by \(M(x)=|x|\), with reference pair \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Generalized-equation strong regularity via classical linearization is undefined here, while \(M\) also fails strong metric regularity at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: nonsmooth mapping exhibiting the scope boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmoothness prevents unqualified transfer between linearization-based and mapping-level terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(M(x)=|x|\) has no classical derivative at \(0\), so Robinson strong regularity based on the affine derivative linearization cannot be asserted without choosing another generalized derivative or model. Moreover, for every sufficiently small \(y>0\), \[M^{-1}(y)=\{-y,y\},\] so \(M^{-1}\) has no single-valued localization on a neighborhood of \(0\). Thus cross-framework terminology requires explicit differentiability, normal-cone, and linearization conventions; the labels are not interchangeable without those hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a specified differentiable model, linearization-based strong regularity may be undefined and need not coincide with mapping-level regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Framework Scope Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container. The example correctly shows both the absence of a classical derivative at zero and failure of strong metric regularity through the two-valued inverse for positive outputs, but no source or standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Smooth Equation Specialization
children.top_down_role: Reduction to classical local inverse and implicit-function theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Exact Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square continuously differentiable mappings in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), strong metric regularity at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\) holds if and only if \(DF(\bar x)\) is nonsingular. The converse uses the Lipschitz inverse localization to obtain a lower bound on \(DF(\bar x)\); in equal finite dimensions injectivity is equivalent to invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square finite-dimensional C1 equation, strong metric regularity is equivalent to nonsingularity of the Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is strongly metrically regular at }(\bar x,F(\bar x))\iff \det DF(\bar x)\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Exact Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach-Space Forward Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward inverse-function implication for continuously Fréchet differentiable maps between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to Y\) be continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\). If \(DF(\bar x):X\to Y\) is a bounded linear isomorphism, then neighborhoods \(U,V\) exist such that \(F|_U:U\to V\) is bijective and its inverse is continuously differentiable, hence locally Lipschitz. Therefore \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible derivative yields a locally differentiable and Lipschitz inverse, hence strong metric regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(DF(\bar x)\) is a bounded linear isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional variational inequality over a fixed polyhedral convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), with \(0\in f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal Strong-Monotonicity Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space maximal strongly monotone inclusions, including variational inequalities when the sum operator is maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal and strongly monotone with modulus \(m>0\). Then \(\operatorname{ran}A=H\), \(A^{-1}:H\to H\) is single-valued, and \[\|A^{-1}(p)-A^{-1}(q)\|\le m^{-1}\|p-q\|.\] Consequently, whenever \(A=f+N_C\) is maximal and strongly monotone, the corresponding variational inequality has a globally defined strongly metrically regular solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal strongly monotone inclusion has an everywhere-defined unique inverse with Lipschitz constant at most the reciprocal strong-monotonicity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone and strongly monotone with modulus \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{-1}\) is defined on \(H\), single-valued, and \(1/m\)-Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space strong-monotonicity specialization, conditional on existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any solvable parameters \(p_1,p_2\), let \(x_i\) satisfy \(p_i\in f(x_i)+N_C(x_i)\). Monotonicity of \(N_C\) and strong monotonicity of \(f\) give \[m\|x_1-x_2\|^2\le \langle p_1-p_2,x_1-x_2\rangle.\] Hence \[\|x_1-x_2\|\le m^{-1}\|p_1-p_2\|.\] Thus every solvable parameter has at most one solution, and the solution mapping \(s:p\mapsto x\) is \(1/m\)-Lipschitz on its domain. If solvability holds throughout a neighborhood of a reference parameter, the variational inequality is strongly metrically regular there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes a solvable variational inequality uniquely solvable and gives a Lipschitz solution bound of modulus at most \(1/m\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Variational-Inequality Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness and reciprocal strong-monotonicity estimate are mathematically plausible, and the theorem kind fits the specialization. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Complementarity Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar convex program with a weakly active constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_x\ \tfrac12x^2\quad\text{subject to }x\le0,\] the KKT point is \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)=(0,0)\), so strict complementarity fails. Its KKT mapping is \[M(x,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}x+\lambda\\-x\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\N_{\mathbb R_+}(\lambda)\end{pmatrix}.\] For every nearby \((p,q)\), the unique solution of \((p,q)\in M(x,\lambda)\) is \[\lambda=\max\{0,p+q\},\qquad x=p-\lambda.\] This inverse is piecewise affine and Lipschitz, so \(M\) is strongly metrically regular despite failure of strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex scalar program has a strongly metrically regular KKT mapping at an active constraint with zero multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong metric regularity holds at \((0,0)\), although strict complementarity fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Complementarity Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local covering of closed-graph multifunctions between Asplund spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood covering criterion for single-valued Lipschitz mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Lipschitz specialization using Fréchet subgradients of scalarizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a single-valued mapping between Asplund spaces that is Lipschitz continuous around $\bar x$. Then $f$ has local covering around $(\bar x,f(\bar x))$ if and only if $\widehat a(f,\bar x)>0$, and its exact covering bound equals $\widehat a(f,\bar x)$, where
$$\widehat a(f,\bar x)=\sup_{\eta>0}\inf\left\{\|x^*\|:\ x^*\in\widehat\partial\langle y^*,f\rangle(x),\ x\in B_\eta(\bar x),\ \|y^*\|=1\right\}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz mapping between Asplund spaces is locally covering exactly when the neighborhood infimum of the Fréchet-subgradient norms of its unit scalarizations is positive; this quantity is the exact covering bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semi-local covering near a domain point, uniformly over graph values above nearby domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F:X\rightrightarrows Y$ be a set-valued mapping between Asplund spaces whose graph is closed near $\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F$. Define

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F:X\rightrightarrows Y$ satisfy the Asplund-space and local closed-graph assumptions of the local covering theorem at $(\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F$, and suppose that $\operatorname{gph}F$ is convex. Then $F$ has local covering around $(\bar x,\bar y)$ if and only if $\widehat a(F,\bar x,\bar y)>0$, and $\operatorname{cov}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\widehat a(F,\bar x,\bar y)$, where

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the strong slope at a point where \(\varphi(x)<+\infty\) by \[|\nabla\varphi|(x):=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }x\text{ is a local minimizer of }\varphi,\\ \displaystyle\limsup_{z\to x,\ z\ne x}\frac{[\varphi(x)-\varphi(z)]_+}{d(x,z)},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] Under the stated uniform lower bound, there exists \(\rho>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\frac{\varphi(x)}{\alpha}\qquad\text{for every }x\in B(\bar x,\rho).\] Thus the positive strong-slope bound is a sufficient local residual error-bound criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a specified zero of a lower-semicontinuous residual on a complete metric space, a uniform positive strong slope away from the zero set guarantees a local error bound with reciprocal slope constant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\ge0\) if and only if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\qquad(x\in U).\] With the convention \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,\varnothing)=+\infty\), this is precisely a local error bound for the residual \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\), whose zero set is \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity is the local error bound comparing distance to the solution set with the generalized-equation residual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Set of the Distance Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification needed when identifying the zero set of a distance residual with the exact inverse image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\), \[r^{-1}(0)=\{x:\bar y\in\operatorname{cl}F(x)\}.\] Hence \(r^{-1}(0)=F^{-1}(\bar y)\) locally whenever the relevant values \(F(x)\) are closed at \(\bar y\). Without this qualification, the distance residual can vanish at a point that is not an exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical distance residual has the exact solution set as its zero set only when closure at the reference value does not add solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \(\bar y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual zero set equals \(\{x:\bar y\in\operatorname{cl}F(x)\}\), with equality to \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\) under local closedness of the values at \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Set of the Distance Residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Residual Error-Bound Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real ratio representation of the exact metric-subregularity modulus for the canonical residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\) and \(S=F^{-1}(\bar y)\). With \(a/0=+\infty\) for \(a>0\), \[\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{r(x)},\] where the value is zero when no points outside \(S\) occur locally. This is the infimum of all constants admissible in the local residual error bound; the infimum need not itself be attained on one fixed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact metric-subregularity modulus is the local upper limit of solution-set distance divided by the canonical residual.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact local residual error-bound modulus equals the displayed extended-real limsup.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Power-Residual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-residual family generalizing the immutable quadratic boundary example and identifying the surviving sharp Hölder exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p>1\), let \(\varphi_p(x)=|x|^p\) and \(S=\{0\}\). For \(x\ne0\), \[|\nabla\varphi_p|(x)=p|x|^{p-1}\longrightarrow0\quad(x\to0).\] No local linear error bound \(|x|\le\kappa\varphi_p(x)\) holds at zero. A local Hölder estimate \[|x|\le\kappa\varphi_p(x)^q\] holds precisely for \(0<q\le1/p\); at \(q=1/p\), its least constant is one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every power residual of order greater than one has vanishing slope and no linear error bound, but has sharp Hölder exponent one over its order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear error bounds fail, while the largest admissible Hölder exponent is \(1/p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that, for some \(\kappa>0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\varphi(x)\) fails in every neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then there are \(x_n\to\bar x\) and \(u_n\to\bar x\) such that \[0<\varphi(x_n),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x_n,S)>\kappa\varphi(x_n),\] and \[0<\varphi(u_n)\le\varphi(x_n),\qquad d(u_n,x_n)\le\kappa\varphi(x_n),\qquad |\nabla\varphi|(u_n)\le\kappa^{-1}.\] Thus repeated failure of the proposed constant produces arbitrarily nearby positive-residual points of small slope.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical derivative is given by \[DF(x\mid y)(h):=\{k\in Y:(h,k)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x,y)\}.\] If the displayed covering inclusion holds uniformly at all nearby graph points, then for every \(c'<c\) the mapping \(F\) is open at linear rate \(c'\) near \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Equivalently, \(F\) is metrically regular there and \[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\le c^{-1}.\] Pointwise surjectivity only at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is not substituted for the required uniform nearby condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform surjectivity of nearby graphical derivatives implies linear openness and hence metric regularity with reciprocal modulus.
