knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability and directional sensitivity of parametric projection-type solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space parametric problem (5.87) with twice continuously differentiable data and Robinson constraint qualification at the reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a Hilbert space. Suppose \psi and G are twice continuously differentiable, \psi(u_0)\in\Phi(u_0), x_0=\psi(u_0), and Robinson's constraint qualification holds at x_0 for G(\cdot,u_0) and K. Then there is a neighborhood \mathcal V_U of u_0 such that problem (5.87) has a unique optimal solution \bar x(u) for every u\in\mathcal V_U, \|\bar x(u)-x_0\|=O(\|u-u_0\|), and, for some \kappa>0, \|\bar x(u)-\bar x(u')\|\leq\kappa\|u-u'\|^{1/2} for all u,u'\in\mathcal V_U. If D_xG(x_0,u_0) is onto, then \bar x is Lipschitz continuous near u_0. Moreover, \bar x is directionally differentiable at u_0, and \bar x'(u_0;d) is an optimal solution of \[\min_{h\in X}\|D\psi(u_0)d-h\|\quad\text{subject to}\quad DG(x_0,u_0)(h,d)\in T_K(G(x_0,u_0)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under twice continuous differentiability and Robinson qualification, the nearby problem has a unique solution map that is stable at the reference parameter and Hölder continuous with exponent one half. Surjectivity of the partial constraint derivative strengthens this to local Lipschitz continuity. The solution map is directionally differentiable, with its derivative determined by the stated tangent-cone-constrained approximation problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal V_U\ni u_0:\ \bar x(u)\text{ is unique for all }u\in\mathcal V_U,\ \|\bar x(u)-x_0\|=O(\|u-u_0\|),\ \|\bar x(u)-\bar x(u')\|\leq\kappa\|u-u'\|^{1/2};\quad D_xG(x_0,u_0)\text{ onto}\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ is locally Lipschitz};\quad \bar x'(u_0;d)\text{ solves the stated tangent-cone-constrained minimization problem}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivatives of strongly regular KKT solution operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise directional sensitivity characterized by the referenced linearized generalized KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the generalized equation (5.24) and assume that $(\mathrm{SRC})$ holds at $(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)$. Then the solution operators $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3$ are directionally differentiable at $x_0$. For every $h\in\mathbb R^n$, the vector
\[(\sigma_1'(x_0;h),\sigma_2'(x_0;h),\sigma_3'(x_0;h))=(v,w,u)\]
is the unique solution of
\[0\in \begin{bmatrix}\mathcal J_x\mathcal L(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\\ \mathcal J_xH(x_0,y_0)\\-\mathcal J_xG_{I^+}(x_0,y_0)\\-\mathcal J_xG_{I^0}(x_0,y_0)\end{bmatrix}h+D_{(I)}(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)\begin{bmatrix}v\\w\\u_{I^+}\\u_{I^0}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0_{\mathbb R^n}\\0_{\mathbb R^e}\\0_{\mathbb R^{a^+}}\\N_{\mathbb R_+^{a^0}}(u_{I^0})\end{bmatrix},\qquad u_L=0,\]
where $D_{(I)}(x_0,y_0,\mu_0,\lambda_0)$ is the operator specified in (5.27).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under SRC, the three localized KKT solution operators are directionally differentiable. Their derivatives in any parameter direction uniquely solve the stated linearized generalized KKT system, including the normal-cone condition and u sub L equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\sigma_1'(x_0;h),\sigma_2'(x_0;h),\sigma_3'(x_0;h))\text{ exists and is the unique }(v,w,u)\text{ satisfying the displayed system and }u_L=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidifferentiable Solution Branches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semidifferentiable implicit-function criterion for a locally unique residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(X\) be finite-dimensional normed spaces and let \(F:P\times X\to X\) be locally Lipschitz and semidifferentiable at \((\bar p,\bar x)\), with \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\). Suppose \(F(p,x)=0\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization \(x=s(p)\), and for every \(h\in P\) the equation \(F'((\bar p,\bar x);(h,k))=0\) has a unique solution \(k=k(h)\) that depends continuously and positively homogeneously on \(h\). Then \(s\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar p\), with \[F'((\bar p,\bar x);(h,k(h)))=0,\qquad s'(\bar p;h)=k(h).\] Equivalently, as \(h'\to h\) and \(t\downarrow0\), \[s(\bar p+th')=\bar x+t k(h)+o(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a Lipschitz implicit branch is semidifferentiable when every semidifferentiated residual equation has a unique solution depending continuously and positively homogeneously on the direction.
assumptions_latex: \(F:P\times X\to X\) is locally Lipschitz and semidifferentiable at \((\bar p,\bar x)\), with \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\).
The equation \(F(p,x)=0\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization \(x=s(p)\).
For every \(h\in P\), the equation \(F'((\bar p,\bar x);(h,k))=0\) has a unique solution \(k=k(h)\), continuously and positively homogeneously dependent on \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar p\), and \(s'(\bar p;h)=k(h)\) for every \(h\in P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidifferentiability of a Solution Branch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semiderivative definition for a localized single-valued branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(s:P\to X\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar p\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(H:P\to X\) such that \[s(\bar p+h)=s(\bar p)+H(h)+o(\|h\|)\quad(h\to0).\] Equivalently, \[\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{s(\bar p+t h')-s(\bar p)}t=H(h)\quad\text{for every }h\in P.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oscillating Difference Quotients Need Not Be Proto-Differentiable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar map whose difference-quotient graphs have incompatible subsequential limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(S(0)=0\) and \(S(p)=p\sin(\log|p|)\) for \(p\ne0\). Then \[S_t(q)=\frac{S(tq)}t=q\sin(\log t+\log|q|)\quad(q\ne0).\] Subsequences for which \(\log t\) approaches different phases modulo \(2\pi\) yield different graphical subsequential limits. Thus \(S_t\) has no graphical limit as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous scalar map can fail proto-differentiability because its graphical difference quotients oscillate between distinct subsequential limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is not proto-differentiable at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillating Difference Quotients Need Not Be Proto-Differentiable

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proto-Differentiability by Graphical Difference Quotients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graphical proto-differentiability of a solution map at a fixed graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), define \(S_t(h):=(S(\bar p+th)-\bar x)/t\) for \(t>0\). The map \(S\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) when \(S_t\) converges graphically as \(t\downarrow0\), equivalently when \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}S_t=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}S_t.\] The common limit is \(T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar p,\bar x)=\operatorname{gph}DS(\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution map is proto-differentiable when its graphical difference quotients have one common inner and outer graph limit, namely the graph of its graphical derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\), \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), and the graphical limits are taken in finite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{g-lim}_{t\downarrow0}S_t=DS(\bar p,\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graphical proto-differentiability at a fixed solution pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution map \(S\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) when the mappings \(S_t\), for \(t>0\), converge graphically as \(t\downarrow0\). Equivalently, the outer and inner graphical limits coincide:
\[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}S_t=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{gph}S_t.\]
Their common graph defines \(DS(\bar p,\bar x)\), so
\[u\in DS(\bar p,\bar x)(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(q,u)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar p,\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution map is proto-differentiable when its graphical difference quotients have a common inner and outer limit, which is its graphical derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative sufficient condition for stability of irregular generalized equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aubin stability under PSNC, SNC, and two normal-coderivative qualification conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S(x):=\{y\mid0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\}, let (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}S, and set \bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y). Suppose X,Y,Z are Asplund, f is continuous around (\bar x,\bar y) and PSNC there, and Q has locally closed graph and is SNC at (\bar x,\bar y,\bar z). Assume [(x^*,0)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)]\Rightarrow x^*=0 and [(x^*,y^*)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)\cap(-D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*))]\Rightarrow(x^*,y^*,z^*)=(0,0,0). Then S is Lipschitz-like around (\bar x,\bar y). If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)\le\sup\{\|x^*\|\mid\exists z^*,\ (x^*,-y^*)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an irregular generalized equation in Asplund spaces, PSNC and SNC together with two normal-coderivative qualification conditions guarantee the Aubin property. A finite-dimensional parameter space gives an upper bound for the Lipschitz modulus.

f\text{ is continuous around and PSNC at }(\bar x,\bar y)
Q\text{ has locally closed graph and is SNC at }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar y),\quad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ satisfies the displayed upper bound.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability criterion for generalized equations with strictly Lipschitzian bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalarized-subdifferential criterion and modulus bound in the irregular generalized-equation framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the Asplund-space framework of the irregular generalized-equation theorem, let S(x):=\{y\mid0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\}, set \bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y), suppose f is strictly Lipschitzian at (\bar x,\bar y), and suppose Q has closed graph and is SNC at (\bar x,\bar y,\bar z). If [(x^*,0)\in\partial\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)]\Rightarrow(x^*,z^*)=(0,0), then S is Lipschitz-like around (\bar x,\bar y). When f is strictly differentiable, this reduces to the corresponding derivative-coderivative condition. If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)\le\sup\{\|x^*\|\mid\exists z^*,\ (x^*,-y^*)\in\partial\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}.

Strict differentiability recovers the smooth condition, and finite-dimensional parameters yield a modulus upper bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-coderivative criterion for an irregular generalized equation with an x-independent field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the framework of the irregular generalized-equation theorem, suppose X,Y,Z are Asplund, f is continuous around (\bar x,\bar y) and PSNC there, and Q=Q(y) has closed graph and is SNC at (\bar y,\bar z), where \bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y). Q=Q(y)\text{ has closed graph and is SNC at }(\bar y,\bar z)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional constraint systems with an exact limiting-normal pullback rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) and \(x^*\in X^*\), the limiting coderivative is represented by
\[D^*S(\bar p,\bar x)(x^*)=\left\{p^*\in P^*\ \middle|\ \exists\lambda\in N_D(g(\bar p,\bar x)):\ p^*=\nabla_p g(\bar p,\bar x)^*\lambda,\ -x^*=\nabla_x g(\bar p,\bar x)^*\lambda\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible-set coderivative consists of parameter covectors generated by constraint normals whose state adjoints equal the negative prescribed state covector.

\(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by \(S(p):=\{x\in X\mid g(p,x)\in D\}\).
The limiting-normal inverse-image rule is exact at \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coderivative is represented by multipliers normal to \(D\) satisfying the displayed adjoint equations.

\((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), \(\bar y:=-f(\bar p,\bar x)\in Q(\bar x)\), and the limiting-coderivative chain rule for this generalized equation is exact at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a composite-field GVI with finite-dimensional range, closedness of the subgradient graph, the two stated qualification conditions, local Lipschitz continuity of the field, and either local Lipschitz continuity of the composite map or finite-dimensional parameter spaces yield the normal and mixed coderivative upper estimates for the solution map.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative Estimates for General Variational Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper estimates for normal and mixed coderivatives of a generalized-equation solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) solve \(0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\), where \(X,Y,Z\) are Asplund spaces, \(f\) is continuous near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and \(\operatorname{gph}Q\) is closed near \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\), with \(\bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y)\). For \(D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}\), \[D^*S(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\{x^*\mid \exists z^*:\ (x^*,-y^*)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\},\] provided either: (a) \(Q\) is SNC and \((0,0,0)\) is the only triple satisfying \((x^*,y^*)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)\cap[-D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)]\); or (b) \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), \(\dim Z<\infty\), and \([0\in\partial\langle z^*,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)]\Rightarrow z^*=0\). If \(f\) is strictly Lipschitzian at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), the qualification in (a) is equivalent to this scalarized implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a general variational system in Asplund spaces, both normal and mixed coderivatives of the solution map have an upper estimate formed from the coderivatives of the base map and the field. The estimate requires one of the stated SNC or finite-dimensional qualification regimes.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is continuous near }(\bar x,\bar y)
\operatorname{gph}Q\text{ is closed near }(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z),\quad \bar z=-f(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*S(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\{x^*\mid \exists z^*:\ (x^*,-y^*)\in D_N^*f(\bar x,\bar y)(z^*)+D_N^*Q(\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\},\quad D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}.

abla_xf( ar x, ar y)\) is surjective, and \(Q\) is independent of \(x\), then \[D_N^*S( ar x, ar y)(y^*)=\{x^*\mid \exists z^*:\ x^*=
abla_xf( ar x, ar y)^*z^*,\ -y^*\in
abla_yf( ar x, ar y)^*z^*+D_N^*Q( ar y, ar z)(z^*)\}.\] Moreover, if \(Q\) is strongly coderivatively normal at \(( ar y, ar z)\), then \(S^{-1}\) is strongly coderivatively normal at \(( ar y, ar x)\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact range-normal representations for solution-map coderivatives when the generalized-equation field has convex graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) solve \(0\in f(x,y)+Q(x,y)\), where \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(\operatorname{gph}Q\) is convex. (i) If \(X,Y,Z\) are Banach spaces, \(\nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y)\) is surjective, and \(Q\) is independent of \(x\), then \(S\) is \(N\)-regular and \[D^*S(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\{\nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y)^*z^*\mid -(y^*,z^*)\in N((0,0);\operatorname{rge}\widetilde M)\},\] where \(\widetilde M(y)=(y-\bar y,\widetilde L(y))\). (ii) If \(X,Y,Z\) are Asplund spaces, \(Q\) is locally closed-graph at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\), either \(\dim Z<\infty\) or \(Q\) is SNC there, and \(N(0;\operatorname{rge}L)=\{0\}\), then \(S\) is \(N\)-regular and \[D^*S(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\{x^*\mid \exists z^*:\ (x^*,-y^*,-z^*)\in N((0,0,0);\operatorname{rge}M)\},\] where \(M(x,y)=(x-\bar x,y-\bar y,L(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For generalized equations with convex-graph fields, the solution map is normally regular and its coderivative has an exact representation through normals to the ranges of associated mappings, subject to the separate hypotheses of the two cases.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is strictly differentiable at }(\bar x,\bar y)
\text{Case (i): }X,Y,Z\text{ are Banach},\ \nabla_xf\text{ is surjective},\ Q\text{ is independent of }x
\text{Case (ii): }X,Y,Z\text{ are Asplund},\ Q\text{ is locally closed-graph},\ [\dim Z<\infty\text{ or }Q\text{ is SNC}],\ N(0;\operatorname{rge}L)=\{0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is }N\text{-regular and has the stated exact range-normal coderivative representation in each case.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order multiplier responses to a parameter direction \(q\in P\) are
\[D\Lambda(\bar p,\bar\lambda)(q):=\{\eta\in L\mid(q,\eta)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}\Lambda}(\bar p,\bar\lambda)\}.\]
The corresponding dual sensitivity is
\[D^*\Lambda(\bar p,\bar\lambda)(\lambda^*):=\{p^*\in P^*\mid(p^*,-\lambda^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}\Lambda}(\bar p,\bar\lambda)\}.\]
Hence isolated multiplier stability in the zero parameter direction requires \(D\Lambda(\bar p,\bar\lambda)(0)=\{0\}\), while nonzero elements of that set expose infinitesimal multiplier nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent directions of the multiplier graph describe primal multiplier responses; normals to the same graph describe their dual sensitivity and detect infinitesimal nonuniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Constraint-System Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical derivative of a smooth finite-dimensional parameterized constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) and \(q\in P\), the graphical derivative is
\[DS(\bar p,\bar x)(q)=\left\{u\in X\ \middle|\ \nabla_p g(\bar p,\bar x)q+\nabla_x g(\bar p,\bar x)u\in T_D(g(\bar p,\bar x))\right\}.\]
Thus \(u\in X\) is a feasible first-order state response precisely when the linearized parameter-state displacement belongs to the tangent cone of \(D\) at the reference image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state velocity is feasible exactly when the linearized parameter-state displacement is tangent to the constraint set at the reference image.
assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, \(g:P\times X\to Y\) is continuously differentiable, and \(D\subset Y\) is geometrically derivable at \(g(\bar p,\bar x)\).
\(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by \(S(p):=\{x\in X\mid g(p,x)\in D\}\), and \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
The tangent inverse-image rule is exact at \((\bar p,\bar x)\), for example under a sufficient metric-subregularity qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible first-order responses are exactly the directions whose linearized constraint displacement lies in the tangent cone to \(D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneous Linearized-VI Test for Isolated Calmness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolated-calmness specialization for a smooth variational inequality over a fixed polyhedral set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral and \(S(p):=\{x\mid 0\in F(p,x)+N_C(x)\}\), where \(F\) is continuously differentiable. At \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), set \(\bar v=-F(\bar p,\bar x)\) and \(K=T_C(\bar x)\cap\bar v^\perp\). Then \(S\) is isolated calm at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if and only if
\[0\in \nabla_xF(\bar p,\bar x)u+N_K(u)\]
has no solution other than \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth polyhedral variational inequality, isolated calmness is equivalent to triviality of its homogeneous critical-cone linearization.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and polyhedral.
\(F\) is continuously differentiable near \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is isolated calm at }(\bar p,\bar x)\iff \{u\mid0\in\nabla_xF(\bar p,\bar x)u+N_K(u)\}=\{0\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical-derivative criterion for isolated calmness of finite-dimensional VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The map \(S\) is isolated calm at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\), \(V\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that
\[S(p)\cap V\subset\{\bar x\}+\kappa\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\mathbb B\qquad\text{for every }p\in U.\]
Under graphical derivability, this property holds if and only if
\[DS(\bar p,\bar x)(0)=\{0\}.\]
Thus no nonzero state velocity may occur while the parameter has zero first-order velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational-inequality solution is isolated calm precisely when its graphical derivative has no nonzero state response to zero parameter velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Calmness for Variational Inequalities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-Cone Graphical Derivative of an Affine Polyhedral VI Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order sensitivity of the right-hand-side solution map for an affine variational inequality over a polyhedral set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and polyhedral, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear, and define \(S(p)=\{x\mid p\in Ax+N_C(x)\}\). For \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), set \(\bar v=\bar p-A\bar x\) and \(K=T_C(\bar x)\cap\bar v^\perp\). Then
\[DS(\bar p,\bar x)(q)=\{u\mid q\in Au+N_K(u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical derivative of an affine polyhedral VI solution map is the solution map of its critical-cone linearized VI.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Cone Graphical Derivative of an Affine Polyhedral VI Map

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and polyhedral, and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is linear.

Solution map of the affine variational inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine variational inequalities over a finite-dimensional polyhedral set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(C\) is polyhedral, \(\operatorname{gph}N_C\) is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets. The identity
\[\operatorname{gph}S=\{(p,x)\mid(x,p-Ax)\in\operatorname{gph}N_C\}\]
therefore makes \(\operatorname{gph}S\) a finite union of polyhedral convex sets. Hence \(S\) is a piecewise-polyhedral multifunction and is calm at every \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\). If, additionally, a localization of \(S\) is single-valued, that localization is piecewise affine and locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine variational inequality over a polyhedral set has a piecewise-polyhedral solution graph, implying local calmness and piecewise-affine behavior for single-valued localizations.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Variational-Inequality Solution Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write the KKT system as \(0\in H(p,z)+Q(z)\), where \(z=(x,\lambda)\). Under LICQ and the strong second-order sufficient condition, this generalized equation is strongly regular at \((\bar p,\bar z)\). Consequently, there are neighborhoods on which its solution map has a unique Lipschitz localization \(z=s(p)\). For every parameter direction \(q\), each directional derivative \(w=s'(\bar p;q)\), when represented through the proto-derivative of \(Q\), is the unique solution of
\[0\in\nabla_pH(\bar p,\bar z)q+\nabla_zH(\bar p,\bar z)w+DQ(\bar z,-H(\bar p,\bar z))(w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ and strong second-order sufficiency yield a locally unique Lipschitz KKT branch whose directional derivative solves the linearized primal-dual generalized equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Reduction of the Second-Order Graphical Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calibration of the parabolic graphical derivative on a twice differentiable single-valued map using the one-half-square convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s:P\to X\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar p\), set \(\bar x=s(\bar p)\), and let \(u=Ds(\bar p)q\). Under the parabolic convention \(\bar p+tq+\tfrac12t^2r\),
\[
D^2s((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))(r)=\{Ds(\bar p)r+D^2s(\bar p)[q,q]\}.
\]
If \(u\ne Ds(\bar p)q\), then \((q,u)\) is not tangent to the graph, so no second-order graph correction exists along that prescribed pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth map, the second-order graphical derivative is single-valued and equals the response to parameter acceleration plus the Hessian response to first-order motion.
assumptions_latex: \(s:P\to X\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^2s((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))(r)=\{Ds(\bar p)r+D^2s(\bar p)[q,q]\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Reduction of the Second-Order Graphical Derivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness Without Second-Order Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar preimage showing strict overestimation by a formal second-order linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=x^2\), \(C=\{0\}\), and \(A=\Phi^{-1}(C)=\{0\}\). At \(x=0\) in direction \(d=0\), \[T_A^2(0;0)=\{0\},\] whereas \[\{e\mid D\Phi(0)e+D^2\Phi(0)[0,0]\in T_C^2(0;0)\}=\mathbb R.\] Thus the second-order preimage inclusion can be strict when a second-order lifting qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the equation x squared equals zero, every acceleration satisfies the formal second-order linearization, but only zero is an actual second-order feasible acceleration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_A^2(0;0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Without Second-Order Lifting

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Preimage Inclusion and Conditional Solution-Graph Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parabolic second-order calculus for a solution graph represented as a smooth preimage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(p)=\{x\mid \Phi(p,x)\in C\}\), where \(\Phi:P\times X\to Y\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(C\subset Y\) is closed. For \(z=(\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) and \(d=(q,u)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(z)\), \[T^2_{\operatorname{gph}S}(z;d)\subseteq\{e\mid D\Phi(z)e+D^2\Phi(z)[d,d]\in T_C^2(\Phi(z);D\Phi(z)d)\}.\] If every acceleration in the right-hand set admits an \(o(t^2)\) correction producing a path in \(\Phi^{-1}(C)\), equality holds. Under that lifting property, \[v\in D^2S((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))(r)\iff D\Phi(z)(r,v)+D^2\Phi(z)[d,d]\in T_C^2(\Phi(z);D\Phi(z)d).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth preimage calculus always gives an outer second-order linearization; it is exact when all formally feasible accelerations lift to actual solution-graph paths.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(C\) is closed.
Equality requires the stated second-order lifting property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inclusion holds; equality and the graphical-derivative formula hold under second-order lifting.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Preimage Inclusion and Conditional Solution-Graph Formula

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Surjective Second-Order Preimage Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact parabolic inverse-image rule for a smooth finite-dimensional solution graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(p)=\{x\mid \Phi(p,x)\in C\}\), where \(\Phi:P\times X\to Y\) is \(C^2\), \(C\subset Y\) is closed, and \(D\Phi(z)\) is surjective at \(z=(\bar p,\bar x)\). For \(d=(q,u)\) with \(D\Phi(z)d\in T_C(\Phi(z))\), the convention \(z+td+\tfrac12t^2e\) gives
\[
T^2_{\operatorname{gph}S}(z;d)=\{e\mid D\Phi(z)e+D^2\Phi(z)[d,d]\in T_C^2(\Phi(z);D\Phi(z)d)\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
v\in D^2S((z);d)(r)\iff D\Phi(z)(r,v)+D^2\Phi(z)[d,d]\in T_C^2(\Phi(z);D\Phi(z)d).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Surjectivity of the smooth constraint derivative makes the parabolic second-order inverse-image formula exact.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is twice continuously differentiable, \(C\) is closed, and \(D\Phi(z)\) is surjective.
Second-order tangents use the one-half-square normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T^2_{\Phi^{-1}(C)}(z;d)=\{e\mid D\Phi(z)e+D^2\Phi(z)[d,d]\in T_C^2(\Phi(z);D\Phi(z)d)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Surjective Second-Order Preimage Rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Implicit Solution Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order sensitivity of a locally single-valued smooth solution branch of an equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:P\times X\to Y\) be \(C^2\), let \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), and suppose \(A:=D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)\) is invertible. The local implicit solution \(s\) satisfies, for parameter velocity \(q\) and acceleration \(r\),
\[
u:=Ds(\bar p)q=-A^{-1}D_pF(\bar p,\bar x)q,
\]
\[
v:=Ds(\bar p)r+D^2s(\bar p)[q,q]=-A^{-1}\left(D_pF(\bar p,\bar x)r+D^2F(\bar p,\bar x)[(q,u),(q,u)]\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth equation with invertible state Jacobian, first- and second-order state responses are obtained from linear systems with that same Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable, \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), and \(D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)v+D_pF(\bar p,\bar x)r+D^2F(\bar p,\bar x)[(q,u),(q,u)]=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Implicit Solution Formula

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic Second-Order Graphical Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-half-square second-order tangent and graphical derivative for a solution multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\subset Z\), \(a\in A\), and \(d\in T_A(a)\), define
\[
T_A^2(a;d):=\left\{e\mid \exists t_k\downarrow0,\ e_k\to e:\ a+t_kd+\tfrac12t_k^2e_k\in A\right\}.
\]
For \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\), \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), and \((q,u)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}S}(\bar p,\bar x)\), its parabolic second-order graphical derivative is defined by
\[
v\in D^2S((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))(r)
\iff
(r,v)\in T^2_{\operatorname{gph}S}((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing a first-order graph direction, the second-order graphical derivative collects all compatible parameter and state accelerations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\in D^2S((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))(r)\iff(r,v)\in T^2_{\operatorname{gph}S}((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u)).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Second-order solution sensitivity is represented by the second-order graphical derivative \(D^2S((\bar p,\bar x);(q,u))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Tangents for Smooth Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth inequality systems under LICQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\mid g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where each \(g_i\) is twice continuously differentiable, and suppose LICQ holds at \(\bar x\in C\). For \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\), set \(I(\bar x;w):=\{i\mid g_i(\bar x)=0,\ \nabla g_i(\bar x)w=0\}\). Then
\[
T_C^2(\bar x;w)=\{z\mid \nabla g_i(\bar x)z+\nabla^2g_i(\bar x)[w,w]\le0\quad(i\in I(\bar x;w))\}.
\]
Constraints with \(\nabla g_i(\bar x)w<0\) impose no second-order restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under LICQ, only constraints remaining active to first order restrict the second-order correction, with their Hessians supplying the curvature shift.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable for every \(i\).
\(\bar x\in C\), LICQ holds at \(\bar x\), and \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^2(\bar x;w)=\{z\mid \nabla g_i(\bar x)z+\nabla^2g_i(\bar x)[w,w]\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x;w))\}\).

assumptions_latex: \(C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid h(x)=0\}\), where \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is twice continuously differentiable.
\(\nabla h(\bar x)\) is surjective and \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constraint manifolds; curvature appears in their parabolic tangent geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order tangent condition is \(
abla h( ar x)w=0\). The parabolic second-order tangent set in direction \(w\) is
\[T_C^2( ar x;w)=\left\{z\in\mathbb R^n\ \middle|\ 
abla h( ar x)z+
abla^2h( ar x)[w,w]=0ight\}.\]
Thus the admissible second-order correction is not generally tangent to the linearized constraint: it must compensate for the quadratic curvature term generated by the first-order direction. For affine constraints this Hessian term vanishes, recovering the purely linear tangent equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along an equality-constraint manifold, second-order feasible corrections must cancel the Hessian curvature produced by the first-order direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The critical cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is
\[K_C(\bar x,\bar v):=T_C(\bar x)\cap\bar v^\perp=\{w\in T_C(\bar x)\mid\langle\bar v,w\rangle=0\}.\]
It consists exactly of feasible first-order directions on which the normal \(\bar v\) has zero first-order work. Since \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\), every tangent direction satisfies \(\langle\bar v,w\rangle\le0\), and critical directions are those attaining equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical cone contains tangent directions orthogonal to the selected normal, equivalently feasible directions with zero first-order normal work.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Cone Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed-Face Structure of the Critical Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural geometry of the convex critical cone defined by the accepted seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed and convex, \(\bar x\in C\), and \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\), then
\[
K_C(\bar x,\bar v)=\{w\in T_C(\bar x)\mid\langle\bar v,w\rangle=0\}
\]
is the exposed face of \(T_C(\bar x)\) on which the functional \(w\mapsto\langle\bar v,w\rangle\) attains its maximum zero. Hence \(K_C(\bar x,\bar v)\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical cone is the closed convex exposed face of the tangent cone on which the selected normal has zero pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) and \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_C(\bar x,\bar v)\) is a closed convex exposed face of \(T_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical second-order sensitivity of a smooth implicit solution branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter direction \(q\in P\), differentiating the implicit equation gives the unique first-order response \(u\in X\) satisfying
\[
abla_xF( ar p, ar x)u+
abla_pF( ar p, ar x)q=0.\]
The second-order response \(v\in X\) is the unique solution of
\[
abla_xF( ar p, ar x)v+
abla_{pp}^2F( ar p, ar x)[q,q]+2
abla_{px}^2F( ar p, ar x)[q,u]+
abla_{xx}^2F( ar p, ar x)[u,u]=0.\]
Thus both sensitivities are computed with the same invertible state Jacobian, while curvature supplies the second-order forcing term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth implicit branch has first and second directional responses obtained by solving two linear systems with the same state Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Branch Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the kernel-critical sense of degeneracy for a linearized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the generalized equation \(0\in M(p,x)\), a direction \(w\in X\) is a degenerate critical direction at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if \(w\ne0\) and
\[
0\in DM((\bar p,\bar x),0)(0,w).
\]
Thus the homogeneous graphical linearization has a nonzero solution. Equivalently, the zero parameter direction does not isolate the zero solution direction in the linearized generalized equation. This condition identifies directions along which first-order sensitivity cannot determine a unique local branch and higher-order curvature information may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical direction is degenerate when the homogeneous graphical linearization of the generalized equation has a nonzero solution direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Critical Directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular State Derivative Is Inconclusive
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that invertibility is sufficient but not necessary, while singularity can also destroy differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_1(p,x)=x^3-p^3\), the unique solution map is \(s_1(p)=p\), which is smooth although \(D_xF_1(0,0)=0\). For \(F_2(p,x)=x^3-p\), the unique solution map is \(s_2(p)=\sqrt[3]{p}\), which is not differentiable or locally Lipschitz at \(0\), again with \(D_xF_2(0,0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of state-derivative invertibility neither precludes smoothness nor guarantees it; additional structure is decisive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_xF_i(0,0)=0\) for both examples, while \(s_1\) is smooth and \(s_2\) is not differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Singular State Derivative Is Inconclusive

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Banach-Space Implicit Solution Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical smooth single-valued equation; the absence of a locator does not undermine this standard theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,X,Y\) be Banach spaces. If \(F:P\times X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \((\bar p,\bar x)\), \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), and \(D_xF(\bar p,\bar x):X\to Y\) is a bounded linear isomorphism, then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and a unique continuously Fréchet differentiable map \(s:U\to V\) such that \[F(p,s(p))=0.\] After shrinking \(U\) if necessary, \[Ds(p)=-D_xF(p,s(p))^{-1}D_pF(p,s(p))\qquad(p\in U).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible state derivative yields a locally unique continuously differentiable solution map with the classical implicit derivative formula.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
\(D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)\) is a bounded linear isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists!s\in C^1(U,V):F(p,s(p))=0\) and \(Ds(p)=-D_xF(p,s(p))^{-1}D_pF(p,s(p))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P,X,Y\) be Banach spaces. If \(F:P\times X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \((\bar p,\bar x)\), \(F(\bar p,\bar x)=0\), and \(D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)\) is a bounded linear isomorphism, then neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) admit a unique continuously Fréchet differentiable map \(s:U\to V\) satisfying
\[
F(p,s(p))=0,
\qquad
Ds(\bar p)=-D_xF(\bar p,\bar x)^{-1}D_pF(\bar p,\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible solution-variable derivative yields a locally unique continuously differentiable solution map whose derivative is given by the implicit-function formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Solution-Map Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical-derivative representation under an explicit tangent preimage equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P,X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(M:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\), and suppose \(0\in M(\bar p,\bar x)\). Define \(S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in M(p,x)\}\). If
\[
T_{M^{-1}(0)}(\bar p,\bar x)=\{(q,w)\in P\times X:0\in DM((\bar p,\bar x),0)(q,w)\},
\]
then, for every \(q\in P\),
\[
DS(\bar p,\bar x)(q)=\{w\in X:0\in DM((\bar p,\bar x),0)(q,w)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the stated tangent preimage equality holds, the graphical derivative of the solution map consists exactly of the solution directions satisfying the graphically linearized generalized equation.

\(T_{M^{-1}(0)}(\bar p,\bar x)=\{(q,w)\in P\times X:0\in DM((\bar p,\bar x),0)(q,w)\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DS(\bar p,\bar x)(q)=\{w\in X:0\in DM((\bar p,\bar x),0)(q,w)\}\) for every \(q\in P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{0\}\), \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), and \(M(x)=\{x^2\}\). The generalized equation \(0\in M(x)\) has solution set \(S=\{0\}\), so its tangent solution directions consist only of \(0\). However, \[DM(0,0)(w)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb R,\] and therefore \[\{w\mid0\in DM(0,0)(w)\}=\mathbb R.\] Thus the graphically linearized inclusion can contain spurious directions unless the tangent-preimage equality in the seed holds.

children.title: Lyusternik–Graves Theorem Family

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\)
\(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\), and \(\kappa\lambda<1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\) with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces. Suppose \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\), and \(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\). If \(\kappa\lambda<1\), then \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\). Its local modulus can be chosen no larger than
\[
\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}.
\]
Equivalently, the covering rate loses at most the perturbation slope \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity survives a sufficiently small Lipschitz perturbation, with the regularity modulus inflated by the reciprocal small-gain margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Lyusternik–Graves Theorem Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Small-Gain Boundary for Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional sharpness of the strict Lyusternik–Graves perturbation inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\kappa>0\), let \(F(x)=x/\kappa\) and \(g(x)=-x/\kappa\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)=\kappa\), \(\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1/\kappa\), and \(F+g\equiv0\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\). Thus \(\kappa\lambda<1\) cannot generally be weakened to \(\kappa\lambda\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equality in the small-gain condition, exact cancellation can destroy metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\) and \(F+g\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Small-Gain Boundary for Metric Regularity

\(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\), and \(\kappa\lambda<1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\), with inverse-localization constant at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz modulus of the localized inverse of the unperturbed mapping

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the localization of \(F^{-1}\) around \((\bar y,\bar x)\) be single-valued and Lipschitz with constant \(\kappa\). Let \(g:X\to Y\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\). If \(\kappa\lambda<1\), then the localization of
\[
y\mapsto(F+g)^{-1}(y)
\]
around \((\bar y+g(\bar x),\bar x)\) is also single-valued and Lipschitz. Consequently, \(F+g\) is strongly metrically regular there, with inverse-localization modulus bounded by \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity and local inverse uniqueness persist when the perturbation satisfies the inverse-map small-gain inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Robinson Strong-Regularity Perturbation Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Small-Gain Boundary for Strong Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a single-valued inverse localization at equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\kappa>0\), define \(F(x)=x/\kappa\) and \(g(x)=-x/\kappa\) on \(\mathbb R\). The inverse \(F^{-1}(y)=\kappa y\) is single-valued and Lipschitz, but \(F+g\equiv0\) has no single-valued inverse localization at \((0,0)\). Hence strong metric regularity may fail when \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact cancellation at the small-gain threshold can destroy the unique local inverse branch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\), but \(F+g\) is not, while \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Small-Gain Boundary for Strong Metric Regularity

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\)
\(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\), and \(\kappa\lambda<1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\) with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz perturbation theorem for an isolated inverse image at one reference value.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that near \(\bar x\),
\[
\|x-\bar x\|\leq\kappa\,\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x)).
\]
If \(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\) and \(\kappa\lambda<1\), then near \(\bar x\),
\[
\|x-\bar x\|\leq\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}\operatorname{dist}(\bar y+g(\bar x),(F+g)(x)).
\]
Thus \(F+g\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity at a fixed reference value survives a Lipschitz perturbation whose slope is below the reciprocal subregularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Subregularity Perturbation Family

Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\) with exact modulus \(\kappa\), whereas \(F+g\equiv0\) is not strongly metrically subregular there. Thus preservation can fail when \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cancellation at equality can eliminate the isolated residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\), but \(F+g\) is not, while \(\kappa\operatorname{lip}g(0)=1\).

children.title: Additive Perturbation Stability

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\)
\(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda<1/\kappa\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum \(H:=F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\), with \(\operatorname{reg}H\leq\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued Lipschitz additive perturbations; set-valued additions require additional selection or excess estimates.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(H(x):=F(x)+g(x)\), metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is stable under a locally Lipschitz additive perturbation \(g\) whenever its Lipschitz constant \(\lambda\) satisfies \(\kappa\lambda<1\). Specifically, \(H\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\), and
\[
\operatorname{reg}H(\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\leq\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}.
\]
The denominator is the quantitative small-gain margin for the addition operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a sufficiently small Lipschitz mapping preserves metric regularity and yields an explicit inflated regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Perturbation Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-Valued Additive Perturbation Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric regularity of a sum under local sum-stability and an Aubin-small set-valued summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar w=\bar y+\bar z\), with \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\) and \(\bar z\in G(\bar x)\). Suppose \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\), \(G\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) with modulus \(\lambda\), \(\kappa\lambda<1\), and \((F,G)\) is locally sum-stable there: every nearby \(w\in(F+G)(x)\) near \(\bar w\) admits \(w=y+z\) with \(y\in F(x)\) near \(\bar y\) and \(z\in G(x)\) near \(\bar z\). Then \(F+G\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar w)\), with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small Aubin set-valued summand preserves metric regularity when nearby sum values possess compatible local decompositions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\)
\(G\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) with modulus \(\lambda\)
\((F,G)\) is locally sum-stable at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}(F+G)(\bar x\mid\bar y+\bar z)\leq\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Additive Perturbation Stability

children.title: Composite-Mapping Stability
children.top_down_role: Regularity behavior under composition of component mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicative Linear Openness Under Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of multifunctions under uniform local openness and intermediate-neighborhood control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\) and \(\bar z\in G(\bar y)\). Suppose there are neighborhoods \(U,V,W\), constants \(\alpha,\beta>0\), and \(r_0>0\) such that the following estimates hold whenever the indicated balls remain in the neighborhoods: for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and \(0<r<r_0\), \[B_Y(y,\alpha r)\subset F(B_X(x,r));\] and for every \((y,z)\in\operatorname{gph}G\cap(V\times W)\) and \(0<\rho<\alpha r_0\), \[B_Z(z,\beta\rho)\subset G(B_Y(y,\rho)).\] Then \(G\circ F\) is locally open at linear rate \(\alpha\beta\) near \((\bar x,\bar z)\), and hence is metrically regular there with modulus at most \(1/(\alpha\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform compatible linear openness of two mapping stages composes multiplicatively.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\) and \(\bar z\in G(\bar y)\)
\(F\) is uniformly linearly open with rate \(\alpha\) at nearby compatible graph points
\(G\) is uniformly linearly open with rate \(\beta\) at nearby compatible graph points
The openness balls remain inside common intermediate neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\circ F\) is linearly open with rate \(\alpha\beta\) and \(\operatorname{reg}(G\circ F)(\bar x\mid\bar z)\leq1/(\alpha\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Linear Openness Under Composition

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is locally open at linear rate \(\alpha>0\), uniformly at intermediate graph points
\(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) is locally open at linear rate \(\beta>0\), uniformly at compatible graph points
Nearby values of \(G\circ F\) admit compatible intermediate points in the stated neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\circ F\) is locally open at linear rate \(\alpha\beta\), hence metrically regular with modulus at most \(1/(\alpha\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-openness composition principle with explicit intermediate-point compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\). Suppose \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\), \(\bar z\in G(\bar y)\), and the stated openness estimates hold uniformly at all compatible nearby graph points. If nearby composition values possess intermediate points remaining in those neighborhoods, then for all sufficiently small \(r>0\),
\[
B_Z(\bar z,\alpha\beta r)\subset (G\circ F)(B_X(\bar x,r)).
\]
Consequently, \(G\circ F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) with modulus at most \(1/(\alpha\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform linear openness of two compatible mapping stages composes multiplicatively, producing metric regularity of the composite mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite-Mapping Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicative openness principle is plausible, but phrases such as “the stated openness estimates” and “compatible intermediate points” do not specify a checkable theorem hypothesis. An authoritative composition theorem is needed before the rate and metric-regularity conclusion can be trusted.

children.title: Nested Generalized-Equation Stability
children.top_down_role: Regularity behavior in nested generalized-equation constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Nested Fixed-Point Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive evaluation of the two localized component solution maps for a fixed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p\), choose \(x_0\) in the invariant neighborhood and iterate \[y_k=s(p,x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=t(p,y_k).\] Under the hypotheses of the parameterized nested small-gain theorem, \[\|x_k-x(p)\|\leq q^k\|x_0-x(p)\|,\qquad q=L_sL_t<1,\] and \(y_k\to y(p)\) geometrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating the two localized solution maps converges geometrically with contraction factor equal to the product of the cross-Lipschitz constants.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the parameterized nested small-gain theorem hold
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The alternating iteration converges geometrically to the unique nested solution pair with factor \(q=L_sL_t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Nested Fixed-Point Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Product Threshold for Nested Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar loss of uniqueness at the unit cross-sensitivity product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), let \(s(x)=x\) and \(t(y)=y\). Then \(L_s=L_t=1\), so \(L_sL_t=1\), and every pair \((x,y)\) with \(x=y\) solves \(y=s(x)\), \(x=t(y)\). Thus local uniqueness and contraction may fail at the unit product threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At cross-sensitivity product one, a nested system can have a continuum of local solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_sL_t=1\) and the coupled system is not locally unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Product Threshold for Nested Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameterized Nested Small-Gain Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two localized component solution maps on invariant complete neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a metric space and \(X,Y\) Banach spaces. Suppose \(s:P\times X\to Y\) and \(t:P\times Y\to X\) preserve fixed closed reference neighborhoods and satisfy \[\|s(p,x)-s(p',x')\|\leq M_s d(p,p')+L_s\|x-x'\|,\] \[\|t(p,y)-t(p',y')\|\leq M_t d(p,p')+L_t\|y-y'\|.\] If \(q:=L_sL_t<1\), then the coupled equations \(y=s(p,x)\), \(x=t(p,y)\) have a unique local solution pair \((x(p),y(p))\). Moreover, \[\operatorname{lip}x\leq\frac{M_t+L_tM_s}{1-q},\qquad \operatorname{lip}y\leq\frac{M_s+L_sM_t}{1-q}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nested localized solution maps yield a unique Lipschitz solution pair when their cross-sensitivity product is below one.
assumptions_latex: \(s\) and \(t\) preserve fixed closed reference neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nested system has a unique local Lipschitz solution pair with the stated parameter moduli.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Nested Small-Gain Theorem

assumptions_latex: \(s:P\times X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz in \(x\) with constant \(L_s\)
\(t:P\times Y\to X\) is locally Lipschitz in \(y\) with constant \(L_t\)
\(L_sL_t<1\) and both maps preserve chosen reference neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled equations \(y=s(p,x)\), \(x=t(p,y)\) have a locally unique Lipschitz solution pair \((x(p),y(p))\).

notation.meaning: localized solution maps of the inner and outer generalized equations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-gain theorem for two nested generalized equations represented by localized solution maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let localized inner and outer generalized equations define maps \(y=s(p,x)\) and \(x=t(p,y)\) near \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\). Suppose \(s\) and \(t\) are locally Lipschitz, their cross-variable constants satisfy \(L_sL_t<1\), and the maps preserve fixed reference neighborhoods. Then
\[
x=t(p,s(p,x))
\]
is a contraction in \(x\). Hence the coupled system
\[
y=s(p,x),\qquad x=t(p,y)
\]
has a locally unique solution \((x(p),y(p))\), and this solution pair is locally Lipschitz in \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested pair of locally stable generalized equations remains uniquely Lipschitz stable when the product of their cross-sensitivity constants is below one.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Generalized-Equation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contraction argument supports local uniqueness for each fixed parameter, but the claimed Lipschitz dependence on the parameter requires explicit joint or parameterwise Lipschitz assumptions and neighborhood conditions. No source is supplied to determine the intended precise version.

children.title: Chain-Rule Qualification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Qualification limits governing stability transfer through composition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\Phi^{-1}(C)}(0)=\mathbb R\) but \(D\Phi(0)^*N_C(0)=\{0\}\), so the normal-cone chain formula fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of inverse-image normal calculus when the chain-rule qualification is violated.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(C:=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(\Phi(x):=x^2\). At \(\bar x=0\), the qualification
\[
N_C(\Phi(0))\cap\ker D\Phi(0)^*=\{0\}
\]
fails because both sets on the left equal \(\mathbb R\). Moreover, \(\Phi^{-1}(C)=\{0\}\), so
\[
N_{\Phi^{-1}(C)}(0)=\mathbb R,
\qquad
D\Phi(0)^*N_C(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus the unqualified inverse-image normal formula, and hence the corresponding coderivative chain rule, can be strictly false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the inverse image of zero under the squaring map, failure of the normal qualification makes the formal chain-rule right side strictly too small.
knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Qualification Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualified Normal-Cone Preimage Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth inverse-image calculus; generally an inclusion in the nonconvex setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), and let \(C\subset\mathbb R^m\) be locally closed at \(\Phi(\bar x)\). If \[N_C(\Phi(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla\Phi(\bar x)^*=\{0\},\] then \[N_{\Phi^{-1}(C)}(\bar x)\subset\nabla\Phi(\bar x)^*N_C(\Phi(\bar x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excluding nonzero abnormal target normals annihilated by the adjoint derivative yields the limiting-normal preimage inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\Phi^{-1}(C)}(\bar x)\subset\nabla\Phi(\bar x)^*N_C(\Phi(\bar x))\).

The product spaces carry the maximum norm

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(X_1\times X_2\) and \(Y_1\times Y_2\) with maximum norms. If \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\) with modulus \(\kappa_i\) for \(i=1,2\), then the Cartesian product mapping
\[
(F_1\times F_2)(x_1,x_2):=F_1(x_1)\times F_2(x_2)
\]
is metrically regular at the product reference point. Its modulus satisfies
\[
\operatorname{reg}(F_1\times F_2)\leq\max\{\kappa_1,\kappa_2\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under maximum product norms, a finite product of metrically regular mappings is metrically regular with modulus bounded by the largest component modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Metric Regularity of Finite Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-metric-regularity counterpart of Cartesian-product stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite maximum-norm product spaces, \(F_1\times\cdots\times F_m\) is strongly metrically regular at the product reference pair if and only if every \(F_i\) is strongly metrically regular at its component reference pair. If \(\kappa_i\) is the exact Lipschitz modulus of the localized inverse of \(F_i\), then the exact modulus of the localized product inverse is \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\kappa_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite uncoupled product is strongly metrically regular exactly when every component is, and its localized inverse modulus is the largest component modulus.
assumptions_latex: The Cartesian product has finitely many factors.
The domain and range carry maximum product norms.
Localized component inverses are taken at the component reference pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1\times\cdots\times F_m\text{ is strongly metrically regular}\iff F_i\text{ is strongly metrically regular for every }i\), with inverse modulus \(\max_i\kappa_i\).

notation.meaning: exact Lipschitz modulus of the localized inverse of component \(i\)

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Metric Regularity of Finite Products

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Necessity and Exact Product Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse component implication and exact modulus for finite uncoupled products under maximum norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_m\) act between finite maximum-norm product spaces. If \(F\) is metrically regular at the product reference pair, then every \(F_i\) is metrically regular at its component reference pair and \[\operatorname{reg}F_i\le \operatorname{reg}F.\] Together with product preservation, this yields \[\operatorname{reg}(F_1\times\cdots\times F_m)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\operatorname{reg}F_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity of a finite uncoupled product is equivalent to componentwise metric regularity, and under maximum norms its exact modulus is the largest component modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(F=F_1\times\cdots\times F_m\) is a finite Cartesian product.
The domain and range carry maximum product norms.
The reference pair is the Cartesian product of the component reference pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is metrically regular}\iff F_i\text{ is metrically regular for every }i\), with \(\operatorname{reg}F=\max_i\operatorname{reg}F_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Necessity and Exact Product Modulus

children.title: Block-System Stability
children.top_down_role: Regularity behavior of block-structured generalized equations.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-System Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite block systems with a strongly metrically regular diagonal part and a small single-valued Lipschitz coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) and \(\mathcal Y:=Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_m\) be Banach product spaces. Let \(D:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_m:\mathcal X\rightrightarrows\mathcal Y\), and let \(\bar y\in D(\bar x)\). Suppose \(D\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), with a localized inverse having Lipschitz constant \(\kappa\). If \(C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\) and \(\kappa\lambda<1\), then \(H:=D+C\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+C(\bar x))\). Its localized inverse can be chosen with Lipschitz constant at most
\[
\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite diagonal block mapping with a strongly regular local inverse remains strongly metrically regular after adding a Lipschitz coupling whose slope satisfies the inverse-map small-gain condition.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) and \(\mathcal Y:=Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_m\) are Banach product spaces

\(D:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_m:\mathcal X\rightrightarrows\mathcal Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), where \(\bar y\in D(\bar x)\), and its localized inverse has Lipschitz constant \(\kappa\)
\(C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H:=D+C\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+C(\bar x))\), with inverse-localization constant at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: finite product domain and range spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Triangular Block Stability Without Small Gain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequentially solvable triangular coupling of two strongly metrically regular blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) be strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\), with localized inverse Lipschitz moduli \(\kappa_i\), and let \(C:X_1\to Y_2\) be locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x_1\) with modulus \(L\). Define \[H(x_1,x_2):=\big(F_1(x_1),F_2(x_2)+C(x_1)\big).\] Then \(H\) is strongly metrically regular at \(((\bar x_1,\bar x_2),(\bar y_1,\bar y_2+C(\bar x_1)))\). Under maximum product norms, a localized inverse has Lipschitz modulus at most \[\max\{\kappa_1,\kappa_2(1+L\kappa_1)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triangularly coupled block system remains strongly metrically regular without a small-gain restriction because its blocks admit sequential inversion.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is strongly metrically regular at its reference pair.
\(C\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x_1\) with modulus \(L\).
The product spaces carry maximum norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is strongly metrically regular with localized-inverse modulus at most \(\max\{\kappa_1,\kappa_2(1+L\kappa_1)\}\).

children.title: Coupling-Induced Regularity Loss
children.top_down_role: Loss of componentwise regularity after introduction of cross-block coupling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Two-Block Coupling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-block linear family showing that regular diagonal blocks do not ensure regularity after cross-coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), define \[H_{a,b}(x_1,x_2):=(x_1+a x_2,\,x_2+b x_1).\] The two diagonal blocks are identities. The coupled mapping is strongly metrically regular, equivalently metrically regular, exactly when \(1-ab\ne0\). With Euclidean norms, in that regime \[\operatorname{reg}H_{a,b}=\|H_{a,b}^{-1}\|=\sigma_{\min}(H_{a,b})^{-1}.\] If \(ab=1\), the coupled mapping is not metrically regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two regular identity blocks lose regularity when their cross-coupling makes the block matrix singular; the exact boundary is one minus the coupling product equal to zero.
assumptions_latex: The product spaces carry Euclidean norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_{a,b}\text{ is metrically regular}\iff1-ab\ne0\), and otherwise coupling destroys regularity.

notation.meaning: smallest singular value of the block matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Two-Block Coupling Boundary

assumptions_latex: The component spaces are \(\mathbb{R}\), with the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled mapping is metrically regular exactly when \(1-ab\ne 0\); regularity is lost when \(ab=1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional linear metric regularity is equivalent to invertibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete two-block linear boundary showing that individually regular diagonal blocks do not ensure coupled regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(H_{a,b}:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \(H_{a,b}(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+a x_2,x_2+b x_1)\). Each uncoupled diagonal block is the identity and hence strongly metrically regular. The coupled mapping is strongly metrically regular precisely when its matrix is nonsingular, equivalently when \(1-ab\ne0\). In that case its exact regularity modulus is \(\operatorname{reg}H_{a,b}=1/\sigma_{\min}(H_{a,b})\). If \(ab=1\), the matrix has a nonzero kernel, so metric regularity fails despite regularity of both diagonal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two regular identity blocks can lose regularity after coupling: the coupled linear system is regular exactly when its determinant, one minus the coupling product, is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Induced Regularity Loss

children.title: Fixed-Point Representation Stability
children.top_down_role: Preservation of regularity under fixed-point reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Representation Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global contraction version of stability transfer from a fixed-point representation to its residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(q\in[0,1)\), and let \(T:X\to X\) satisfy \(\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\). For the residual mapping \(R:=I-T\), every equation \(R(x)=u\), with \(u\in X\), has a unique solution. Hence \(R\) is bijective and \[\|R^{-1}(u)-R^{-1}(v)\|\le \frac{1}{1-q}\|u-v\|\qquad(u,v\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a contraction on a Banach space, the fixed-point residual is bijective and its inverse is globally Lipschitz with modulus at most one over one minus the contraction modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) satisfies \(\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual \(R=I-T\) is bijective and \(\operatorname{lip}(R^{-1})\le (1-q)^{-1}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniformly Contractive Parametric Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz stability of fixed points under a uniformly contractive parameterized representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a metric space, \(X\) a Banach space, and \(T:P\times X\to X\). Suppose that for some \(q\in[0,1)\) and \(L\ge0\), \[\|T(p,x)-T(p,x')\|\le q\|x-x'\|,\qquad \|T(p,x)-T(p',x)\|\le Ld(p,p')\] for all admissible \(p,p',x,x'\). Then every \(T(p,\cdot)\) has a unique fixed point \(x(p)\), and \[\|x(p)-x(p')\|\le \frac{L}{1-q}d(p,p').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly contractive fixed-point equations have unique solutions that depend Lipschitz-continuously on the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(P\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}x(\cdot)\le L/(1-q)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Contractive Parametric Fixed Points

children.title: Regularized-Equation Stability
children.top_down_role: Preservation of regularity under regularized representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Monotonicity Contraction of the Resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative resolvent stability for a maximal strongly monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal and \(m\)-strongly monotone, where \(m>0\). For every \(\lambda>0\), the resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}:=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is everywhere defined and \[\|J_{\lambda A}u-J_{\lambda A}v\|\le \frac{1}{1+\lambda m}\|u-v\|\qquad(u,v\in H).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a maximal strongly monotone operator is globally contractive with factor at most one over one plus the regularization parameter times the monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}J_{\lambda A}\le(1+\lambda m)^{-1}<1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Contraction of the Resolvent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Yosida Inverse Representation and Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse identity and quantitative inverse stability of Yosida regularization under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\), \(A\), \(m\), and \(\lambda\) satisfy the assumptions above, and define \(A_\lambda:=\lambda^{-1}(I-J_{\lambda A})\). Then, as mappings on \(H\), \[A_\lambda^{-1}=A^{-1}+\lambda I.\] In particular, \(A_\lambda^{-1}\) is single-valued and globally Lipschitz, with \[\operatorname{lip}(A_\lambda^{-1})\le m^{-1}+\lambda.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of the Yosida regularization is the inverse of the original operator plus a scaled identity, so strong-monotonicity inverse stability is retained with modulus increased by at most the regularization parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal and \(m\)-strongly monotone with \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_\lambda^{-1}=A^{-1}+\lambda I\) and \(\operatorname{lip}(A_\lambda^{-1})\le m^{-1}+\lambda\).

notation.meaning: inverse mapping of the Yosida regularization

knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Inverse Representation and Stability

assumptions_latex: The operator \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is maximal and \(m\)-strongly monotone for some \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Yosida regularization satisfies \(A_\lambda^{-1}=A^{-1}+\lambda I\) and \(\operatorname{lip}(A_\lambda^{-1})\le m^{-1}+\lambda\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent identities and strong-monotonicity inverse estimate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly monotone maximal-operator version of stability under Yosida regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in X\), the inclusion \(y=A_\lambda x\) holds exactly when there exists \(z=J_{\lambda A}x\) such that \(y\in A z\) and \(x=z+\lambda y\). Consequently, \(A_\lambda^{-1}(y)=A^{-1}(y)+\lambda y\). Strong monotonicity makes \(A^{-1}\) single-valued on its range and Lipschitz with modulus at most \(m^{-1}\). Therefore \(A_\lambda^{-1}\) is Lipschitz with modulus at most \(m^{-1}+\lambda\), so the regularized equation retains stable inverse solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Yosida regularization preserves stable inverse solvability of a strongly monotone maximal operator, with inverse Lipschitz bound increased by at most the regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Equation Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits regularized-equation stability and the Yosida inverse identity is standard, but the identity, surjectivity implications, and Lipschitz estimate lack an inspectable supporting source. The statement also includes derivational text.

children.title: Representation-Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring stability conclusions between original and transformed representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Identical Zero Sets Without Error-Bound Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample separating zero-set equivalence from preservation of Lipschitz conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r,s:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(r(x)=x\) and \(s(x)=x^3\). Both residual equations have the zero set \(\{0\}\), and \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})=|r(x)|.\] However, there are no \(\kappa<\infty\) and neighborhood \(U\) of zero such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})\le \kappa |s(x)|\qquad(x\in U).\] Thus equality of zero sets alone does not preserve metric subregularity or a local Lipschitz error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the residual x by its cube preserves the solution set but destroys every local Lipschitz error bound at zero.
assumptions_latex: The residual equations are considered locally at \(0\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^{-1}(0)=s^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), while only \(r\) has a local Lipschitz error bound at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Identical Zero Sets Without Error-Bound Transfer

assumptions_latex: Residual equations are considered locally at the common solution \(0\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent zero sets need not transfer metric subregularity or Lipschitz error bounds between residual representations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample separating solution-set equivalence from preservation of Lipschitz conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equations \(r(x)=0\) and \(s(x)=0\), where \(r(x)=x\) and \(s(x)=x^3\), have the identical solution set \(\{0\}\). The residual \(r\) satisfies the exact local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})=|r(x)|\). No finite \(\kappa\) and neighborhood of zero can satisfy \(|x|\le\kappa|s(x)|\), because this would require \(1\le\kappa x^2\) for every sufficiently small nonzero \(x\). Thus a non-bi-Lipschitz residual transformation can destroy metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical solution sets do not preserve conditioning: replacing the residual x by its cube destroys every local Lipschitz error bound at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Transfer Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar example correctly targets a representation-transfer failure boundary, but no inspectable source is supplied and the statement contains the argument establishing failure of the error bound.
