knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocity with the Exact Linear-Openness Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quantitative equivalence among metric regularity, inverse Aubin behavior, and local linear openness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). With compatible local definitions of the exact moduli, \[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)}.\] Here \(\operatorname{lop}F\) is the supremum of admissible local linear covering rates, with \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity and inverse-Aubin moduli coincide and are reciprocal to the exact linear-openness rate.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is a multifunction between metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The exact regularity, inverse-Aubin, and linear-covering moduli use compatible local neighborhoods and metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}=1/\operatorname{lop}F\) at the reference graph point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\kappa(F;\bar x\mid\bar y)\) as the infimum of all \(\kappa\ge0\) for which neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) exist such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\) for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\). This exact metric-regularity modulus equals the exact Lipschitz-like, or Aubin, modulus of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). The value is \(+\infty\) when no such finite bound exists.

children.title: Radius of Regularity
children.top_down_role: Perturbation-radius theory for loss of regularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small-Gain Lower Bound for the Regularity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive single-valued Lipschitz perturbations fixing the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) between Banach spaces, with \(\kappa=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)<+\infty\). For admissible \(h:X\to Y\) satisfying \(h(\bar x)=0\), measured by their local Lipschitz modulus, every \(h\) with \(\operatorname{lip}h(\bar x)<1/\kappa\) preserves metric regularity of \(F+h\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{Lip}}\operatorname{reg}F\ge\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},\] with \(1/0:=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal exact regularity modulus is a guaranteed lower bound on the additive Lipschitz perturbation needed to destroy metric regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
Perturbations are single-valued, fix the reference value, and are measured by local Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{Lip}}\operatorname{reg}F\ge1/\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Regularity radius for the stated additive Lipschitz class

assumptions_latex: A normed perturbation class \((\mathcal P,\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal P})\) is fixed.
Each \(P\in\mathcal P\) defines a perturbed multifunction \(F_P\), with \(F_0=F\).
The reference graph point is transported by a specified rule \(P\mapsto(\bar x_P,\bar y_P)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to an explicitly chosen perturbation model and reference-point transport rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal P\) consist of perturbations \(P\) for which \(F_P\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x_P,\bar y_P)\). The radius of regularity is defined by \[\operatorname{rad}_{\mathcal P}\operatorname{reg}F:=\inf\{\|P\|_{\mathcal P}:P\in\mathcal P\setminus\mathcal R\}.\] The infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Because both admissibility and perturbation size depend on \(\mathcal P\), this radius is not intrinsic until the perturbation class, norm, and reference-point convention have been fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radius of regularity is the smallest admissible perturbation size that destroys metric regularity, relative to a fixed perturbation model and norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Radius of Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perturbation-relative definition fits the radius-of-regularity topic and introduces the necessary perturbation model, norm, and transported reference point, but it has no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended Eckart–Young formula for positively homogeneous multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation distance to loss of bounded inverse behavior, with rank-one and weak-star continuity refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F:X\rightrightarrows Y$ be a positively homogeneous multifunction between Banach spaces. Then
\[\inf_{g\in\mathcal L(X,Y)}\{\|g\|\mid \|(F+g)^{-1}\|=\infty\}=\frac{1}{\|F^{-1}\|}.\]
The infimum is unchanged if $g$ is restricted to rank-one bounded linear operators. If $X=Z^*$ for some Banach space $Z$, the perturbations may additionally be restricted to weak$^*$-to-norm continuous rank-one operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positively homogeneous multifunction, the least norm of a linear perturbation making the inverse unbounded equals the reciprocal inverse norm. Rank-one perturbations suffice, including weak-star-to-norm continuous ones when the domain is a dual space.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the final refinement, }X=Z^*\text{ for some Banach space }Z
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{g\in\mathcal L(X,Y)}\{\|g\|\mid\|(F+g)^{-1}\|=\infty\}=1/\|F^{-1}\|,\text{ with the stated rank-one and weak}^*\text{-continuity restrictions.}

children.title: Distance to Ill-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Distance from a generalized equation to loss of stable local solvability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Properties of Distance to Ill-Posedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of distance to a nonempty ill-posed subset of a metric model space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varnothing\ne\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal M\), let \(\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M)=d_{\mathcal M}(M,\Sigma)\). Then \[|\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M)-\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(N)|\le d_{\mathcal M}(M,N)\] and \[\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M)=0\iff M\in\overline\Sigma.\] In particular, if \(\Sigma\) is closed, every model outside \(\Sigma\) has positive distance from ill-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the ill-posed set is 1-Lipschitz and vanishes exactly on its closure.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,d_{\mathcal M})\) is a metric model space.
\(\varnothing\ne\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal M\) is the selected ill-posed model class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M)-\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(N)|\le d_{\mathcal M}(M,N)\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}^{-1}(0)=\overline\Sigma\).

notation.meaning: Distance to the ill-posed model class

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Properties of Distance to Ill-Posedness

assumptions_latex: The model space \((\mathcal M,d_{\mathcal M})\) parametrizes generalized equations.
The subset \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal M\) consists exactly of models lacking the selected stable local solvability property.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: metric distance to the complement of the well-posed model class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-space definition; the selected solvability property and model metric must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a model \(M\in\mathcal M\), define \[\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M):=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal M}(M,\Sigma)=\inf_{N\in\Sigma}d_{\mathcal M}(M,N).\] If \(\Sigma\) is empty, set \(\delta_{\mathrm{ill}}(M)=+\infty\). A positive value means that every model within that distance retains the chosen stable local solvability property. When \(d_{\mathcal M}(M,M_P)=\|P\|_{\mathcal P}\) and every nearby model is represented by an admissible perturbation, this distance coincides with the corresponding radius of regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to ill-posedness is the model-space distance from a generalized equation to the set of equations lacking the chosen stable local solvability property.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The model-space distance definition fits the leaf, but no source is supplied. children.title: Representation-Dependent Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Variation of condition measures across equivalent equation forms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditioning Under Invertible Linear Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-modulus bounds for linear changes of variable and residual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:=B\circ F\circ A^{-1}\). Then \(G^{-1}(v)=A F^{-1}(B^{-1}v)\), metric regularity is preserved, and \[\frac{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)}{\|A^{-1}\|\,\|B\|}\leq \operatorname{reg}G(A\bar x\mid B\bar y)\leq \|A\|\,\|B^{-1}\|\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).\] Consequently, equivalent linear representations may have arbitrarily different numerical moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible linear coordinate changes preserve metric regularity but can alter its modulus by the conditioning of the coordinate transformations.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to X\) and \(B:Y\to Y\) are invertible linear maps
\(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=B\circ F\circ A^{-1}\) is metrically regular and its exact modulus satisfies the stated two-sided bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Under Invertible Linear Reparameterization

assumptions_latex: The spaces \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
The linear maps \(A:X\to X\) and \(B:Y\to Y\) are invertible.
The multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(G=B\circ F\circ A^{-1}\), the condition moduli satisfy \(\kappa/(\|A^{-1}\|\|B\|)\le\kappa_G\le\|A\|\|B^{-1}\|\kappa\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: inverse Aubin moduli transform under linear bi-Lipschitz coordinate changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning under invertible linear changes of variables and residual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse of the transformed multifunction satisfies \(G^{-1}(v)=A F^{-1}(B^{-1}v)\). Consequently, composition estimates for exact Lipschitz-like moduli give \[\frac{\kappa}{\|A^{-1}\|\,\|B\|}\le \kappa_G\le \|A\|\,\|B^{-1}\|\kappa.\] Thus invertible coordinate changes preserve metric regularity but generally change its numerical condition measure. In particular, algebraically equivalent representations can be arbitrarily differently conditioned when the coordinate transformations are poorly conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible linear reformulations preserve regularity but scale its modulus according to the conditioning of the variable and residual transformations.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-change bounds fit representation-dependent conditioning and are mathematically plausible, but the exact-modulus inequalities lack an inspectable source. The statement also includes derivational text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Convergence and Quadratic Rate of Newton's Method

children.title: Exact Newton Generalized-Equation Methods
children.top_down_role: Newtonian methods using exact local generalized-equation models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Newton Generalized-Equation Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine linearization of the smooth term while retaining the multifunction unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, \(f:X\to Y\) be Fréchet differentiable on a neighborhood of the iterates, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\). Starting from \(x_0\), choose at each iteration the prescribed localized solution \(x_{k+1}\) of \[0\in f(x_k)+Df(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}).\] The method is defined while this localized model has a solution; it terminates when the chosen stopping rule is met. Exactness means that no residual is admitted in the model inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact generalized-equation Newton solves each affine derivative model exactly, retaining the set-valued term at the new point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable near the iterates.
\(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), an initial point \(x_0\), a localization rule, and a stopping rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted iterate satisfies the exact affine generalized equation.

notation.meaning: Exact Fréchet derivative used at iteration k.
Set-valued term retained in the model.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Newton Generalized-Equation Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Quadratic Convergence of Exact Newton Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Robinson-type convergence theorem for the exact generalized-equation Newton iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\in f(\bar x)+F(\bar x)\), and define \(L(x):=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+F(x)\). Suppose \(Df\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and \(L^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization around \((0,\bar x)\). Then every sufficiently close initial point generates uniquely localized exact Newton iterates, and for some \(C>0\), \[\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le C\|x_k-\bar x\|^2\] whenever the iterates are sufficiently close to \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity of the reference affine model and a Lipschitz derivative give locally well-defined, quadratically convergent exact Newton steps.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(0\in f(\bar x)+F(\bar x)\).
\(L^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization around \((0,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le C\|x_k- ar x\|^2\) locally for the uniquely localized exact Newton sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Quadratic Convergence of Exact Newton Steps

assumptions_latex: The mapping \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable near the current iterate.
The multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) admits a solution of each local Newton inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration solves the exact affine generalized-equation model and returns an iterate satisfying a prescribed stopping test.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Newton linearization for generalized equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Newton iteration for the generalized equation \(0\in f(x)+F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in X\) and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), at iteration \(k\) choose \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying the exact linearized generalized equation \[0\in f(x_k)+Df(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}).\] Stop and output \(x_k\) when the selected computable residual measure \(\rho(x_k)\) satisfies \(\rho(x_k)\le\varepsilon\); otherwise continue. If the local inclusion has multiple solutions, a prescribed localization selects the solution near \(x_k\). The method is exact because no error is admitted in solving the local generalized-equation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each step, exact Newton solves the generalized equation obtained by affine linearization of the smooth term while retaining the set-valued term unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Newton Generalized-Equation Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct knowledge kind, but no generalized-equation Newton source is cited. The spaces and mapping type of the set-valued term, the residual measure, and the localization rule are not fully specified.

children.title: Inexact Newton Generalized-Equation Methods
children.top_down_role: Newtonian methods allowing controlled local-model solution errors.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Controlled Inexact Newton Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact solution of the affine generalized-equation model with a prescribed residual gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, \(f:X\to Y\) be Fréchet differentiable near the iterates, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\). Given \(x_0\), prescribed tolerances \(\delta_k\ge0\), a localization rule, and a stopping rule, choose \((x_{k+1},r_k)\) satisfying \[r_k\in f(x_k)+Df(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}),\qquad \|r_k\|\le\delta_k.\] Exact Newton is recovered when \(\delta_k=0\). Relative-forcing variants specify \(\delta_k\) using a step, current-error, or computable residual gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact Newton admits a controlled residual in each otherwise exact affine generalized-equation model.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\(x_0\), \((\delta_k)\), localization, and stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted model residual satisfies \(\|r_k\|\le\delta_k\).

notation.meaning: Admitted residual in the affine model.
Prescribed absolute or gauge-derived residual tolerance.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Controlled Inexact Newton Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forcing-Term Rate Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local rate consequences for current-error-relative model residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the reference affine generalized equation is strongly regular at \((\bar x,0)\), \(Df\) is locally Lipschitz, and localized inexact steps satisfy \[r_k\in f(x_k)+Df(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}),\qquad \|r_k\|\le\eta_k\|x_k-\bar x\|.\] Then locally there are \(C_1,C_2>0\) such that \[\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le\bigl(C_1\eta_k+C_2\|x_k-\bar x\|\bigr)\|x_k-\bar x\|.\] Uniformly sufficiently small \(\eta_k\) yields Q-linear convergence, while \(\eta_k\to0\) yields Q-superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed small forcing level gives a linear rate, whereas a vanishing forcing level restores superlinear convergence.
assumptions_latex: The reference affine generalized equation is strongly regular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le(C_1\eta_k+C_2\|x_k-\bar x\|)\|x_k-\bar x\|\), with the stated linear and superlinear consequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Forcing-Term Rate Transfer

assumptions_latex: The mapping \(f:X\to Y\) is Fréchet differentiable near the iterates.
A forcing sequence \((\eta_k)\) with \(\eta_k\ge0\) and an error gauge \(\psi_k\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration permits a model residual \(e_k\) satisfying \(\|e_k\|\le\eta_k\psi_k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: inexact generalized Newton steps use controlled residual inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-controlled inexact Newton template; convergence requires a separately specified forcing rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\), choose at iteration \(k\) a pair \((x_{k+1},e_k)\) such that \[e_k\in f(x_k)+Df(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}),\qquad \|e_k\|\le\eta_k\psi_k.\] The gauge may be chosen as \(\psi_k=\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\) or as a computable current residual, but that choice is part of the algorithm specification. Stop and output \(x_k\) when the prescribed residual measure is at most \(\varepsilon\). Exact Newton is recovered when \(e_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact Newton approximately solves each affine generalized-equation model, with a forcing rule bounding the admitted model residual.

children.title: Quasi-Newton Generalized-Equation Methods
children.top_down_role: Generalized-equation methods using approximate derivative models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-Newton Generalized-Equation Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine generalized-equation models using prescribed bounded-linear derivative approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, \(f:X\to Y\) be differentiable near the iterates, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\). Given \(x_0\), \(B_0\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), a prescribed update rule \(B_{k+1}=\mathcal U_k(B_k,x_k,x_{k+1},f)\), localization, and stopping rules, choose \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying \[0\in f(x_k)+B_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}),\] and then apply the update rule. Taking \(B_k=Df(x_k)\) recovers exact Newton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-Newton generalized-equation methods replace the exact derivative by updated bounded-linear models.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0,B_0\), an update rule, localization, and stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each step solves the generalized-equation model determined by \(B_k\), after which \(B_k\) is updated.

notation.meaning: Approximate derivative used in iteration k.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Newton Generalized-Equation Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dennis–Moré Superlinear Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local directional-accuracy criterion for quasi-Newton generalized-equation models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), and suppose \[0\in f(x_k)+B_ks_k+F(x_{k+1}).\] Assume the localized models are uniformly strongly regular, \(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), and \(\|s_k\|=O(\|x_k-\bar x\|)\). If, along nonzero steps, \[\frac{\|(B_k-Df(x_k))s_k\|}{\|s_k\|}\longrightarrow0,\] then \[\frac{\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|}{\|x_k-\bar x\|}\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform model stability and vanishing derivative-model error along realized steps imply Q-superlinear quasi-Newton convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\to\bar x\) and the quasi-Newton inclusions hold.
The localized models are uniformly strongly regular.
\(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable and \(\|s_k\|=O(\|x_k-\bar x\|)\).
The displayed Dennis–Moré condition holds on nonzero steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Dennis–Moré Superlinear Criterion

assumptions_latex: The mapping \(f:X\to Y\) is differentiable near the iterates.
A sequence of bounded linear derivative approximations \(B_k:X\to Y\) and a model-solution rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method replaces \(Df(x_k)\) by \(B_k\) in each local generalized-equation model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: quasi-Newton generalized equations replace the exact derivative by an updated linear model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract quasi-Newton template with a Dennis-Moré-type local accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\) and \(B_0\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(x_{k+1}\) satisfying \[0\in f(x_k)+B_k(x_{k+1}-x_k)+F(x_{k+1}),\] then construct \(B_{k+1}\) from the prescribed secant or approximation update. Stop when the selected residual or step test meets its tolerance. A standard local superlinear-accuracy requirement along nonzero steps \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) is \[\frac{\|(B_k-Df(x_k))s_k\|}{\|s_k\|}\longrightarrow0.\] The update rule and localization of the model solution are required algorithmic inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Newton Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semismooth residual-equation interface with Clarke generalized Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz and semismooth near \(\bar x\), with \(R(\bar x)=0\), and suppose every matrix in the Clarke generalized Jacobian \(\partial R(\bar x)\) is nonsingular. For every sufficiently close initial point \(x_0\), the iteration obtained by selecting \(V_k\in\partial R(x_k)\), solving \(V_kd_k=-R(x_k)\), and setting \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\) is locally well-defined and converges superlinearly to \(\bar x\). If \(R\) is strongly semismooth with a second-order remainder, the convergence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a root, a semismooth residual whose Clarke generalized Jacobians are all nonsingular admits locally well-defined generalized-Jacobian Newton steps with superlinear convergence; strong semismoothness with a second-order remainder yields quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz and semismooth near \(\bar x\).
Every matrix in the Clarke generalized Jacobian \(\partial R(\bar x)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every sufficiently close \(x_0\), the generalized-Jacobian Newton iteration is locally well-defined and converges superlinearly to \(\bar x\); under strong semismoothness with a second-order remainder, it converges quadratically.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Semismooth Newton Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-controlled inexact solution of generalized-Jacobian Newton systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace the exact Newton equation by \[V_kd_k=-R(x_k)+r_k,\qquad V_k\in\partial R(x_k),\] and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\). Under local semismoothness and uniform inverse bounds, a sufficiently small uniform forcing bound \(\|r_k\|\leq\eta\|R(x_k)\|\) yields local linear convergence; \(\|r_k\|\leq\eta_k\|R(x_k)\|\) with \(\eta_k\to0\) preserves superlinear convergence. Under strong semismoothness, \(\|r_k\|=O(\|R(x_k)\|^2)\) preserves quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-controlled inexact Newton solves retain linear, superlinear, or quadratic local convergence according to the forcing sequence.
assumptions_latex: R\text{ is locally Lipschitz and semismooth at a root }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta_k\to0\text{ preserves superlinear convergence; strong semismoothness and }\|r_k\|=O(\|R(x_k)\|^2)\text{ preserve quadratic convergence.}
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Semismooth Newton Interface

assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\iff F_C(z)=0\) under the displayed variable correspondence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-set normal-map formulation and its Newton equation.

source_refs.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_C(z):=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz\). The correspondences \(x=P_Cz\), \(z=x-F(x)\), and \(z-x=-F(x)\in N_C(x)\) identify the solutions of \(F_C(z)=0\) with the solutions of \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\). A normal-map Newton interface selects \(A_k\in\partial F_C(z_k)\), solves \(A_kd_k=-F_C(z_k)\), sets \(z_{k+1}=z_k+d_k\), and obtains the associated constrained point \(x_k=P_Cz_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constrained generalized equation is represented equivalently by a normal-map equation, and generalized Newton steps for that equation produce associated constrained points through projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Newton Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Map Newton Matrix Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting derivative matrices used by Newton steps for a convex-set normal map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be \(C^1\), set \(x=P_Cz\), and let \(B\in\partial_B P_C(z)\), so that \(P_C'(z_j)\to B\) along differentiability points \(z_j\to z\). Then the corresponding limiting Jacobian of \(F_C(z)=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz\) is \[A=F'(x)B+I-B.\] A normal-map Newton step solves \(Ad=-F_C(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting projector derivative gives the normal-map Newton matrix \(F'(x)B+I-B\).
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(x)B+I-B\in\partial_B F_C(z)\text{ along the corresponding differentiability sequence.}
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Newton Matrix Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Normal-Map Models Do Not Define Unique Newton Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematically correct but canonically owned by the dedicated normal-map irregularity leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an admissible normal-map Newton matrix \(A\) is singular, \(Ad=-F_C(z)\) may be inconsistent or have multiple solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular normal-map derivative need not define a unique Newton step.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an admissible normal-map Newton matrix}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ad=-F_C(z)\text{ need not have a unique solution.}
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Normal-Map Models Do Not Define Unique Newton Steps

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z_k\), choose an active smooth selection \(H_{i_k}\) satisfying \(H_{i_k}(z_k)=H(z_k)\), and form the affine model \(L_k(z_k+d):=H(z_k)+H_{i_k}'(z_k)d\). Solve \(L_k(z_k+d_k)=0\); if no solution exists, report model failure. Otherwise set \(z_{k+1}:=z_k+d_k\). Stop with output \(z_k\) when \(H(z_k)=0\), or with an approximate solution when a prescribed residual tolerance \(\lVert H(z_k)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an active smooth piece, solve its affine Newton model, update, and stop when the residual meets the prescribed tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Piece Solvability Does Not Ensure Model Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for arbitrary active-selection Newton steps at interfaces between pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solving \(H(z_k)+H_{i_k}'(z_k)d=0\) certifies only a zero of the selected affine model. If \(z_k+d\) is outside a region on which \(H_{i_k}\) represents \(H\), then \(H(z_k+d)=0\) is not guaranteed. A consistency or residual test is therefore required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solvable active-piece model may extrapolate beyond its valid region and need not solve the original equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_k+d\text{ outside the selected piece's validity region}\ \Longrightarrow\ H(z_k+d)=0\text{ is not guaranteed.}
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Solvability Does Not Ensure Model Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Step on a Consistent Affine Piece
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness of active-piece Newton linearization for a piecewise-affine equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(H(z)=A_i z+b_i\) on a selection region \(P_i\), where \(A_i\) is nonsingular. If \(z_k,z_*\in P_i\) and \(H(z_*)=0\), then \[H(z_k)+A_i d_k=0\] has the unique solution \(d_k=z_*-z_k\), and hence \(z_{k+1}=z_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On one nonsingular affine piece containing the iterate and root, the active-piece Newton step reaches the root exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_k=z_*-z_k\quad\text{and}\quad z_{k+1}=z_*.

notation.meaning: linear part of the selected affine piece

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Step on a Consistent Affine Piece

children.title: Implicit-Function Theorems for Newton Iterations
children.top_down_role: Implicit-mapping principles specialized to Newton iteration maps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of the Small-Perturbation Condition Can Destroy Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure at the contraction boundary for an implicit Newton update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(y)=y\), which is strongly metrically regular with inverse modulus \(\kappa=1\), and let \(g(x,y)=-y\), whose state Lipschitz modulus is \(L_y=1\). Then \(\kappa L_y=1\) and \(0=g(x,y)+G(y)\) for every \(y\), so no locally unique solution branch exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state perturbation that cancels the strongly regular base mapping destroys uniqueness at the contraction boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0=g(x,y)+G(y)\text{ for every }y,\text{ so no unique implicit update exists.}

notation.meaning: state Lipschitz modulus of the perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of the Small-Perturbation Condition Can Destroy Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Regularity Newton Update Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precise perturbation theorem defining a locally unique Newton update from a strongly regular base equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y,Z\) be normed spaces, let \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) be strongly metrically regular at \((\bar y,-g(\bar x,\bar y))\) with inverse-localization modulus \(\kappa\), and define \(\Phi(x,y)=g(x,y)+G(y)\), where \(0\in\Phi(\bar x,\bar y)\). Suppose locally \[\|g(x,y)-g(x',y)\|\leq L_x\|x-x'\|,\qquad \|g(x,y)-g(x,y')\|\leq L_y\|y-y'\|,\] with \(\kappa L_y<1\). Then locally \(0\in\Phi(x,y)\) has a unique solution \(y=s(x)\), and \[\|s(x)-s(x')\|\leq\frac{\kappa L_x}{1-\kappa L_y}\|x-x'\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity plus a sufficiently small state perturbation yields a unique Lipschitz Newton update.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is strongly metrically regular at }(\bar y,-g(\bar x,\bar y))\text{ with modulus }\kappa
g\text{ is locally uniformly }L_x\text{-Lipschitz in }x\text{ and }L_y\text{-Lipschitz in }y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,s(x):0\in g(x,s(x))+G(s(x)),\qquad \operatorname{lip}s\leq\frac{\kappa L_x}{1-\kappa L_y}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Regularity Newton Update Theorem

assumptions_latex: y\mapsto\Phi(\bar x,y)\text{ is strongly metrically regular at }(\bar y,0)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique local solution mapping \(s\) with \(0\in\Phi(x,s(x))\), and \(s\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-regularity implicit theorem used to define locally single-valued Newton iterates.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Implicit-function theorems p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume additionally that parameter perturbations satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(w,\Phi(x,y))\leq\operatorname{dist}(w,\Phi(x',y))+L\lVert x-x'\rVert\) locally. Then neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) exist such that, for every \(x\in U\), the inclusion \(0\in\Phi(x,y)\) has exactly one solution \(y=s(x)\) in \(V\). Moreover, \(s(\bar x)=\bar y\) and \(\lVert s(x)-s(x')\rVert\leq\kappa L\lVert x-x'\rVert\), where \(\kappa\) is a strong-regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity and Lipschitz parameter dependence yield a unique local Lipschitz solution map, which can serve as a Newton update.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Function Theorems for Newton Iterations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Implicit-function theorems p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Strong metric regularity of the frozen mapping in the solution variable, together with the displayed pointwise distance estimate in the parameter, does not transparently guarantee uniqueness for every parameterized mapping without a more precise perturbation or contraction hypothesis. The exact implicit-function theorem and its required local quantifiers must be checked against the cited source before this theorem can be retained.

children.title: Metric Regularity of Newton Iterations
children.top_down_role: Regularity analysis of Newtonian iteration mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed error bound characterizes metric regularity of the Newton relation near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood error-bound condition for a set-valued Newton iteration relation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relation \(T\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,T^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,T(x))\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\), with distance to the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). For a Newton iteration relation, this condition bounds the distance to an admissible next iterate by the residual of its defining generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds distance to an admissible Newton iterate by the residual of the iteration-defining generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity of Newton Iterations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Regularity Does Not Make the Newton Relation Single-Valued
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between metric regularity and locally unique Newton updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(T(x)=\{x,-x\}\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,T^{-1}(y))=\min\{|x-y|,|x+y|\}=\operatorname{dist}(y,T(x)),\] so \(T\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(1\). Nevertheless, for every \(y\ne0\), \(T^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metrically regular two-branch Newton relation has two nearby admissible iterates for every nonzero target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is metrically regular at }(0,0),\quad T^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\text{ for }y\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity Does Not Make the Newton Relation Single-Valued

children.title: Sequential Implicit-Function Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Sequential implicit-mapping theory for Newton-type processes.

assumptions_latex: \Phi_k\text{ satisfy uniform local strong regularity and parameter-Lipschitz bounds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local implicit solutions \(y=s_k(x)\) exist uniquely and obey a uniform Lipschitz estimate.

notation.meaning: localized solution map for the kth model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform sequential version of an implicit-mapping principle for changing Newton models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose common neighborhoods \(U\) and \(V\), and constants \(\kappa,L>0\), certify strong metric regularity in \(y\) and Lipschitz dependence on \(x\) for every \(\Phi_k\), with \(K:=\kappa L\). Then, after possibly shrinking \(U\) and \(V\) uniformly, each inclusion \(0\in\Phi_k(x,y)\) has a unique local solution \(y=s_k(x)\), and
\[\lVert s_k(x)-s_k(x')\rVert\leq K\lVert x-x'\rVert\]
for all \(x,x'\in U\) and all \(k\). Thus a changing sequence of Newton models defines uniformly controlled implicit iteration maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform strong regularity and parameter bounds give uniformly Lipschitz local solution maps for a sequence of changing Newton models.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Implicit-Function Frameworks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record asserts a uniform sequential implicit-function principle without any citation. Common moduli alone may not supply uniform neighborhoods unless the reference points, localization radii, graph behavior, and perturbation hypotheses are controlled uniformly. An exact sequential theorem source is required.

x\text{ lies in the certified neighborhood of }\bar x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Metric subregularity provides a neighborhood \(U\subset X\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x))\qquad(x\in U).\] Consequently, an evaluated residual bound \(\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x))\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\varepsilon\). This certificate applies only when \(x\in U\) and the stated modulus bound have been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mapping between normed spaces, metric subregularity converts a locally computed generalized-equation residual into an upper bound on distance to the solution set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Residual Without a Linear Error Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of residual-to-distance conversion without metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(G(x)=x^2\), one has \(S=G^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x))=x^2\), but no \(\kappa<\infty\) and \(\delta>0\) satisfy \(|x|\leq\kappa x^2\) for all \(|x|<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the squared residual, residuals vanish quadratically while solution distance vanishes linearly, so no local linear certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,\kappa<\infty,\delta>0\ \forall |x|<\delta:\ \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the inverse localization of \(d\mapsto A_kd+Q_k(d)\) at \((\bar d_k,-a_k)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz with modulus \(\kappa_k\), then every sufficiently small \(\Delta a\in\mathbb{R}^m\) determines exactly one nearby step \(d(\Delta a)\) satisfying \(0\in a_k+\Delta a+A_kd(\Delta a)+Q_k(d(\Delta a))\). The sensitivity estimate is \[\lVert d(\Delta a)-d(0)\rVert\leq\kappa_k\lVert\Delta a\rVert.\] Thus strong regularity certifies local solvability and isolation of the perturbed linearized subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity at the consistent reference point certifies that each sufficiently small perturbation of the linearized Newton subproblem has one isolated nearby step with controlled sensitivity.

assumptions_latex: \lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert\leq q\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\text{ eventually}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration converges locally \(Q\)-linearly, with asymptotic error ratio at most \(q\).

source_refs.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((x_k)\) is in a local \(Q\)-linear rate regime at \(\bar x\) when there exist \(k_0\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(q\in[0,1)\) such that \[\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert\leq q\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\qquad(k\geq k_0).\] Hence \(\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\leq q^{k-k_0}\lVert x_{k_0}-\bar x\rVert\), and \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert/\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\leq q<1\) whenever the quotient is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eventually contracting the error by one fixed factor below one is precisely the local Q-linear regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Rate Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: R-Linear Majorants and Their Separation from Q-Linear Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: R-linear formulation and its strict distinction from the accepted Q-linear regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) converges R-linearly if there are \(C>0\), \(q\in(0,1)\), and \(k_0\) such that \(\|x_k-\bar x\|\le Cq^k\) for \(k\ge k_0\). Every Q-linearly convergent sequence is R-linearly convergent. The converse fails: with \(a_{2m}=2^{-m}\) and \(a_{2m+1}=2^{-2m}\), one has \(a_k\le2(2^{-1/2})^k\), while \(a_{2m+2}/a_{2m+1}=2^{m-1}\). Thus \((a_k)\) is R-linear but not Q-linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: R-linear convergence requires a geometric majorant, whereas Q-linear convergence controls successive errors and is strictly stronger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q-linear convergence implies R-linear convergence, but the converse fails.

notation.meaning: Scalar sequence separating the two rate notions.

knowledge_statements.title: R-Linear Majorants and Their Separation from Q-Linear Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Q- and R-Convergence Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a nonstationary convergent sequence in finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^k\to x^\infty\) in \(\mathbb R^n\), with \(x^k\ne x^\infty\) for every \(k\). The convergence is at least Q-linear if \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{\|x^{k+1}-x^\infty\|}{\|x^k-x^\infty\|}<\infty\); Q-superlinear if this ratio tends to \(0\); Q-quadratic if \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{\|x^{k+1}-x^\infty\|}{\|x^k-x^\infty\|^2}<\infty\); and R-linear if \(0<\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x^k-x^\infty\|^{1/k}<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sequence converging to a distinct limit at every finite iterate, Q-linear, Q-superlinear, and Q-quadratic rates are defined through successive-error ratios, while R-linear convergence is defined through the asymptotic kth root of the error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x^k\}\) is classified as Q-linear, Q-superlinear, Q-quadratic, or R-linear according to the stated limits.

children.title: Superlinear Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local convergence behavior classified as superlinear.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is locally \(Q\)-superlinear exactly when consecutive-error ratios converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard local Q-superlinear regime for Newton-type iterates.

source_refs.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every sufficiently large \(k\), define \(\rho_k:=\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert/\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\). The convergence \(x_k\to\bar x\) is \(Q\)-superlinear precisely when \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\rho_k=0.\] Equivalently, for every \(q\in(0,1)\), there exists \(k(q)\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert\leq q\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert\) whenever \(k\geq k(q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Superlinear convergence means the ratio of successive errors tends to zero, eventually beating every fixed positive linear contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Rate Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Q-Order Greater Than One and Quadratic Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-order subclasses of the local Q-superlinear regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_k=\|x_k-\bar x\|>0\) eventually. Convergence has Q-order at least \(p>1\) if \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{e_{k+1}}{e_k^p}<\infty,\] equivalently, \(e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^p\) eventually for some \(C>0\). Every such sequence is Q-superlinear. The case \(p=2\) is Q-quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error estimate of order p greater than one is quantitatively superlinear; order two is quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^p)\), then \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\); \(p=2\) gives Q-quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Q-Order Greater Than One and Quadratic Convergence

children.title: Rate-Transition Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Regularity or approximation thresholds separating local rate classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Coefficient Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract threshold separating linear and superlinear behavior in a local error recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(e_k\to0\) and eventually \[\|e_{k+1}\|\le(\alpha_k+c\|e_k\|^p)\|e_k\|,\qquad c\ge0,\quad p>0.\] If \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\alpha_k<1\), then the errors are eventually contracted by some fixed factor \(q<1\), giving Q-linear convergence. If \(\alpha_k\to0\), then \[\frac{\|e_{k+1}\|}{\|e_k\|}\longrightarrow0,\] giving Q-superlinear convergence whenever the quotient is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order coefficient uniformly below one yields a linear regime; its vanishing yields a superlinear regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup\alpha_k<1\) implies Q-linear convergence, while \(\alpha_k\to0\) implies Q-superlinear convergence.

notation.meaning: First-order coefficient in the local error recursion.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Coefficient Transition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Strict Contraction Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-one boundary for the generic local error recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_0\ne0\) and \(e_{k+1}=e_k\). This satisfies the generic recursion with \(\alpha_k\equiv1\) and \(c=0\), but \(e_k=e_0\) for every \(k\). Hence replacing \(\limsup\alpha_k<1\) by \(\limsup\alpha_k\le1\) cannot guarantee convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At coefficient one, a nonexpansive error bound need not decrease the error, so strict contraction is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weak threshold \(\limsup\alpha_k\le1\) does not ensure convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Strict Contraction Threshold

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform coefficient below one gives a linear regime, while \(\alpha_k\to0\) gives a superlinear regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold classification derived from a generic local Newton error recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the displayed recursion holds eventually and \(e_k\to0\). If \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\alpha_k<1\), then for some \(q<1\), \(\lVert e_{k+1}\rVert\leq q\lVert e_k\rVert\) eventually, giving \(Q\)-linear convergence. If instead \(\alpha_k\to0\), then
\[\frac{\lVert e_{k+1}\rVert}{\lVert e_k\rVert}\leq\alpha_k+c\lVert e_k\rVert^p\longrightarrow0,\]
so convergence is \(Q\)-superlinear. The threshold is therefore whether the first-order approximation coefficient merely remains below one or vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the local error recursion, a first-order coefficient bounded below one yields linear convergence; its vanishing yields superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Transition Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold conclusions follow plausibly from the displayed recursion, but the record has no source for that recursion or for its interpretation as a Newton approximation coefficient. Because this is a nontrivial rate-transition condition rather than a bare rate definition, an authoritative source for the exact hypotheses is required.

children.title: Approximation-Quality Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence of the attainable rate class on local approximation quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Relative Accuracy Need Not Be Superlinear
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar sharpness example for fixed nonzero model-solution tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x\) on \(\mathbb R\), admit an inexact Newton residual \(r_k=x_{k+1}\) satisfying \(|r_k|\le\eta|x_k|\), where \(\eta\in(0,1)\) is fixed. Choosing \(x_{k+1}=\eta x_k\) gives \[\frac{|x_{k+1}|}{|x_k|}=\eta\] for every nonzero iterate. The convergence is Q-linear but not Q-superlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed nonzero relative solve tolerance can limit even a linear equation to linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Relative Accuracy Need Not Be Superlinear

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rate Dependence on Relative Approximation Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic transfer from a stable local error recursion to linear, superlinear, and higher-order rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e_k:=x_k-\bar x\), and suppose eventually \[\|r_k\|\le\eta_k\|e_k\|,\qquad \|e_{k+1}\|\le\kappa\bigl(\|r_k\|+c\|e_k\|^{1+p}\bigr),\] where \(\kappa>0\), \(c\ge0\), and \(p>0\). Then \[\|e_{k+1}\|\le\kappa(\eta_k+c\|e_k\|^p)\|e_k\|.\] If \(\limsup\kappa\eta_k<1\), sufficiently small errors give Q-linear convergence. If \(\eta_k\to0\), convergence is Q-superlinear. If \(\eta_k=O(\|e_k\|^p)\), then \(\|e_{k+1}\|=O(\|e_k\|^{1+p})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed sufficiently small relative approximation error supports a linear rate; vanishing error supports a superlinear rate, and matched higher-order accuracy yields order at least 1+p.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed combined recursion yields the stated linear, superlinear, and order-\(1+p\) regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Rate Dependence on Relative Approximation Quality

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local rate is controlled by \(\kappa\eta_k\) and the higher-order model error.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of Newton convergence rates on relative model-solution accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Combining the residual and stability bounds gives
\[\lVert e_{k+1}\rVert\leq\kappa(\eta_k+c\lVert e_k\rVert^p)\lVert e_k\rVert.\]
If \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\kappa\eta_k<1\), sufficiently small errors produce a \(Q\)-linear regime. If \(\eta_k\to0\), the quotient \(\lVert e_{k+1}\rVert/\lVert e_k\rVert\) tends to zero and the regime is \(Q\)-superlinear. If \(\eta_k=O(\lVert e_k\rVert^p)\), then \(\lVert e_{k+1}\rVert=O(\lVert e_k\rVert^{1+p})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed relative model accuracy supports linear convergence; vanishing accuracy tolerances support superlinear convergence, with matched higher-order accuracy giving order above one.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Quality Dependence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic rate classifications are plausible under the displayed stability and residual bounds, but neither the inexact-Newton bound nor the meanings and domains of the constants are sourced. An exact source is required before accepting this approximation-quality property.

children.top_down_role: Local rate classifications associated with semismooth equation forms.

assumptions_latex: H:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is locally Lipschitz and semismooth at }\bar x
\partial H\text{ denotes the Clarke generalized Jacobian}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized Newton iteration is locally \(Q\)-superlinear; strong semismoothness yields a quadratic error bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semismooth Newton rate theorem using uniformly invertible Clarke generalized Jacobians.

source_refs.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{k+1}:=x_k-V_k^{-1}H(x_k)\), where \(V_k\in\partial H(x_k)\), and assume \(\sup\{\lVert V^{-1}\rVert:V\in\partial H(x),\ x\text{ near }\bar x\}<\infty\). Then every sufficiently close initial point generates well-defined iterates converging to \(\bar x\), with \[\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert=o(\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert).\] If \(H\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\), then \(\lVert x_{k+1}-\bar x\rVert=O(\lVert x_k-\bar x\rVert^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform invertibility of the Clarke generalized Jacobians and semismoothness give local superlinear Newton convergence; strong semismoothness gives a quadratic rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Local Rate Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5.1 Linear Newton approximation schemes p. 703
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order-Semismooth Newton Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermediate local convergence orders between ordinary superlinear and quadratic regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(\bar x)=0\), and suppose the admissible matrices \(V\in\partial H(x)\) near \(\bar x\) are invertible with uniformly bounded inverses. If, uniformly for such \(V\), \[\|H(x)-H(\bar x)-V(x-\bar x)\|=O(\|x-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha}),\qquad 0<\alpha\leq1,\] then \(x_{k+1}=x_k-V_k^{-1}H(x_k)\) satisfies \[\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|=O(\|x_k-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha}).\] For \(\alpha=1\), this is the quadratic regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-Jacobian remainder of order one plus alpha yields Newton convergence of the same order.
assumptions_latex: \|H(x)-H(\bar x)-V(x-\bar x)\|=O(\|x-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha})\text{ uniformly for admissible }V
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Semismooth Newton Rate Regimes

children.title: Metric-Space Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity theory based on purely metric arguments.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) precisely when the stated local error bound holds.

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to positive infinity.
Inverse image of a point under the multifunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely metric definition; no linear, differentiable, or dual-space structure is assumed.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\) if \(\kappa\ge 0\) and there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that \[d_X\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le \kappa d_Y\bigl(y,F(x)\bigr)\] for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\). Its exact regularity modulus is the infimum of all such \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity is a local error bound comparing distance to a solution of the inverse inclusion with distance from the target to the multifunction value.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Space Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Regularity–Aubin Inverse Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure-free metric equivalence between regularity of a multifunction and Lipschitz-like behavior of its inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For metric spaces \(X,Y\), a multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\): there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\), \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
F^{-1}(y_1)\cap U\subseteq\{x\in X:d_X(x,F^{-1}(y_2))\leq\kappa d_Y(y_1,y_2)\}
\]
for all \(y_1,y_2\in V\). Their exact moduli satisfy
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is metrically regular exactly when its inverse is Lipschitz-like, with equal exact moduli.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is metrically regular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff F^{-1}\text{ has the Aubin property at }(\bar y,\bar x),\quad \operatorname{reg}F=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}.

notation.meaning: exact Aubin modulus of the inverse multifunction

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularity–Aubin Inverse Equivalence

assumptions_latex: X and Y are Banach spaces.
F:Xightrightarrows Y has locally closed graph at (ar x,ar y).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform positive lower bound on adjoint coderivative action yields metric regularity of F near (ar x,ar y).

review_flags: exact Banach-space hypotheses may require an Asplund or smooth-renorming qualification

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Banach-space coderivative regularity condition at (ar x,ar y) is the existence of neighborhoods U and V and a constant c>0 such that \|x^*\|\ge c whenever (x,y) belongs to \operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V), y^* belongs to Y^* with \|y^*\|=1, and x^* belongs to \widehat D^*F(x,y)(y^*). Under the applicable coderivative criterion, this lower bound implies metric regularity with modulus at most c^{-1}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Banach spaces, regularity can be certified by uniformly preventing unit dual perturbations from producing coderivative images near zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Banach-Space Regularity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the standard Asplund-space compactness qualification for the coderivative criterion, F is metrically regular around (ar x,ar y) if and only if \ker D^*F(ar x,ar y)=\{0\}. Equivalently, 0 belongs to D^*F(ar x,ar y)(y^*) only when y^*=0. The conclusion is local metric regularity of the inverse relation, with a quantitative modulus obtained from the corresponding positive coderivative lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the qualified Asplund setting, metric regularity is equivalent to the limiting coderivative having no nonzero dual vector in its kernel.

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity theory with finite-dimensional compactness and limiting-normal characterizations.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exactly when its limiting coderivative kernel is trivial.

notation.meaning: Limiting coderivative defined through limiting normals to the graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich criterion, where compactness removes additional sequential qualifications.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \[0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(v)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v=0.\] Equivalently, there is no nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \((0,-v)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\). Thus failure of regularity is witnessed by a nonzero vertical limiting normal to the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, metric regularity holds exactly when the graph has no nonzero vertical limiting normal at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Regularity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Inverse-Coderivative Formula for Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative finite-dimensional form of metric regularity through the inverse multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\lVert D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)\rVert^+,
\]
where
\[
\lVert D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)\rVert^+:=\sup\{\lVert v\rVert:v\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(u),\ \lVert u\rVert\leq1\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) when this set is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the exact regularity modulus equals the Aubin modulus of the inverse and the outer norm of the inverse limiting coderivative.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\lVert D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)\rVert^+.

notation.meaning: outer norm of the limiting coderivative of the inverse

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Inverse-Coderivative Formula for Regularity

The graph-normal criterion gives metric regularity of \(F\) at \(( ar x, ar y)\) exactly when every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^q\) satisfying \(
abla_x h( ar x, ar y)^	op\lambda=0\) and \(
abla_y h( ar x, ar y)^	op\lambda=-v\) for some \(v\in\mathbb R^m\) must have \(v=0\). Because \(Dh( ar x, ar y)\) has full row rank, this is equivalent to \[\ker 
abla_x h( ar x, ar y)^	op=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smoothly equality-defined graph, regularity means that no nonzero graph-normal multiplier can generate a purely vertical normal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Regularity Modulus of a Manifold Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative normal-space form of the manifold-graph regularity criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive and Uniform Positive Definiteness on a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a matrix-valued mapping over a parameter set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let O:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and \Xi\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n. The map O is positive definite on \Xi if \langle d,O(z)d\rangle>0 for every z\in\Xi and every d\in\mathbb{R}^m\setminus\{0\}. It is uniformly positive definite on \Xi if there exists \alpha>0 such that \langle d,O(z)d\rangle\geq\alpha\|d\|^2 for every z\in\Xi and every d\in\mathbb{R}^m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-valued map is positive definite on a set when every matrix value has a strictly positive quadratic form on every nonzero direction. It is uniformly positive definite when one positive quadratic lower bound works for all points and directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Branching Without Prox-Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed graph with arbitrarily near points having multiple nearest graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
G=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\subset\mathbb R^2,
\]
viewed as the graph of the multifunction \(F\) defined by \(F(x)=\{0\}\) for \(x\neq0\) and \(F(0)=\mathbb R\). For every \(t>0\), the point \((t,t)\) has the two distinct nearest graph points \((t,0)\) and \((0,t)\). Hence no neighborhood of the origin admits a single-valued metric projection onto \(G\), and the graph is not prox-regular at the origin in the uniform local sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of the coordinate axes is a closed multifunction graph whose nearest-point projection branches arbitrarily close to the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_G(t,t)\supseteq\{(t,0),(0,t)\}\text{ for every }t>0,\text{ so }P_G\text{ has no single-valued localization at the origin}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Localized Projection Stability of a Prox-Regular Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-point consequence of finite-dimensional prox-regular graph geometry at a designated graph-normal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=\operatorname{gph}F\subset\mathbb R^{n+m}\) be locally closed and prox-regular at \(\bar z\in G\) for \(\bar v\in N_G(\bar z)\). For every sufficiently small \(t>0\), the metric projection \(P_G\) admits a single-valued Lipschitz localization around \((\bar z+t\bar v,\bar z)\); in particular,
\[
P_G(\bar z+t\bar v)=\{\bar z\}
\]
within that localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a sufficiently short displacement along the designated normal, a prox-regular graph has a unique locally Lipschitz nearest-point projection back to the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent Stability Below the Hypomonotonicity Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional resolvent consequence for an operator whose monotone shift is maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) satisfy that \(T+\rho I\) is maximal monotone for some \(\rho\geq0\). If \(\rho=0\), let \(\lambda>0\); if \(\rho>0\), let \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\). Then \(I+\lambda T\) is strongly monotone with modulus \(1-\lambda\rho\) and is surjective. Its resolvent
\[
J_{\lambda T}:=(I+\lambda T)^{-1}
\]
is single-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\) and satisfies
\[
\lVert J_{\lambda T}(u)-J_{\lambda T}(v)\rVert\leq\frac{1}{1-\lambda\rho}\lVert u-v\rVert.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the monotone shift is maximal, a hypomonotone operator has a globally single-valued Lipschitz resolvent below the reciprocal hypomonotonicity threshold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent Failure at the Hypomonotonicity Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar failure of resolvent invertibility at the reciprocal hypomonotonicity threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\rho>0\) and \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(T(x)=-\rho x\). Then \(T+\rho I=0\) is maximal monotone, so \(T\) is maximally \(\rho\)-hypomonotone. At \(\lambda=1/\rho\),
\[
I+\lambda T=0.
\]
Consequently \((I+\lambda T)^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\), while \((I+\lambda T)^{-1}(u)=\varnothing\) for \(u\neq0\); the resolvent is neither a globally defined single-valued map nor locally isolated at zero.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (I+\lambda T)^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\text{ and }(I+\lambda T)^{-1}(u)=\varnothing\text{ for }u\neq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Failure at the Hypomonotonicity Threshold

children.title: Singular Linearized Generalized Equations

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Linearized Generalized Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous-kernel singularity of the graphical linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linearizing \(0\in f(x)+Q(x)\) at \((\bar x,\bar q)\) gives the positively homogeneous mapping \(u\mapsto \nabla f(\bar x)u+DQ(\bar x\mid\bar q)(u)\). Singularity is detected by a nontrivial solution of its homogeneous zero-inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical linearization is singular when its homogeneous generalized equation has a nonzero primal solution.
assumptions_latex: \(Q:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), \(0\in f(\bar x)+Q(\bar x)\), and \(\bar q=-f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linearized generalized equation is singular when \[0\in \nabla f(\bar x)u+DQ(\bar x\mid\bar q)(u)\] has a nonzero solution \(u\). Such a direction belongs to the kernel of the graphical linearization and prevents that linearization from having an isolated inverse at zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Trivial Primal Kernel Does Not Ensure Full Inverse Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the leaf's injectivity-type singularity test and surjectivity or metric-regularity obstructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear mapping \(L:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\), \(L(u)=(u,0)\), the homogeneous equation \(L(u)=0\) has only \(u=0\). Thus the graphical linearization has no nonzero primal kernel direction. Nevertheless, \(L\) is not surjective, and right-hand sides \((0,\varepsilon)\) have no inverse image. Hence a trivial homogeneous primal kernel does not by itself imply metric regularity or a locally defined inverse for every nearby right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absence of a nonzero primal kernel direction is only an injectivity-type test; it does not exclude a missing-range obstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L^{-1}(0)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{rge}L\ne\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad L\text{ is not metrically regular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero horizontal tangent \((u,0)\) represents first-order motion in the primal variable without first-order motion in the image. By the definition of the graphical derivative, this is exactly the homogeneous inclusion stated in the conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangential degeneracy is a nonzero horizontal graph tangent, so the image has no first-order change along a primal direction.

The graph then has a nonzero horizontal tangent direction, obstructing injectivity of its graphical linearization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\). Consequently, any nonzero \(u\) satisfying \(0\in DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u)\) rules out strong metric subregularity.

children.title: Abnormal Dual Directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abnormal Covectors of a Nonsurjective Linear Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear realization of an abnormal coderivative direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear with \(\operatorname{rge}A\neq\mathbb R^m\), and let \(F(x)=Ax\). Choose \(0\neq y^*\in(\operatorname{rge}A)^\perp=\ker A^*\). For every \((x,Ax)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), \[D^*F(x\mid Ax)(y^*)=\{A^*y^*\}=\{0\}.\] Thus \(y^*\) is a nonzero abnormal dual direction. Moreover, \(F\) is not metrically regular because its range contains no neighborhood of any of its values in \(\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonsurjective finite-dimensional linear map has a nonzero adjoint-kernel covector realizing an abnormal coderivative direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y^*\neq0:\ D^*F(x\mid Ax)(y^*)=\{0\},\quad\text{and }F\text{ is not metrically regular}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary separating failure of active-gradient independence from stronger constraint-qualification and multiplier pathologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constraints \(g_1(x)=x\le0\) and \(g_2(x)=2x\le0\) at \(\bar x=0\), both constraints are active and their gradients are linearly dependent. Nevertheless, \(d=-1\) satisfies \(\nabla g_i(0)d<0\) for both active indices, so MFCQ holds. Jacobian whose rows are active constraint gradients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth inequality-system meaning of constraint degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(\bar x):=\{i\mid g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The feasible system is constraint-degenerate at \(\bar x\) when there exists a nonzero vector \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{I(\bar x)}\) such that
\[\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\alpha_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)=0.\]
Equivalently, the active-constraint Jacobian \(A(\bar x)\) has rank strictly smaller than \(|I(\bar x)|\). This definition concerns linear dependence of active normals and does not by itself require existence of a Lagrange multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint degeneracy occurs when the gradients of the active smooth inequality constraints are linearly dependent.

children.title: Multiplier Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-Compatible Kernel Characterization of Multiplier Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact geometry of a non-singleton multiplier fiber for a smooth inequality KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_I\) have rows \(\nabla g_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}\) for active indices. The multiplier set \(\Lambda(\bar x)\) is non-singleton if and only if there exist \(\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) and \(d\ne0\), supported on the active indices, such that \(A_I^{\mathsf T}d=0\) and \(\lambda+d\ge0\). Then both \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda+d\) are KKT multipliers. Thus active-gradient dependence is necessary but becomes multiplier degeneracy only when a kernel displacement is compatible with dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier nonuniqueness is exactly a nonzero active-gradient kernel displacement that keeps a multiplier dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\Lambda(\bar x)|>1\iff\exists\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar x),\ \exists d\ne0:\ A_I^{\mathsf T}d=0,\ d_{I^c}=0,\ \lambda+d\ge0.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Compatible Kernel Characterization of Multiplier Nonuniqueness

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is feasible and admits at least one KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplier degeneracy at \(\bar x\) is the failure of the multiplier set \(\Lambda(\bar x)\) to be a singleton.

notation.meaning: Set of nonnegative KKT multipliers at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness form of multiplier degeneracy for smooth inequality-constrained optimization.

Define
\[\Lambda( ar x):=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\ \middle|\ 
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)=0,\quad \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\ 	ext{for all }iight\}.\]
The KKT system is multiplier-degenerate at \( ar x\) when \(\Lambda( ar x)\) contains at least two distinct elements. Equivalently, there exist \(\lambda^1,\lambda^2\in\Lambda( ar x)\) with \(\lambda^1
e\lambda^2\); their difference is a nonzero linear dependence among active constraint gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier degeneracy means that the same primal solution admits more than one KKT multiplier vector.
