children.title: Primal–Dual Degeneracy Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between constraint geometry and multiplier instability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Singularity Need Not Come from Multiplier Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse boundary for the primal-dual block coupling statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(1\ \ 0)\) and \(H=0\) in the KKT matrix \(K=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\). The active Jacobian has full row rank, so \(\ker A^{\mathsf T}=\{0\}\), but \(u=(0,1)\in\ker A\) satisfies \(Hu=0\). Hence \(K(u,0)=0\) and \(K\) is singular. Therefore KKT singularity can arise from a primal reduced-curvature null direction without multiplier degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint dependence always gives a dual KKT null direction, but the converse fails because reduced-curvature degeneracy can produce a purely primal null direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker A^{\mathsf T}=\{0\}\quad\text{and}\quad \ker K\ne\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Singularity Need Not Come from Multiplier Degeneracy

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is the active-constraint Jacobian of an equality-constrained KKT system.
\(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is its primal Hessian block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any nonzero \(z\in\ker A^{\mathsf T}\) produces the primal-dual null direction \((0,z)\in\ker K\), so dual nonuniqueness forces singular linearization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic coupling in the linearized equality-constrained KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual linearization
\[K:=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{pmatrix},\]
constraint dependence means that some \(z\ne0\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}z=0\). Consequently,
\[K\binom{0}{z}=\binom{A^{\mathsf T}z}{0}=0.\]
Thus the same dependence that permits a dual multiplier direction also makes the full primal-dual linearization singular. This implication is independent of the curvature block \(H\); additional primal null directions may arise from the behavior of \(H\) on \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dependence among active constraint normals creates a dual null direction in the KKT matrix, coupling multiplier nonuniqueness to singular primal-dual linearization.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Degeneracy Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block-matrix calculation correctly identifies a dual null direction caused by row dependence of the active-constraint Jacobian, and property is the appropriate knowledge kind. A supporting source and locator are absent.

children.title: Branch-Multiplicity Consequences
children.top_down_role: Multiple or unstable local branches associated with primal-dual degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Persistent Nearby Multiplicity Precludes a Single-Valued Localization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General local consequence of two distinct solution branches converging to the same reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there are parameters \(p_k\to\bar p\) and distinct solutions \(x_k^1,x_k^2\in S(p_k)\) such that \(x_k^1\to\bar x\) and \(x_k^2\to\bar x\). Then no neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) make \(S(p)\cap V\) a singleton for every \(p\in U\). In particular, \(S\) has no single-valued Lipschitz localization through \((\bar p,\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Nearby Multiplicity Precludes a Single-Valued Localization

assumptions_latex: Consider the parameterized scalar equation \(0=x^2-p\) near \((\bar x,\bar p)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution map has two local branches for \(p>0\), one solution at \(p=0\), and no real solution for \(p<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar model showing branch creation at a singular generalized-equation linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(p):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\mid x^2=p\}\). At \((\bar p,\bar x)=(0,0)\), the derivative of the residual with respect to \(x\) is zero, so the linearized equation is singular. Explicitly,
\[S(p)=\begin{cases}\{-\sqrt p,\sqrt p\},&p>0,\\\{0\},&p=0,\\\varnothing,&p<0.\end{cases}\]
Hence no single-valued Lipschitz localization of \(S\) exists around \((0,0)\). The degeneracy is accompanied by coalescing solution branches and loss of local solvability on one side of the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singular equation x²=p has two branches for positive parameters, one at zero, and none for negative parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Multiplicity Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar example and its branch structure are correct, and counterexample appropriately realizes the consequence-oriented leaf. No cited source or locator is provided.

children.title: Loss of Neighborhood Uniformity
children.top_down_role: Pointwise behavior that fails to extend uniformly across nearby graph points.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is a set-valued mapping between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise metric subregularity fails to become neighborhood-uniform when no common modulus and neighborhoods establish metric regularity near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a reference-value error bound from metric regularity uniform in nearby values.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric subregularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) requires neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\) such that
\[d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\le\kappa d(\bar y,F(x))\quad\text{for all }x\in U.\]
Neighborhood uniformity is lost when this estimate holds at the fixed value \(\bar y\), but for every choice of neighborhoods \(U,V\) and \(\kappa\), some \((x,y)\in U\times V\) violates
\[d(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\kappa d(y,F(x)).\]
Then \(F\) is subregular at the reference pair but not metrically regular there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-value error bound may hold at the reference pair while no common bound works uniformly for nearby right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Neighborhood Uniformity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Mapping with a Fixed-Value Error Bound but No Uniform Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar separation of metric subregularity at a fixed value from metric regularity for nearby right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=\max\{x,0\}\). Then \(F^{-1}(0)=(-\infty,0]\), and for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[d(x,F^{-1}(0))=\max\{x,0\}=d(0,F(x)).\] Hence \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(1\). However, for every \(y<0\), \(F^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\). Thus arbitrarily near \((0,0)\), \[d(0,F^{-1}(y))=+\infty>d(y,F(0))=|y|,\] so no neighborhoods and common finite modulus establish metric regularity around \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-part mapping has an exact fixed-value error bound at zero but is not metrically regular because nearby negative right-hand sides have no preimages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{subreg}F(0\mid0)=1,\qquad F\text{ is not metrically regular around }(0,0).

notation.meaning: distance from x to S, with distance to the empty set equal to positive infinity

children.title: Subregularity Representation Fragility

children.title: Perturbation Fragility of Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Loss of subregularity under perturbations tolerated by stronger properties.

assumptions_latex: Define \(F(x)=x\) and the Lipschitz perturbation \(h(x)=-x+x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\), \(F+h=x^2\) is not metrically subregular there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows failure without a perturbation-size condition relative to the original subregularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=x\),
\[d(x,F^{-1}(0))=|x|=|F(x)|,\]
so \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\) with modulus one. The locally Lipschitz perturbation \(h(x)=-x+x^2\) gives \(G(x):=F(x)+h(x)=x^2\). If \(G\) were metrically subregular at \((0,0)\), some \(\kappa\) and neighborhood of zero would satisfy \(|x|\le\kappa|x|^2\). This is impossible for arbitrarily small nonzero \(x\). Thus unrestricted Lipschitz perturbations need not preserve subregularity; a quantitative smallness condition is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz perturbation can turn the subregular residual x into x², destroying its local linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Fragility of Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly shows that an unrestricted Lipschitz perturbation can destroy even strong metric subregularity; it does not claim robustness against quantitatively small perturbations. The counterexample kind fits, but no source is cited.

children.title: Composition Fragility of Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Failure of reference-value regularity to pass through mapping operations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both component mappings are metrically subregular at their reference pairs, while \(H\circ G\) is not metrically subregular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete composition failure caused by tangency to the outer zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(G\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,(0,0))\), since \(G^{-1}(0,0)=\{0\}\) and \(\|G(x)\|=|x|\). The mapping \(H\) is metrically regular, hence subregular, near \(((0,0),0)\) because its derivative in the \(v\)-direction equals one. Nevertheless,
\[(H\circ G)(x)=x^2,\qquad (H\circ G)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}.\]
Metric subregularity of the composition would require \(|x|\le\kappa|x|^2\) near zero, which is impossible. Componentwise subregularity therefore does not pass through composition without a transversality qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two subregular mappings can compose to x², whose residual has no local linear error bound at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Fragility of Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The component mappings have the asserted regularity properties while their composition is the non-subregular residual x squared. The counterexample fits the leaf, but a source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Representation Dependence of Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Variation of residual error bounds across equivalent formulations.

assumptions_latex: Consider the equivalent equations \(R_1(x)=0\) and \(R_2(x)=0\), where \(R_1(x)=x\) and \(R_2(x)=x^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two representations have the same solution set, but only \(R_1\) admits a local Lipschitz error bound at zero.

notation.meaning: Common solution set of the two residual equations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent zero-set representations with inequivalent residual growth.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both residual equations define the same solution set \(S=\{0\}\). For \(R_1(x)=x\), the exact global estimate
\[d(x,S)=|x|=|R_1(x)|\]
holds. For \(R_2(x)=x^2\), a local Lipschitz error bound would require constants \(\kappa,\delta>0\) such that
\[|x|\le\kappa|x|^2\quad\text{whenever }|x|<\delta.\]
No such constants exist. Thus equivalence of feasible sets does not preserve metric subregularity of a chosen residual representation; nonlinear rescaling can flatten residual growth at the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The equations x=0 and x²=0 have the same solutions, but only the first supplies a linear residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of Error Bounds

children.title: Compactness Loss in Limiting-Normal Calculus
children.top_down_role: Compactness defects that obstruct limiting-normal constructions in infinite-dimensional settings.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional Asplund space and \(C\subset X\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without sequential normal compactness, weak-star vanishing of regular normals need not imply norm vanishing, obstructing norm-compact limiting-normal arguments.

notation.meaning: Fréchet normal cone to the set.
Weak-star convergence in the dual space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Sequential normal compactness at \(\bar x\) would force \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\) whenever \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\), and \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\). Compactness loss occurs when a sequence satisfying these three conditions instead obeys
\[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x_k^*\|>0.\]
Such weak-star invisible normal mass cannot be discarded by norm-convergent subsequence arguments. Consequently, limiting-normal calculus rules that require an SNC qualification cannot generally be asserted after that qualification is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-star vanishing normal sequences may retain positive norm, invalidating limiting-normal calculus steps that depend on sequential normal compactness.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space with orthonormal sequence \((e_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The singleton \(C\) is not sequentially normally compact at zero in the infinite-dimensional ambient norm topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the singleton \(C=\{0\}\), every dual vector is a Fréchet normal, so after identifying \(H^*\) with \(H\),
\[\widehat N_C(0)=H.\]
Choose \(x_k=0\) and \(x_k^*=e_k\). Then \(x_k\to0\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\), and the orthonormal sequence satisfies \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\). However, \(\|e_k\|=1\) for every \(k\). Hence weak convergence of normal vectors to zero does not force norm convergence, and \(C\) fails sequential normal compactness at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space singleton, orthonormal normal vectors converge weakly to zero while retaining unit norm.

children.top_down_role: Structural dependence of SNC-based calculus on compactness properties.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed implication is the sequential normal compactness requirement for \(C\) at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\) when every pair of sequences \((x_k,x_k^*)\) satisfying
\[x_k\xrightarrow{C}\bar x,\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k),\qquad x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}0\]
also satisfies
\[\|x_k^*\|\longrightarrow0.\]
Here \(x_k\xrightarrow{C}\bar x\) means \(x_k\in C\) and \(x_k\to\bar x\) in norm. In finite-dimensional spaces the implication follows from equivalence of weak and norm convergence, whereas in infinite dimensions it is an additional compactness requirement.

children.title: Nonclosed-Range Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Range obstructions to openness and stable inversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Range Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal Hilbert-space operator exhibiting nonclosed range and failure of stable inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\ell^2\to\ell^2\) be defined by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\). The operator \(T\) is injective and bounded. Its range contains every finitely supported sequence and is therefore dense, but it is not closed: \(y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\ell^2\), while its formal preimage \((1,1,\ldots)\) does not. Moreover, for the standard unit vectors \(e_n\), \[\|e_n\|=1,\qquad \|Te_n\|=1/n\longrightarrow0.\] Hence no constant \(c>0\) satisfies \(\|Tx\|\ge c\|x\|\). Consequently, \(T\) is neither metrically subregular nor metrically regular at \((0,0)\), linear openness fails there, and \(T^{-1}\) has no Lipschitz-like stable-inversion estimate around \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagonal operator with entries 1/n has dense nonclosed range, is not metrically subregular or regular at zero, and has no Lipschitz-like stable inverse.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\ell^2\to\ell^2\) is the bounded linear operator defined by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\).
The generalized equation is \(y=Tx\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The range of \(T\) is nonclosed, \(T\) is neither metrically subregular nor metrically regular at \((0,0)\), and \(T^{-1}\) lacks a Lipschitz-like stable-inversion estimate around \((0,0)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Banach-space range characterization illustrated by the diagonal seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. Metric subregularity at any graph point is equivalent to the existence of \(c>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\ker T)\le c\|Tx\|\quad(x\in X),\] and is equivalent to \(\operatorname{ran}T\) being closed. Metric regularity additionally requires \(\operatorname{ran}T=Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the single-valued linear mapping \(F(x)=\{Tx\}\), one has \(D^*F(0,0)(y^*)=\{T^*y^*\}\) for every \(y^*\in H\). Since \(T^*=T\) is injective, \(\{y^*\in H:0\in D^*F(0,0)(y^*)\}=\{0\}\), so the pointwise coderivative kernel condition holds. Nevertheless, \(T(H)\) is dense and nonclosed in \(H\), and \(T\) is not surjective. Consequently, \(F\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\). Thus this finite-dimensional pointwise coderivative implication does not transfer without additional infinite-dimensional hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct quantitative replacement for pointwise adjoint injectivity for bounded linear operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), the following are equivalent: \(T\) is metrically regular; \(T\) is surjective; and there exists \(c>0\) such that \[\|T^*y^*\|\ge c\|y^*\|\quad(y^*\in Y^*).\] At every graph point, \[\operatorname{reg}T=\left(\inf_{\|y^*\|=1}\|T^*y^*\|\right)^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear metric regularity requires a uniform positive adjoint lower bound, not merely a trivial adjoint kernel.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation Lower Bound for the Radius of Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of the metric-regularity radius under a single-valued Lipschitz perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(g:X\to Y\). Suppose \(X\) is Asplund, \(\dim Y<\infty\), \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and \(F^{-1}\) is coderivatively normal at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). If \(\operatorname{lip}g(\bar x)<\operatorname{rad}F(\bar x,\bar y)\), then \[\operatorname{rad}(F+g)(\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\ge \operatorname{rad}F(\bar x,\bar y)-\operatorname{lip}g(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an Asplund-domain mapping with finite-dimensional range, a locally closed graph, and coderivative normality of its inverse, a Lipschitz perturbation whose local Lipschitz modulus is smaller than the original metric-regularity radius decreases that radius by at most the perturbation modulus.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance of the Metric-Regularity Radius under First-Order Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of metric-regularity radii for a mapping and its first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) satisfy: \(X\) is Asplund, \(\dim Y<\infty\), \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and \(F^{-1}\) is coderivatively normal at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). If \(G:X\rightrightarrows Y\) furnishes a first-order approximation to \(F\) around \((\bar x,\bar y)\), then \[\operatorname{rad}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\operatorname{rad}G(\bar x,\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated Asplund-space, finite-dimensional-range, local closedness, and coderivative-normality assumptions, a first-order approximation of a set-valued mapping at the reference graph point has the same radius of metric regularity as the original mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower bound for perturbations destroying metric regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary Lipschitz-modulus threshold for loss of metric regularity under additive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F:X\rightrightarrows Y$ have locally closed graph around $(\bar x,\bar y)$, and let $g:X\to Y$ be Lipschitz continuous around $\bar x$. If $F+g$ is not metrically regular around $(\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))$, then
\[\operatorname{lip}g(\bar x)\geq\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x,\bar y)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every locally Lipschitz additive perturbation that destroys metric regularity must have local Lipschitz modulus at least the reciprocal of the original exact regularity bound.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is locally closed around }(\bar x,\bar y)
g:X\to Y\text{ is Lipschitz continuous around }\bar x
F+g\text{ is not metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lip}g(\bar x)\geq 1/\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x,\bar y).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(H_s\) with \(\|x\|_s^2=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{2s}|x_n|^2\). Then \(\|Ax\|_{s-1}=\|x\|_s\), so \(A:H_s\to H_{s-1}\) is an isometric isomorphism. By contrast, for \(u^{(n)}=n^{-s}e_n\), one has \(\|u^{(n)}\|_s=1\) and \(\|Au^{(n)}\|_s=n\). Hence \(A
otin\mathcal L(H_s,H_s)\). A generalized equation whose derivative contains \(A\) therefore possesses a bounded derivative only after lowering the codomain regularity by one level; same-scale derivative criteria are inapplicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagonal first-order operator is bounded only after lowering the codomain by one regularity level; on a fixed level its norm is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by measuring perturbations in a scale incompatible with the derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: As a mapping \(A:H_s\to H_{s-1}\), the operator is bijective and satisfies \(\|x-A^{-1}y\|_s=\|Ax-y\|_{s-1}\); hence its inverse has Lipschitz modulus one in the compatible scale. However, \(A(H_s)\not\subset H_s\), and the sequence \(u^{(n)}=n^{-s}e_n\) satisfies \(\|u^{(n)}\|_s=1\) while \(\|Au^{(n)}\|_s=n\). Thus neither the same-scale residual nor a same-scale derivative bound is generally available. Regularity established in \(H_s\to H_{s-1}\) cannot be transferred by merely replacing the residual norm with \(\|\cdot\|_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The equation is perfectly regular between adjacent scale levels, but its residual and derivative are not controlled when both variables use the stronger level.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Scale Mismatch

children.title: Cross-Scale Inverse Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure of inverse mechanisms when domain, range, or derivative estimates occupy incompatible scales.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inverse \(J^{-1}:J(H_s)\to H_s\) is unbounded, so \(J\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Canonical embedding from the stronger to the weaker scale level.
Weighted Hilbert space at scale level s.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Injectivity across scale levels does not ensure a bounded inverse in the stronger norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The embedding \(J\) is bounded and injective, but its range is dense and nonclosed in \(H_{s-1}\). For \(u^{(n)}=n^{-s}e_n\), one has \(\|u^{(n)}\|_s=1\) and \(\|Ju^{(n)}\|_{s-1}=n^{-1}\). If a locally Lipschitz inverse estimate \(\|x\|_s\le\kappa\|Jx\|_{s-1}\) held near zero, positive scalar multiples of \(u^{(n)}\) would imply \(1\le\kappa/n\) for every \(n\), a contradiction. Thus cross-scale injectivity does not provide metric regularity or a Lipschitz inverse into the stronger space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical embedding is bounded and injective, yet high-frequency vectors make its inverse unbounded and destroy metric regularity across scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Scale Inverse Failure
